docs.title: Actor Spring Boot Starter
docs.text:
The actor model for Spring Boot, on Apache Pekko (the open-source fork of Akka).

Actors are Spring beans. You spawn them, send them messages, and scale them across a cluster, and the API you compile against has no Pekko types.

docs.title: Why actors in a Spring application
docs.text:
Most Spring services are stateless: every request reads its state from a database. Some problems are stateful by nature, and an actor fits them better:

  • A chat room or a game session that many users talk to at once
  • A user session, a cart or a device that receives a stream of events
  • A workflow or a long-running AI agent that waits for timers, tools, model replies and approvals

An actor owns its state and handles one message at a time, so you write plain code with no locks. A failed actor is restarted by its supervisor. Sharding spreads thousands of actors over a cluster, and event sourcing brings an actor's state back after a restart.

docs.text: Area What's included Start here Core Actors as beans, tell and ask, supervision, timers, routers, pub/sub topics, receptionist, dispatchers, logging with actor context Actors Cluster Sharding, singletons, replicated data, split brain resolver and leases; join through seed nodes, Kubernetes, a database or Redis Sharded actors Data Actor state in your database, event-sourced actors, projections into Spring Data or Kafka State in a database Streaming Reactor Mono/Flux, SSE, WebSocket and gRPC Reactor streams Operations Graceful shutdown, Actuator health, metrics, tracing, dashboards, rolling/canary/blue-green deployments Running in production Kotlin suspend ask and spawn, reified helpers Kotlin Testing @ActorTest slice, multi-node cluster helpers Testing AI agents Agents as sharded actors with tools, streaming and approvals AI agents

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
Start with actor-spring-boot-starter, and add the others when you need them. All are published as io.github.seonwkim:<module>:1.0.0 and need Java 21+ and Spring Boot 3.5+.

Module What it adds actor-spring-boot-starter The actor system, actors as beans, messaging, routers, topics, receptionist actor-spring-boot-starter-cluster Cluster mode: sharding, singletons, replicated data, split brain resolver (use it instead of the starter above) actor-jdbc Cluster join and leases through your DataSource actor-redis Cluster join and leases through Redis actor-persistence Event-sourced actors, with journal and snapshots on your DataSource actor-projection Projections of persisted events into Spring Data or Kafka actor-streams Reactor bridges, and SSE, WebSocket and gRPC streaming actor-metrics Micrometer meters for actors, mailboxes, dispatchers, cluster and sharding actor-kotlin Kotlin coroutines and reified helpers actor-test @ActorTest, cluster test helpers and store contract tests (test scope)

Using several? Import actor-bom to set the version once (see Getting started).

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This page takes you from an empty Spring Boot application to an actor that answers HTTP requests.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Java 21 or higher
  • Spring Boot 3.5 or higher

Spring Boot 2 users stay on the 0.x line (spring-boot-starter-actor). See Migrating from 0.x.

docs.title: 1. Add the dependency
Several modules: import the BOM
docs.text:
From 1.1.0, io.github.seonwkim:actor-bom lists every module at one version. Import it and leave the version off each module. It manages only this project's modules; Spring Boot keeps managing Pekko's dependencies such as Jackson.

GradleMaven 
implementation platform('io.github.seonwkim:actor-bom:1.1.0')
implementation 'io.github.seonwkim:actor-spring-boot-starter'
implementation 'io.github.seonwkim:actor-metrics'
testImplementation 'io.github.seonwkim:actor-test'

<dependencyManagement>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>io.github.seonwkim</groupId>
      <artifactId>actor-bom</artifactId>
      <version>1.1.0</version>
      <type>pom</type>
      <scope>import</scope>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.seonwkim</groupId>
    <artifactId>actor-spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.seonwkim</groupId>
    <artifactId>actor-metrics</artifactId>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.seonwkim</groupId>
    <artifactId>actor-test</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>

Note

Spring Boot 3.5 manages Jackson 2.18+, which satisfies Pekko. No jackson-bom override is needed.

docs.title: 2. Start the application
docs.text:
The starter is a Spring Boot auto-configuration: with the dependency on the classpath, a @SpringBootApplication starts one actor system for the Spring context and stops it when the context closes. spring.actor.enabled=false keeps the starter on the classpath without starting one.

JavaKotlin 
@SpringBootApplication
public class MyApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(MyApplication.class, args);
    }
}

@SpringBootApplication
class MyApplication

fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    runApplication<MyApplication>(*args)
}

@EnableActorSupport is optional

Applications written for 1.0.0 have @EnableActorSupport on the application class. It still works and adds nothing in a Spring Boot application, so you can remove it. Keep it only where auto-configuration is off, such as a context built without @EnableAutoConfiguration.

docs.title: 3. Write an actor
docs.text:
An actor is a Spring bean that implements SpringActor<Command>. Command is the type of message it accepts. A message that expects an answer extends AskCommand<Reply> and answers with reply(...).

JavaKotlin 
@Component
public class GreeterActor implements SpringActor<GreeterActor.Command> {

    public interface Command {}

    public static class Greet extends AskCommand<String> implements Command {
        public final String name;

        public Greet(String name) {
            this.name = name;
        }
    }

    @Override
    public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
        return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                .onMessage(Greet.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                    msg.reply("Hello, " + msg.name + "!");
                    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                })
                .build();
    }
}

@Component
class GreeterActor : SpringActor<GreeterActor.Command> {

    sealed interface Command

    class Greet(val name: String) : AskCommand<String>(), Command

    override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
        behavior<Command>(actorContext) {
            onMessage<Greet> { msg ->
                msg.reply("Hello, ${msg.name}!")
                same()
            }
        }
}

The actor handles one message at a time, so state inside it needs no locks. Because it's a bean, its constructor can take any other bean (a repository, a client).

docs.title: 4. Talk to it
docs.text:
Inject SpringActorSystem. getOrSpawn returns the running actor with that id, or starts it. ask sends a message and waits for the reply, up to the timeout.

JavaKotlin 
@RestController
public class GreeterController {

    private final SpringActorSystem actorSystem;

    public GreeterController(SpringActorSystem actorSystem) {
        this.actorSystem = actorSystem;
    }

    @GetMapping("/greet")
    public CompletionStage<String> greet(@RequestParam String name) {
        return actorSystem.getOrSpawn(GreeterActor.class, "greeter")
                .thenCompose(greeter -> greeter.ask(new GreeterActor.Greet(name))
                        .withTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
                        .execute());
    }
}

@RestController
class GreeterController(private val actorSystem: SpringActorSystem) {

    @GetMapping("/greet")
    suspend fun greet(@RequestParam name: String): String =
        actorSystem.awaitGetOrSpawn<GreeterActor, _>("greeter")
            .awaitAsk(GreeterActor.Greet(name), timeout = 5.seconds)
}

In Kotlin, awaitGetOrSpawn and awaitAsk suspend instead of returning a CompletionStage. A suspend controller method needs Spring WebFlux, or Spring MVC with kotlinx-coroutines-reactor on the classpath.

Run the application and call it:

curl 'http://localhost:8080/greet?name=Ada'
# Hello, Ada!

docs.title: 5. Configure (optional)
docs.text:
Nothing is required. Every key lives under spring.actor:

spring:
  actor:
    name: orders        # actor system name, shown in logs and node addresses
    provider: local     # local (default) or cluster

The configuration reference lists every key.

docs.title: Migrating from 0.x
docs.text: 1.0 renames the artifacts and packages, requires Java 21+ and Spring Boot 3.5+, and removes Pekko types from the public API. Spring Boot 2 users stay on the 0.x line.

docs.title: New coordinates
Step by step
docs.text:
1. Upgrade to Java 21 and Spring Boot 3.5 or later. Boot 2 applications stay on 0.x.
  2. Remove the com.fasterxml.jackson:jackson-bom override from your build.
  3. Depend on io.github.seonwkim:actor-spring-boot-starter (and actor-metrics if you use metrics). If you run with pekko.actor.provider=cluster (sharding, singletons, cluster events, management), depend on actor-spring-boot-starter-cluster instead; without it the application fails at startup and says so. If your code uses Pekko Cluster classes directly, declare org.apache.pekko:pekko-cluster-sharding-typed_3 yourself, and code that uses any Pekko class (through unwrap(...) or SpringActorBehavior.wrap(...)) declares org.apache.pekko:pekko-actor-typed_3: the starters no longer export Pekko.
  4. Replace io.github.seonwkim.core with io.github.seonwkim.actor and io.github.seonwkim.metrics with io.github.seonwkim.actor.metrics in your imports. If you extended RootGuardian or used other classes now under internal, import them from io.github.seonwkim.actor.internal.
  5. Behaviors: handlers return SpringActorBehavior, not Pekko's Behavior.
  6. Behaviors.same(), Behaviors.stopped(), Behaviors.unhandled() → SpringActorBehavior.same(), .stopped(), .unhandled(). Keep a raw Pekko behavior with SpringActorBehavior.wrap(behavior).
  7. onSignal(PreRestart.class, ...) and onSignal(PostStop.class, ...) take io.github.seonwkim.actor.PreRestart and io.github.seonwkim.actor.PostStop.
  8. SupervisorStrategy.restart() / .resume() / .stop() → SupervisionStrategy.restart() / .resume() / .stop(), with restart().withLimit(maxRetries, within) as before. withSupervisionStrategy takes the new type.
  9. MailboxConfig, DispatcherConfig and TagsConfig keep their factory methods (MailboxConfig.bounded(n), DispatcherConfig.blocking(), TagsConfig.of(...), ...). They are now sealed records and enums, so their Pekko conversions (toMailboxSelector(), toProps(), applyToProps(...)) and describe() are gone; TagsConfig.getTags() → tags().
  10. Refs and handles: getUnderlying() → unwrap(ActorRef.class), getPath() → path(), SpringActorSystem.getRaw() → unwrap(ActorSystem.class), a behavior context's getUnderlying() → unwrap(ActorContext.class). AskCommand.replyTo is a SpringActorRef. Messages that carry a reply address declare a SpringActorRef<T> field; it serializes across the cluster. SpringActorRefBuilder is removed: use ask(...) on the handle.
  11. SpringActorSystem, SpringActorSpawnBuilder, SpringChildActorBuilder and SpringChildActorReference are interfaces. Code that constructed them must get them from the actor system instead. ActorSpawner and ActorTypeRegistry moved to internal.
  12. Cluster: getCluster(), getClusterSharding() and getClusterSingleton() are removed. Use isClusterMode(), or unwrap(Cluster.class) (and the other Pekko classes) for raw access.
  13. Cluster events: ClusterEventBehavior.ClusterDomainWrappedEvent is removed. Listen for io.github.seonwkim.actor.cluster.ClusterEvent or one of its records (@EventListener void on(ClusterEvent.MemberUp event)). Member addresses are strings and statuses are the MemberStatus enum.
  14. Sharded actors:
    • EntityTypeKey<T> typeKey() → ShardedEntityType<T> entityType(), built with ShardedEntityType.of(Command.class, "name"). Keep the same name so running clusters route to the same entities.
    • create(...) returns SpringActorBehavior<T> built with SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, ctx); SpringShardedActorBehavior is removed. Sharded entities get supervision, signals and MDC like local actors.
    • extractor() → sharding(), returning ShardingStrategy.hashed(numberOfShards). The shard ids are the same as DefaultShardingMessageExtractor produced.
    • SpringShardedActorContext.getEntityContext() is removed; getEntityId() stays.
    • SpringShardedActorHandle is an interface; getUnderlying() → unwrap(EntityRef.class). Set the ask timeout with sharded(...).withId(id).withTimeout(d).get(); SpringShardedActorHandle.builder(...) is removed.
  15. Topics: topicManager.topic(Message.class).withName("news") → topicManager.topic(TopicName.of(Message.class, "news")); withTimeout, create() and getOrCreate() are unchanged. SpringTopicManager and SpringTopicRef are interfaces you get as beans. SpringTopicRef.getTopicName() → name().name(), getUnderlying() → unwrap(ActorRef.class).
  16. Receptionist: ServiceKey<T> → ServiceName<T>, and SpringReceptionist.serviceKey(Message.class, "id") → ServiceName.of(Message.class, "id"). register and deregister take any SpringActorRef, so the ActorRef overload is removed: pass the actor's handle or ctx.self(). In a behavior, ctx.registerWithReceptionist(ServiceName.of(...)). SpringReceptionist is an interface you get as a bean; SpringReceptionistSubscription.getServiceKey() → serviceName(), and getHelperPath() is removed.
  17. Routers: RoutingStrategy.roundRobin(), .random(), .broadcast() and .consistentHashing(n) are unchanged. The router.strategy classes (RoundRobinRoutingStrategy, ...) are removed, and RoutingStrategy is a sealed type: getName() and applyToPool(...) are gone. Code that branched on getName() can switch on the type.

docs.title: After migrating
docs.text:
• Move raw spring.actor.pekko.* keys that have a typed equivalent to the typed keys (spring.actor.name, provider, remote.*, cluster.*). See the configuration reference.
  • New in 1.0 and worth a look: health checks and metrics, graceful shutdown, @ActorTest and the Kotlin API.

The full list of changes is in the changelog.

docs.title: Bugs, questions and proposals
docs.text:
Use GitHub Issues for all of them:

  • Bug: what you did, what you expected, what happened, and the versions (starter, Spring Boot, Java). A small project or test that reproduces it helps most.
  • Feature or API change: the problem first (what you're trying to do and why the current API makes it hard), then the change you'd like. Discuss it in the issue before opening a large PR.
  • Question: Discussions or Discord work too.

Search existing issues first; add to one that already covers your case.

docs.title: Pull requests
docs.text:
1. Open or pick an issue, and say in it that you're working on it.
  2. Branch from main, and run ./gradlew spotlessApply build before pushing.
  3. Link the issue in the PR (Closes #123).

ARCHITECTURE.md explains the modules, and AGENTS.md the testing rules.

docs.title: More
docs.text: • Spring conventions: how the starter compares with other Spring projects

docs.title: Spring conventions: how this starter compares
docs.text:
This page compares the starter with the conventions Spring users already know from Spring Boot, Spring for Apache Kafka, Spring Data, Spring Cloud Stream, Micrometer, Resilience4j and Temporal. Each row says what we keep and what we change. Changes are proposed and tracked in GitHub Issues.

Snapshot

"This starter today" describes the 0.10.0 release (the last 0.x main), before the 1.0 refactor. The 1.0 changes are in the changelog. The core configuration is ActorConfiguration, which is imported by @EnableActorSupport. core-boot3 is generated from core sources by the syncAllBoot3Sources Gradle task, so anything said about core also holds for core-boot3.

docs.title: How to read a row
docs.text:
Every row has four parts:

  • Reference libraries: how the named libraries do it.
  • This starter today: what the code does now.
  • Verdict: one of
    • Keep: we already follow the convention, or we depart from it on purpose (the reason is given).
    • Change: we should follow the convention.
    • Tracked: the gap is already tracked by an open issue. The row links the issue.
  • Source: a link to the official documentation of the reference.

Rows 1 to 17 cover the eight topics of issue #105. Rows 18 to 24 are other conventions found in the same libraries that apply to this starter; each names the library it comes from.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Issue links are in each row below.

Row Convention Verdict 1 Auto-configuration registration (Boot 2 and 3) Change, done (#184) 2 @Enable* annotations Change, done (#184) 3 @ConditionalOn* back-off Change 4 *Customizer beans Change 5 @ConfigurationProperties and metadata Tracked (#97) 6 Property namespace Keep 7 SmartLifecycle phases and graceful shutdown Tracked (#99) 8 Micrometer meters Keep 9 Micrometer Observation Change 10 Actuator health indicator Tracked (#100) 11 Actuator endpoint Change 12 Test artifact Change 13 Test slice Change 14 BOM Change 15 Native image hints Change 16 Starter and auto-configure module split Keep 17 Optional dependencies Keep 18 Global on/off switch (Spring Boot, Spring Cloud, Spring for Apache Kafka) Change 19 Registries scoped to the application context (Spring for Apache Kafka) Change 20 Starter artifact naming (Spring Boot) Change 21 FailureAnalyzer for startup errors (Spring Boot) Change 22 Components discovered as beans (Spring for Apache Kafka, Spring Cloud Stream, Temporal) Keep 23 Framework events as ApplicationEvent (Spring for Apache Kafka) Keep 24 Configuration ordering with @AutoConfiguration(after = ...) (Spring Boot) Keep

docs.title: Row 1: Auto-configuration registration (Boot 2 and 3)
docs.text:
• Reference libraries: A Spring Boot starter registers its configuration classes so that adding the dependency is enough. Boot 2.0 to 2.6 read org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.EnableAutoConfiguration keys in META-INF/spring.factories. Boot 2.7 added META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports and the @AutoConfiguration annotation (which also sets proxyBeanMethods = false). Boot 3.0 reads only the .imports file. Spring for Apache Kafka, Spring Data, Resilience4j and Temporal all ship their Boot integration this way: the Kafka and Spring Data auto-configurations live in Spring Boot itself, resilience4j-spring-boot2/-3 and temporal-spring-boot-autoconfigure list theirs in these files.
  • This starter today: core has no src/main/resources at all, so it has neither file. Nothing starts until the app adds @EnableActorSupport. ActorConfiguration and PekkoManagementAutoConfiguration are plain @Configuration classes. The metrics module has a spring.factories entry only, so Boot 3 never loads ActorMetricsAutoConfiguration on its own. The core tests pass without @EnableActorSupport only because the test application sits in the io.github.seonwkim.actor package, and component scanning picks ActorConfiguration up.
  • Verdict: Change. Done in #184: every actor configuration is an @AutoConfiguration listed in actor-autoconfigure's AutoConfiguration.imports, ordered with @AutoConfiguration(after = ...).
  • Source: Spring Boot: Creating your own auto-configuration, Spring Boot 2.7 release notes, Spring Boot 3.0 migration guide.

docs.title: Row 2: @Enable* annotations
docs.text:
• Reference libraries: In a Boot app the @Enable* annotation is optional, because the auto-configuration applies it for you. Boot's Kafka auto-configuration adds @EnableKafka when the app has not, so @KafkaListener works with the dependency alone. Boot enables Spring Data repositories for you; @EnableJpaRepositories is needed only to change the scanned packages or the defaults. Outside Boot (plain Spring Framework), the annotation remains the switch.
  • This starter today: @EnableActorSupport is required. It is the only way to import ActorConfiguration and PekkoManagementAutoConfiguration.
  • Verdict: Change. The annotation stays and is not deprecated; it becomes optional in a Boot app. Done in #184: it is an @ImportAutoConfiguration of the same list, so it adds nothing next to @EnableAutoConfiguration and still starts the actor system where auto-configuration is off.
  • Source: Spring for Apache Kafka: @KafkaListener annotation, Spring Boot: Apache Kafka support, Spring Data JPA: Creating repository instances.

docs.title: Row 3: @ConditionalOn* back-off
docs.text:
• Reference libraries: Every bean an auto-configuration defines backs off when the user defines one (@ConditionalOnMissingBean). Each class that touches an optional library is guarded with @ConditionalOnClass, so it never loads when the library is absent. Boot's Kafka auto-configuration backs off on KafkaTemplate, ProducerFactory, ConsumerFactory and the listener container factory. Boot also asks that BeanPostProcessor @Bean methods be static, so the configuration class is not created early.
  • This starter today: actorProperties, rootGuardianSupplierWrapper, actorSystemBuilder, actorSystem and topicManager back off. actorRegistrationBeanPostProcessor and clusterShardingInitializer do not, and the post-processor method is not static. PekkoManagementAutoConfiguration is the only class with @ConditionalOnClass.
  • Verdict: Change.
  • Source: Spring Boot: Condition annotations, Spring Framework: BeanPostProcessor @Bean methods.

docs.title: Row 4: *Customizer beans
docs.text:
• Reference libraries: Boot lets an app tweak a bean it builds without replacing it: the app declares one or more *Customizer beans, and the auto-configuration applies them in @Order order through an ObjectProvider. Examples: RestTemplateCustomizer and Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer (Spring Boot); DefaultKafkaProducerFactoryCustomizer and DefaultKafkaConsumerFactoryCustomizer (Boot's Kafka support); CircuitBreakerConfigCustomizer (Resilience4j); TemporalOptionsCustomizer and WorkerFactoryOptionsCustomizer (Temporal); MeterRegistryCustomizer (Micrometer in Boot).
  • This starter today: There is no customizer type. To change one thing (for example a Pekko setting computed at startup, or an extra root guardian behaviour) the app replaces the whole SpringActorSystemBuilder or RootGuardianSupplierWrapper bean.
  • Verdict: Change.
  • Source: Spring Boot: Apache Kafka support, Resilience4j: Spring Boot 2 getting started, Temporal: Spring Boot integration, Spring Boot: Metrics customization.

docs.title: Row 5: @ConfigurationProperties and metadata
docs.text:
• Reference libraries: Properties bind to a typed @ConfigurationProperties class (KafkaProperties, DataSourceProperties, TemporalProperties, Resilience4j's CircuitBreakerProperties). The spring-boot-configuration-processor generates META-INF/spring-configuration-metadata.json, so IDEs complete and document the keys, and deprecated keys are marked.
  • This starter today: ActorProperties is a plain class that binds spring.actor.* into a Map<String, Object> with the Binder. There is no metadata file.
  • Verdict: Tracked: #97. Not re-specified here.
  • Source: Spring Boot: Type-safe configuration properties, Spring Boot: Configuration metadata.

docs.title: Row 6: Property namespace
docs.text:
• Reference libraries: Spring Boot asks third-party starters to keep their keys in their own namespace and not to use spring, server or management. Resilience4j uses resilience4j.*. Temporal's own starter uses spring.temporal.*, and Spring-team projects (Kafka, Cloud Stream) use spring.kafka.* and spring.cloud.stream.*.
  • This starter today: All keys live under spring.actor.*, and spring.actor.pekko.* maps to the Pekko configuration.
  • Verdict: Keep. Moving every key breaks every user's configuration, and Temporal shows that a spring.* prefix is accepted in practice. If the typed properties work in #97 wants to revisit the prefix, it should do so there, with deprecation metadata for the old keys.
  • Source: Spring Boot: Creating your own starter, configuration keys, Temporal: Spring Boot integration.

docs.title: Row 7: SmartLifecycle phases and graceful shutdown
docs.text:
• Reference libraries: Components that run work start and stop in a SmartLifecycle phase, not in a constructor or destroy(). Spring for Apache Kafka's listener containers are SmartLifecycle beans with autoStartup and a phase, and stop before the beans they use are destroyed. Boot's web server graceful shutdown runs in its own phase with a bounded timeout (spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase).
  • This starter today: The Pekko actor system starts when the actorSystem bean is built. SpringActorSystem implements DisposableBean, and destroy() calls terminate() and then waits on getWhenTerminated() with no timeout.
  • Verdict: Tracked: #99. Not re-specified here.
  • Source: Spring Framework: Startup and shutdown callbacks, Spring for Apache Kafka: Message listener containers, Spring Boot: Graceful shutdown.

docs.title: Row 8: Micrometer meters
docs.text:
• Reference libraries: Libraries register meters on the app's MeterRegistry bean, backed off with @ConditionalOnClass(MeterRegistry.class) and @ConditionalOnBean(MeterRegistry.class). Spring for Apache Kafka binds client meters through MicrometerConsumerListener; Resilience4j ships resilience4j-micrometer.
  • This starter today: The separate metrics module (an instrumentation agent) registers actor meters on the MeterRegistry through ActorMetricsAutoConfiguration, guarded with @ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnBean, @ConditionalOnMissingBean and spring.actor.metrics.enabled.
  • Verdict: Keep. Its missing Boot 3 registration file is part of row 1; this change does not touch the metrics module.
  • Source: Spring Boot: Metrics, Spring for Apache Kafka: Monitoring.

docs.title: Row 9: Micrometer Observation
docs.text:
• Reference libraries: Since Micrometer 1.10 and Boot 3, libraries instrument a unit of work once with the Observation API, and Boot turns it into a timer and a trace span. Spring for Apache Kafka enables it with observationEnabled on the template and the container (Boot properties spring.kafka.template.observation-enabled, spring.kafka.listener.observation-enabled) and lets the app plug in its own ObservationConvention.
  • This starter today: tell and ask create actor.send and actor.receive Observations when an ObservationRegistry bean exists, and the trace crosses nodes. Actor spawn is not observed.
  • Verdict: Change.
  • Source: Micrometer: Observation API, Spring for Apache Kafka: Monitoring.

docs.title: Row 10: Actuator health indicator
docs.text:
• Reference libraries: A library with a remote dependency contributes a HealthIndicator (Spring Data's Redis, Mongo and Cassandra indicators; the Spring Cloud Stream binders indicator), enabled by management.health.<name>.enabled.
  • This starter today: No health indicator. Cluster membership is visible only through Pekko Management HTTP when it is on the classpath.
  • Verdict: Tracked: #100. Not re-specified here.
  • Source: Spring Boot: Actuator endpoints, health.

docs.title: Row 11: Actuator endpoint
docs.text:
• Reference libraries: Libraries with runtime state expose a read-only Actuator @Endpoint: Spring Cloud Stream's bindings and channels endpoints; Spring Integration's integrationgraph; Resilience4j's circuitbreakers and circuitbreakerevents.
  • This starter today: No endpoint. Actor and shard state is available only through Pekko APIs.
  • Verdict: Change.
  • Source: Spring Boot: Implementing custom endpoints, Spring Cloud Stream: Binding visualization and control, Resilience4j: Spring Boot 2 getting started.

docs.title: Row 12: Test artifact
docs.text:
• Reference libraries: Libraries publish a test artifact with a ready-made fixture: spring-kafka-test with @EmbeddedKafka and EmbeddedKafkaBroker; spring-cloud-stream-test-binder with InputDestination and OutputDestination; temporal-testing with TestWorkflowEnvironment, which Temporal's starter wires in when spring.temporal.test-server.enabled=true.
  • This starter today: No test artifact. Users wire Pekko's pekko-actor-testkit-typed by hand, and the core tests use ActorTypeRegistry.clear() to reset static state between contexts.
  • Verdict: Change.
  • Source: Spring for Apache Kafka: Testing applications, Spring Cloud Stream: Testing, Temporal: Spring Boot integration, Apache Pekko: Testing.

docs.title: Row 13: Test slice
docs.text:
• Reference libraries: Boot test slices load one layer of the app and only the auto-configuration it needs: @DataJpaTest (Spring Data), @JsonTest, @WebMvcTest. A library can ship its own slice with @ImportAutoConfiguration and a META-INF/spring/<annotation>.imports file.
  • This starter today: No slice. A test that needs actors uses @SpringBootTest and loads the whole application.
  • Verdict: Change.
  • Source: Spring Boot: Testing Spring Boot applications, auto-configured tests.

docs.title: Row 14: BOM
docs.text:
• Reference libraries: A project with more than one artifact publishes a bill of materials so users pick one version: spring-cloud-dependencies (Spring Cloud Stream), micrometer-bom, resilience4j-bom, temporal-bom, spring-boot-dependencies; Pekko itself ships pekko-bom_<scala>.
  • This starter today: Three published artifacts (spring-boot-starter-actor, spring-boot-starter-actor_3, spring-boot-starter-actor-metrics) and no BOM. Users repeat the version on each.
  • Verdict: Change.
  • Source: Spring Boot: Dependency management, Micrometer: Installing.

docs.title: Row 15: Native image hints
docs.text:
• Reference libraries: Boot 3 libraries that use reflection, resources or proxies register a RuntimeHintsRegistrar in META-INF/spring/aot.factories, so GraalVM native images work. Spring for Apache Kafka ships KafkaRuntimeHints.
  • This starter today: No hints. Pekko loads reference.conf resources and creates extensions, serializers and actor classes by reflection, so a native image cannot start the actor system.
  • Verdict: Change.
  • Source: Spring Framework: Ahead of time optimizations, runtime hints, Spring Boot: GraalVM native images.

docs.title: Row 16: Starter and auto-configure module split
docs.text:
• Reference libraries: Spring Boot describes a starter as two modules, an -autoconfigure module with the code and an empty -starter module with the dependencies, and allows one combined module when there is no need to separate them. Temporal ships both (temporal-spring-boot-autoconfigure and temporal-spring-boot-starter).
  • This starter today: One combined module per Boot line (core, core-boot3).
  • Verdict: Keep. Boot allows a combined module, and the starter has no optional feature large enough to need a separate auto-configure jar.
  • Source: Spring Boot: Creating your own starter.

docs.title: Row 17: Optional dependencies
docs.text:
• Reference libraries: Spring Boot asks auto-configure modules to declare the libraries they configure as optional, so the app chooses them, and to guard the code that uses them with @ConditionalOnClass.
  • This starter today: Pekko Management and Cluster Bootstrap are compileOnly, and PekkoManagementAutoConfiguration is guarded by @ConditionalOnClass on their class names. The metrics module declares Spring Boot compileOnly.
  • Verdict: Keep. The remaining guard gaps are in row 3.
  • Source: Spring Boot: Creating your own starter.

docs.title: Row 18: Global on/off switch
docs.text:
Source libraries: Spring Boot, Spring Cloud, Spring for Apache Kafka.

  • Reference libraries: A starter that starts something can be turned off with one property, without removing the dependency: spring.cloud.discovery.enabled and spring.cloud.config.enabled (Spring Cloud), spring.jmx.enabled (Spring Boot), spring.kafka.listener.auto-startup (Boot's Kafka support).
  • This starter today: spring.actor.pekko.management.enabled turns off Pekko Management and spring.actor.metrics.enabled turns off metrics, but there is no switch for the actor system itself.
  • Verdict: Change.
  • Source: Spring Boot: Condition annotations, property conditions, Spring Cloud Commons.

docs.title: Row 19: Registries scoped to the application context
docs.text:
Source library: Spring for Apache Kafka.

  • Reference libraries: Spring for Apache Kafka keeps its listener endpoints in a KafkaListenerEndpointRegistry bean, one per application context. The Spring TestContext framework caches and reuses contexts, so several contexts can live in one JVM at once, and state kept in static fields leaks between them.
  • This starter today: ActorTypeRegistry and ShardedActorRegistry keep actor factories in static maps. Tests call ActorTypeRegistry.clear() to isolate contexts.
  • Verdict: Change.
  • Source: Spring for Apache Kafka: @KafkaListener lifecycle management, Spring Framework: Context caching.

docs.title: Row 20: Starter artifact naming
docs.text:
Source library: Spring Boot.

  • Reference libraries: Spring Boot reserves the spring-boot prefix for its own modules and asks third-party starters to put the project name first: acme-spring-boot-starter. Temporal follows it (temporal-spring-boot-starter), as does Resilience4j (resilience4j-spring-boot3).
  • This starter today: The artifacts are spring-boot-starter-actor, spring-boot-starter-actor_3 and spring-boot-starter-actor-metrics, under the io.github.seonwkim group.
  • Verdict: Change. The 1.0 release renamed them to actor-spring-boot-starter and friends.
  • Source: Spring Boot: Creating your own starter, naming.

docs.title: Row 21: FailureAnalyzer for startup errors
docs.text:
Source library: Spring Boot.

  • Reference libraries: Boot turns well-known startup failures into a short "Description / Action" report with a FailureAnalyzer registered in spring.factories (for example "Port 8080 was already in use", or a missing bean).
  • This starter today: A Pekko startup failure (remoting port already bound, a bad spring.actor.pekko.* value, a missing seed node) reaches the user as a nested stack trace from the actorSystem bean.
  • Verdict: Change.
  • Source: Spring Boot: Create your own FailureAnalyzer.

docs.title: Row 22: Components discovered as beans
docs.text:
Source libraries: Spring for Apache Kafka, Spring Cloud Stream, Temporal.

  • Reference libraries: The user's handlers are ordinary beans the library finds in the context: @KafkaListener methods, Function/Consumer beans in Spring Cloud Stream, and workflow and activity beans found by Temporal's spring.temporal.workers-auto-discovery.packages.
  • This starter today: Actors are @Component beans implementing SpringActor or SpringShardedActor, found by a BeanPostProcessor. They get dependency injection like any bean.
  • Verdict: Keep.
  • Source: Spring for Apache Kafka: @KafkaListener annotation, Spring Cloud Stream: Functional binding names, Temporal: Spring Boot integration.

docs.title: Row 23: Framework events as ApplicationEvent
docs.text:
Source library: Spring for Apache Kafka.

  • Reference libraries: Spring for Apache Kafka publishes container state changes as Spring application events (ListenerContainerIdleEvent, ConsumerStartedEvent, ConsumerStoppedEvent), so the app reacts with @EventListener.
  • This starter today: In cluster mode, SpringActorSystem publishes Pekko cluster events through the ApplicationEventPublisher.
  • Verdict: Keep.
  • Source: Spring for Apache Kafka: Application events.

docs.title: Row 24: Configuration ordering
docs.text:
Source library: Spring Boot.

  • Reference libraries: An auto-configuration that depends on another declares it with @AutoConfiguration(after = ...) or @AutoConfigureAfter, never by relying on class names or scan order.
  • This starter today: ActorMetricsAutoConfiguration declares @AutoConfigureAfter(CompositeMeterRegistryAutoConfiguration.class). The core classes have no ordering yet because they are not auto-configurations; row 1 adds the ordering they need.
  • Verdict: Keep. The core ordering is part of row 1.
  • Source: Spring Boot: Locating auto-configuration candidates.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The repository's example/ directory holds runnable Spring Boot apps. Each one is a Gradle subproject that uses the library's modules from source, so you can run it from a clone with one command:

git clone https://github.com/seonWKim/actor-spring-boot-starter.git
cd actor-spring-boot-starter
./gradlew :example:simple:bootRun

Cluster examples start several nodes with sh cluster-start.sh <example> <main class> 8080 2551 3 from the repository root and stop them with sh cluster-stop.sh. Each page gives the exact commands.

docs.title: All examples
docs.text: Example What it shows Runs Modules Simple One actor behind REST: spawn, ask, restart, stop Local actor-spring-boot-starter Kotlin The simple example in Kotlin with suspend functions Local actor-spring-boot-starter, actor-kotlin Cluster Sharded actors and a cluster singleton on three nodes Cluster (3 nodes) actor-spring-boot-starter-cluster Synchronization A counter under load: DB lock vs Redis lock vs sharded actor Cluster (3 nodes) + MySQL, Redis actor-spring-boot-starter-cluster Chat WebSocket chat: actor per connection, sharded rooms, pub/sub topics Cluster (3 nodes), Docker Compose actor-spring-boot-starter-cluster, actor-streams, actor-metrics Metrics Actor meters in Prometheus through Actuator Local actor-spring-boot-starter, actor-metrics Logging Static and per-message MDC, tags, request ids, JSON logs Local actor-spring-boot-starter Virtual threads Dispatchers on Java 21 virtual threads Local actor-spring-boot-starter Persistence Order state in JPA: current state, events, snapshots Local + H2 actor-spring-boot-starter Agent LLM agents: sharded agents, rate limit, human approval, recovery Cluster (1 node) actor-spring-boot-starter-cluster Kubernetes The chat app on Kubernetes: discovery, rollouts, monitoring Kubernetes (kind) the chat app's image

docs.title: Suggested learning path
docs.text:
1. Simple (or Kotlin): the basics of defining, spawning and asking an actor, and what supervision does.
  2. Logging and Virtual threads: settings you will want in any app, MDC and dispatchers.
  3. Persistence: keep actor state across restarts with a database.
  4. Cluster: the step to several nodes, with sharded actors and a singleton.
  5. Synchronization: why one actor per key replaces a lock.
  6. Chat: a full app with WebSockets and pub/sub on a cluster.
  7. Metrics and Kubernetes: run it in production.
  8. Agent: a larger design that combines most of the above.

docs.title: Agent Example
docs.text:
LLM agents as actors. Each agent is a sharded actor that keeps its conversation, calls a model and tools without blocking, waits for a human before risky tools, shares a per-node rate limit, and reloads its conversation after a crash or a restart of the whole app.

The model is a scripted fake, so the example runs without an API key or network.

  • Source: example/agent
  • Runs: a one-node cluster (spring.actor.cluster.join-self: true); no HTTP server
  • Modules: actor-spring-boot-starter-cluster, Jackson; no LLM SDK

The AI agents guide explains the design step by step with this example's code. This page is the short tour.

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
• One sharded actor per agent id (AgentActor), reachable from any node
  • pipeToSelf to turn an LLM call's future into a message, so the actor never waits
  • A message adapter (ctx.messageAdapter) so a node-local rate limiter can reply with a message
  • A human approval step: an ask with a timeout to an approval actor, and timers that expire requests
  • Restart supervision that reloads state from a snapshot file
  • Plain node-local actors (RateLimiterActor, ApprovalActor) spawned once per node with spawnAndWait

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
./gradlew :example:agent:bootRun

On start, DemoRunner asks the agent demo-agent "What is the weather in Seoul?" and logs the answer and the whole conversation (user message, tool call, tool result, final answer). Set agent.demo: false to skip it.

The tests drive every feature and are the best way to explore:

./gradlew :example:agent:test
Test What it checks AgentConversationTest A turn with a tool call, and a turn without one ConcurrentAgentsTest 100 agents in parallel each keep their own conversation SlowLlmTest The agent answers GetConversation while an LLM call is pending RateLimiterTest No more than the limit of permits in any one-second window HumanApprovalTest Approved, rejected and unanswered (timed out) tool calls SupervisionTest A crashed agent restarts with its conversation ActorSystemRestartTest The conversation survives a restart of the whole actor system

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
spring:
  actor:
    name: agent-example
    provider: cluster
    remote:
      hostname: 127.0.0.1
      port: 2551
    cluster:
      join-self: true   # a one-node cluster; list seed-nodes instead for more nodes

agent:
  calls-per-second: 20   # LLM calls one node may start per second, across all its agents
  approval-timeout: 30s  # how long an agent waits for a human
  max-tool-steps: 5      # tool calls per turn before the agent gives up
  fake-llm-latency: 200ms
  demo: true

agent.snapshot-dir (default: <java.io.tmpdir>/agent-snapshots) is where each agent's conversation is saved as one JSON file. The agent.* keys are the example's own AgentProperties, not starter properties.

docs.title: Walkthrough
docs.text: Class Role AgentActor The sharded entity: commands Chat (ask, replies AgentAnswer), GetConversation, SimulateCrash AgentBrain The agent loop and its state, run under a restart supervisor AgentService Talks to agents by id AgentRuntime Spawns the node-local rate limiter and approval actors RateLimiterActor Sliding-window permits for LLM calls, per node ApprovalActor, ApprovalService Pending tool calls, and the human side that lists and decides them FakeLlmClient The scripted model behind the LlmClient interface WeatherTool, RefundTool Two tools; refund requires approval FileAgentSnapshotStore One JSON file per agent, replaced atomically

docs.title: Talking to an agent
docs.text:
/** Talks to agents by id. The agent may live on any node of the cluster. */
@Service
public class AgentService {

    private final SpringActorSystem actorSystem;

    public AgentService(SpringActorSystem actorSystem) {
        this.actorSystem = actorSystem;
    }

    public CompletionStage<AgentAnswer> chat(String agentId, String text, Duration timeout) {
        return agent(agentId)
                .ask(new AgentActor.Chat(text))
                .withTimeout(timeout)
                .execute();
    }

    public CompletionStage<ConversationView> conversation(String agentId, Duration timeout) {
        return agent(agentId)
                .ask(new AgentActor.GetConversation())
                .withTimeout(timeout)
                .execute();
    }

    public void simulateCrash(String agentId) {
        agent(agentId).tell(new AgentActor.SimulateCrash());
    }

    private SpringShardedActorHandle<AgentActor.Command> agent(String agentId) {
        return actorSystem.sharded(AgentActor.class).withId(agentId).get();
    }
}

docs.title: The LLM call without blocking
docs.text:
The brain asks the rate limiter for a permit, then calls the model. pipeToSelf delivers the result as an LlmResponded message, so the actor keeps handling other messages while the model works:

ctx.pipeToSelf(deps.llm().complete(List.copyOf(conversation)), LlmResponded::new);

New Chat messages that arrive during a turn wait in a queue inside the state and start when the turn ends.

docs.title: Approval
docs.text:
A tool with requiresApproval() sends RequestApproval to the approval actor with an ask and the configured timeout. A human (here, a test) lists and decides through ApprovalService:

approvals.pending();                    // CompletionStage<List<PendingApproval>>
approvals.decide(requestId, true);      // completes with false if the request is unknown or expired

If no one answers in time, the tool does not run and the model gets "not run: no human answer within ...".

docs.title: Crash and restart
docs.text: AgentBrain is built with SupervisionStrategy.restart().withLimit(10, Duration.ofMinutes(1)). Every change to the conversation is saved before the agent moves on, and the state constructor loads the snapshot, so a restart (or a new actor system) continues the conversation.

docs.title: Things to keep in mind
docs.text:
• The rate limiter and the approval actor are per node. With N nodes, the cluster-wide limit is N times calls-per-second, and a human must decide on the node that holds the request.
  • Snapshots go to a local directory. In a real cluster, use a store every node can read, because a sharded agent can move to another node.

docs.title: Try next
docs.text:
• Replace FakeLlmClient with a real provider behind LlmClient.
  • Ask "refund order-42" from a test and approve it with ApprovalService.
  • Run two nodes (remove join-self, list seed nodes) and check that demo-agent answers from either.

docs.title: Chat Example
docs.text:
A clustered chat app. Each browser connection gets its own actor, each chat room is a sharded actor, and room messages go to every member through a pub/sub topic, across nodes, with no message broker.

  • Source: example/chat
  • Runs: three nodes on one machine, in Docker Compose, or on Kubernetes (Kubernetes example)
  • Modules: actor-spring-boot-starter-cluster, actor-streams (WebSocket bridge), actor-metrics, Spring WebFlux, Actuator with Prometheus; a React frontend in frontend/

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
• One actor per WebSocket connection, with ActorWebSocketHandler from actor-streams
  • A sharded actor per chat room
  • Pub/sub topics (SpringTopicManager) to broadcast to every member of a room, on any node
  • watch and ActorTerminated: the user actor stops when the browser disconnects
  • Sending to a room from a REST endpoint, outside any WebSocket
  • A custom Actuator endpoint that reads the Pekko cluster state
graph LR
    WS1[WebSocket] --> U1[UserActor<br/>node 1]
    WS2[WebSocket] --> U2[UserActor<br/>node 2]
    U1 -->|SendMessage| R[ChatRoomActor<br/>sharded, one per room]
    U2 -->|JoinRoom| R
    R -->|publish| T((Topic<br/>chat-room-id))
    T --> U1
    T --> U2

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
The frontend is not built by default. Build it once so Spring Boot serves it from src/main/resources/static:

cd example/chat/frontend
npm install
npm run build

bootRun builds the actor-metrics Java agent jar and attaches it. One node, from the repository root:

./gradlew :example:chat:bootRun

Three nodes, with the cluster-start.sh script in the repository root:

sh cluster-start.sh chat io.github.seonwkim.example.SpringPekkoApplication 8080 2551 3

Open http://localhost:8080, http://localhost:8081 and http://localhost:8082 in three tabs, join the same room in each, and send messages. Stop the nodes with sh cluster-stop.sh.

For frontend work, npm run dev in frontend/ serves the UI on http://localhost:5173 and proxies /ws and /api to the node on port 8080.

docs.title: With Docker Compose
docs.text:
cd example/chat
sh init-local-docker.sh

The script builds the jar and the chat-app:latest image and starts three containers (chat-app-0 to chat-app-2) on ports 8080 to 8082. They find each other through the SEED_NODES environment variable.

docs.title: Send messages from the command line
docs.text:
POST /api/chat/send sends a message to a room without a WebSocket. send-random-messages.sh uses it for load tests:

curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/chat/send \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"roomId":"room1","userId":"bot","message":"hello"}'

cd example/chat
./send-random-messages.sh room1 -w 50 -r 20 -m 1000 -b   # 1,000 messages, 50 workers, 20 random users
./send-random-messages.sh --help

docs.title: The WebSocket endpoint: ChatWebSocketHandler
docs.text:
ActorWebSocketHandler connects each WebSocket session to actors. For every new session it calls the connector with a client reference: text sent to client goes to the browser. The connector returns where the browser's text frames go.

public ChatWebSocketHandler(ObjectMapper objectMapper, SpringActorSystem actorSystem, ActorStreams streams) {
    this.objectMapper = objectMapper;
    this.bridge = new ActorWebSocketHandler(streams, (session, client) -> actorSystem
            .actor(UserActor.class)
            .withContext(new UserActor.UserActorContext(actorSystem, UUID.randomUUID().toString(), client))
            .spawn()
            .thenApply(this::connect));
}

@Override
public Mono<Void> handle(WebSocketSession session) {
    return bridge.handle(session);
}

private Consumer<String> connect(SpringActorHandle<UserActor.Command> user) {
    user.tell(new Connect());
    return payload -> {
        UserActor.Command command = parse(payload);
        if (command != null) {
            user.tell(command);
        }
    };
}

parse reads the JSON frame's type (join, leave, message) and turns it into a UserActor command. WebSocketConfig maps the handler to /ws/chat.

docs.title: One actor per connection: UserActor
docs.text:
UserActor gets its user id and the client reference through a custom context (SpringActorWithContext with UserActorContext). It watches client; when the browser disconnects, the reference stops and the actor stops too:

@Override
public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(UserActorContext actorContext) {
    return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
            .withState(ctx -> {
                ctx.watch(actorContext.client);
                return new UserActorBehavior(ctx, actorContext.actorSystem, actorContext.userId, actorContext.client);
            })
            .onMessage(JoinRoom.class, UserActorBehavior::onJoinRoom)
            .onMessage(SendMessage.class, UserActorBehavior::onSendMessage)
            .onMessage(SendMessageEvent.class, UserActorBehavior::onSendMessageEvent)
            // ... Connect, LeaveRoom, JoinRoomEvent, LeaveRoomEvent
            .onSignal(ActorTerminated.class, (behavior, signal) -> SpringActorBehavior.stopped())
            .build();
}

Commands from the browser (JoinRoom, SendMessage) go to the room actor. Events from the room (JoinRoomEvent, SendMessageEvent, ...) become JSON text sent to client.tell(json). To join, the user actor passes its own reference so the room can subscribe it:

roomActor.tell(new ChatRoomActor.JoinRoom(userId, context.getSelf()));

docs.title: One sharded actor per room: ChatRoomActor
docs.text:
Each room is a sharded entity that owns a topic named chat-room-<roomId>. The topic manager is injected into the actor bean. The actor asks for the topic with getOrCreateAsync() and gets it as a message (pipeToSelf), so it never blocks its thread; commands that arrive first wait in a list and run once the topic is there:

@Override
public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringShardedActorContext<Command> ctx) {
    final String roomId = ctx.getEntityId();

    return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, ctx)
            .withState(behaviorCtx -> {
                behaviorCtx.pipeToSelf(
                        topicManager
                                .topic(TopicName.of(UserActor.Command.class, "chat-room-" + roomId))
                                .getOrCreateAsync(),
                        TopicReady::new);
                return new ChatRoomBehavior(behaviorCtx, roomId);
            })
            .onMessage(TopicReady.class, ChatRoomBehavior::onTopicReady)
            .onMessage(JoinRoom.class, ChatRoomBehavior::onJoinRoom)
            .onMessage(LeaveRoom.class, ChatRoomBehavior::onLeaveRoom)
            .onMessage(SendMessage.class, ChatRoomBehavior::onSendMessage)
            .build();
}

Joining subscribes the user actor to the topic; a message is published once and reaches every subscriber, on every node:

private SpringActorBehavior<Command> onJoinRoom(JoinRoom msg) {
    roomTopic.subscribe(msg.userActorRef);
    roomTopic.publish(new UserActor.JoinRoomEvent(msg.userId));
    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
}

private SpringActorBehavior<Command> onSendMessage(SendMessage msg) {
    roomTopic.publish(new UserActor.SendMessageEvent(msg.userId, msg.message));
    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
}

Every command that crosses nodes implements JsonSerializable, including JoinRoom, which carries a SpringActorRef.

docs.title: Sending from outside: ChatMessageSenderService
docs.text:
Any Spring bean can send to a room by id:

JavaKotlin 
SpringShardedActorHandle<ChatRoomActor.Command> roomRef =
        springActorSystem.sharded(ChatRoomActor.class).withId(roomId).get();
roomRef.tell(new ChatRoomActor.SendMessage(userId, message));

actorSystem.sharded<ChatRoomActor, _>()
    .withId(roomId)
    .get()
    .tell(ChatRoomActor.SendMessage(userId, message))

docs.title: Operations extras
docs.text:
• ActorClusterStateEndpoint adds /actuator/actor-cluster-state, which lists the cluster members and their status. It reads Pekko's Cluster through springActorSystem.unwrap(Cluster.class), which is why the build declares Pekko Cluster directly.
  • metrics/ClusterShardingMetricsExporter asks Pekko's shard state every second and exports a pekko.shard.entities gauge per shard for HelloActor.
  • /actuator/prometheus exposes the actor meters. Set ACTOR_METRICS_ENABLED=false to turn off the agent's metrics (see config/ActorMetricsConfiguration).
  • config/BlockHoundConfiguration installs BlockHound when you start the JVM with -Dblockhound.enabled=true, to catch blocking calls on actor dispatcher threads.
  • The app also has the cluster example's sharded HelloActor at GET /hello?message=...&entityId=.... The Kubernetes example's load script uses it.

docs.title: Try next
docs.text:
• Open the same room on two nodes, then stop one node (kill $(lsof -t -i:8081)). The room entity moves to a remaining node if it was on the stopped one; users on the remaining nodes rejoin and keep chatting.
  • Run send-random-messages.sh in burst mode and watch /actuator/prometheus on each node.
  • Close a browser tab and check the log: the UserActor for that connection stops.
  • Deploy it to Kubernetes with the Kubernetes example.

docs.title: Cluster Example
docs.text:
A three-node cluster with two kinds of cluster actors: sharded actors (one instance per id, spread over the nodes) and a cluster singleton (one instance in the whole cluster).

  • Source: example/cluster
  • Runs: three nodes on one machine (spring.actor.provider: cluster)
  • Modules: actor-spring-boot-starter-cluster, Spring WebFlux

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
• A sharded actor (SpringShardedActor) addressed by entity id from any node
  • A cluster singleton (asClusterSingleton()) that collects data sent from every node
  • ask with onTimeout for a fallback answer
  • Messages that cross nodes implementing JsonSerializable
  • Seed-node cluster formation on localhost

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
The repository root has scripts that start several nodes of an example in the background:

# from the repository root
sh cluster-start.sh cluster io.github.seonwkim.example.SpringPekkoApplication 8080 2551 3

This starts three nodes: HTTP ports 8080, 8081, 8082 and remoting ports 2551, 2552, 2553. Each node logs to log_cluster_<port>.txt. Give the cluster 10 to 20 seconds to form. Stop all three with:

sh cluster-stop.sh

To start the nodes by hand, use one terminal per node:

./gradlew :example:cluster:bootRun
./gradlew :example:cluster:bootRun --args='--server.port=8081 --spring.actor.remote.port=2552'
./gradlew :example:cluster:bootRun --args='--server.port=8082 --spring.actor.remote.port=2553'

docs.title: Sharded actors
docs.text:
curl "http://localhost:8080/hello?message=Hello&entityId=entity-1"
curl "http://localhost:8081/hello?message=World&entityId=entity-2"
# Received from entity [entity-2] on node [pekko://spring-pekko-example@127.0.0.1:2553]

# The same entity id answers from the same node, whichever node you call
curl "http://localhost:8080/hello?message=First&entityId=shared"
curl "http://localhost:8082/hello?message=Second&entityId=shared"

docs.title: Cluster singleton
docs.text:
# Record a metric from two different nodes
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080/api/singleton/metrics?name=requests&value=100"
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8081/api/singleton/metrics?name=requests&value=200"

# Read everything the singleton holds, from any node
curl http://localhost:8082/api/singleton/metrics
# {"metrics":{...per node...},"singletonNodeAddress":"pekko://spring-pekko-example@127.0.0.1:2551"}

curl -X DELETE http://localhost:8080/api/singleton/metrics

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
spring:
  actor:
    name: spring-pekko-example
    provider: cluster
    remote:
      hostname: 127.0.0.1
      port: 2551
    cluster:
      seed-nodes:
        - pekko://spring-pekko-example@127.0.0.1:2551
        - pekko://spring-pekko-example@127.0.0.1:2552
        - pekko://spring-pekko-example@127.0.0.1:2553
      downing:
        strategy: keep-majority
    pekko:
      actor:
        allow-java-serialization: off

Every node uses the same file; the start script overrides server.port and spring.actor.remote.port. The seed-node addresses use the actor system name (spring.actor.name), so all nodes must share it.

docs.title: A sharded actor: HelloActor
docs.text:
A sharded actor declares an entity type. The cluster runs at most one instance per entity id and routes every message for that id to it.

@Component
public class HelloActor implements SpringShardedActor<HelloActor.Command> {

    public static final ShardedEntityType<Command> TYPE_KEY = ShardedEntityType.of(Command.class, "HelloActor");

    public interface Command extends JsonSerializable {}

    public static class SayHello extends AskCommand<String> implements Command {
        public final String message;

        public SayHello(String message) {
            this.message = message;
        }
    }

    @Override
    public ShardedEntityType<Command> entityType() {
        return TYPE_KEY;
    }

    @Override
    public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringShardedActorContext<Command> ctx) {
        final String entityId = ctx.getEntityId();
        return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, ctx)
                .withState(actorCtx -> new HelloActorBehavior(actorCtx, entityId))
                .onMessage(SayHello.class, HelloActorBehavior::onSayHello)
                .build();
    }
}

The handler replies with the entity id and ctx.nodeAddress(), so you can see where the entity runs.

HelloService gets a handle by id and asks. You never spawn a sharded actor yourself; the first message starts it. The Kotlin tab shows the same call with actor-kotlin, from a suspend function.

JavaKotlin 
public Mono<String> hello(String message, String entityId) {
    SpringShardedActorHandle<HelloActor.Command> actorRef =
            springActorSystem.sharded(HelloActor.class).withId(entityId).get();

    CompletionStage<String> response = actorRef.ask(new HelloActor.SayHello(message))
            .withTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3))
            .onTimeout(() -> "Request timed out for entity: " + entityId)
            .execute();

    return Mono.fromCompletionStage(response);
}

suspend fun hello(message: String, entityId: String): String =
    actorSystem.sharded<HelloActor, _>()
        .withId(entityId)
        .get()
        .ask(HelloActor.SayHello(message))
        .withTimeout(3.seconds)
        .onTimeout { "Request timed out for entity: $entityId" }
        .await()

docs.title: A cluster singleton: ClusterMetricsAggregator
docs.text:
ClusterMetricsAggregator is a plain actor that keeps a map of metrics per node. ClusterSingletonService spawns it as a cluster singleton when the app starts:

JavaKotlin 
// in a @PostConstruct method
metricsAggregator = springActorSystem
        .actor(ClusterMetricsAggregator.class)
        .withId("metrics-aggregator")
        .asClusterSingleton()
        .spawn()
        .toCompletableFuture()
        .get();

// spawnAndWait() blocks until the singleton proxy is ready, like spawn().get() in the Java tab
val metricsAggregator = actorSystem.actor<ClusterMetricsAggregator, _>()
    .withId("metrics-aggregator")
    .asClusterSingleton()
    .spawnAndWait()

Every node runs this code, and every node gets a handle. The actor itself runs on one node only (the oldest member); the handles on the other nodes forward to it. Recording a metric is a tell, reading is an ask with a fallback:

metricsAggregator.tell(new ClusterMetricsAggregator.RecordMetric(nodeAddress, metricName, value, timestamp));

metricsAggregator.ask(new ClusterMetricsAggregator.GetMetrics())
        .withTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3))
        .onTimeout(() -> new ClusterMetricsAggregator.MetricsResponse(Map.of(), "timeout"))
        .execute();

The response includes singletonNodeAddress, the node the singleton runs on.

docs.title: Try next
docs.text:
• Singleton failover. Find the singleton's node in singletonNodeAddress, stop that node (for port 8080: kill $(lsof -t -i:8080)), wait 10 to 20 seconds and read the metrics from another node. The singleton now runs elsewhere, and its map is empty: its state lived in memory.
  • Entity rebalancing. Call several entity ids, stop one node, and call them again. Entities from the stopped node start again on the remaining nodes, with fresh state.
  • Add a field to SayHello and keep it readable by both old and new nodes (see Deployments).

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Cluster does not form: wait 10 to 20 seconds; check that the seed nodes match and that every node uses the same spring.actor.name.
  • Asks time out across nodes: check that the command classes implement JsonSerializable and that Jackson can write and read them.

docs.title: The actor: HelloActor
docs.text:
@Component
class HelloActor : SpringActor<HelloActor.Command> {
    sealed interface Command

    class SayHello : AskCommand<String>(), Command

    class TriggerFailure : AskCommand<String>(), Command

    override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
        actorBehavior<Command>(actorContext)
            .withState { ctx -> HelloBehavior(ctx, actorContext.actorId()) }
            .onMessage(SayHello::class.java) { state, msg -> state.onSayHello(msg) }
            .onMessage(TriggerFailure::class.java) { state, msg -> state.onTriggerFailure(msg) }
            .onSignal(PreRestart::class.java) { state, _ -> state.onPreRestart() }
            .onSignal(PostStop::class.java) { state, _ -> state.onPostStop() }
            .withSupervisionStrategy(SupervisionStrategy.restart().withLimit(10, Duration.ofMinutes(1)))
            .build()

    private class HelloBehavior(
        private val ctx: SpringBehaviorContext<Command>,
        private val actorId: String,
    ) {
        fun onSayHello(msg: SayHello): SpringActorBehavior<Command> {
            msg.reply("Hello from actor $actorId")
            return SpringActorBehavior.same()
        }

        fun onTriggerFailure(msg: TriggerFailure): SpringActorBehavior<Command> {
            msg.reply("Triggering failure - actor will restart")
            throw IllegalStateException("Intentional failure to demonstrate PreRestart signal")
        }

        // onPreRestart() and onPostStop() log and return SpringActorBehavior.same()
    }
}

actorBehavior<Command>(actorContext) is SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command::class.java, actorContext) with a reified type. The supervision strategy uses java.time.Duration, because it is the Java API.

docs.title: The service: HelloService
docs.text:
@Service
class HelloService(
    private val actorSystem: SpringActorSystem,
) {
    suspend fun hello(): String = helloActor().awaitAsk(HelloActor.SayHello(), timeout = 3.seconds)

    suspend fun triggerRestart(): String = helloActor().awaitAsk(HelloActor.TriggerFailure(), timeout = 3.seconds)

    suspend fun stopActor(): String {
        helloActor().stop()
        return "Actor stopped - PostStop signal will be triggered"
    }

    // `_` lets Kotlin infer the command type from HelloActor.
    private suspend fun helloActor() = actorSystem.awaitGetOrSpawn<HelloActor, _>(ACTOR_ID)

    private companion object {
        const val ACTOR_ID = "hello-actor"
    }
}
  • awaitGetOrSpawn<HelloActor, _>("hello-actor") suspends until the actor runs, spawning it if needed.
  • awaitAsk(command, timeout = 3.seconds) takes a kotlin.time.Duration and suspends until the reply. It throws java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException when no reply arrives in time.

docs.title: The controller
docs.text:
@RestController
class HelloController(
    private val helloService: HelloService,
) {
    @GetMapping("/hello")
    suspend fun hello(): String = helloService.hello()

    @GetMapping("/hello/restart")
    suspend fun triggerRestart(): String = helloService.triggerRestart()

    @GetMapping("/hello/stop")
    suspend fun stopActor(): String = helloService.stopActor()
}

docs.title: Kubernetes Example
docs.text:
Kubernetes manifests that run the chat example as a three-pod Pekko cluster, with scripts for a local kind cluster, rolling updates, canary and blue-green rollouts, and monitoring.

  • Source: example/kubernetes (its README has every command)
  • Runs: a local kind cluster, or any Kubernetes cluster
  • Modules: the chat app's image; Pekko Management, Cluster Bootstrap and Kubernetes API discovery (runtime dependencies of example/chat); Kustomize

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
• Cluster formation with no fixed seed nodes: Cluster Bootstrap finds the other pods through the Kubernetes API
  • The same without RBAC: peers found through PostgreSQL or Redis (spring.actor.cluster.join: discovery)
  • Zero-downtime rolling updates (maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1)
  • Canary and blue-green rollouts, and a script that runs all three under load and counts failed requests
  • A ServiceMonitor, alert rules and the Grafana dashboard for the Prometheus Operator
  • Kustomize overlays for local, dev and prod

docs.title: Run it locally
docs.text:
You need Docker (with at least 8 GB of memory), kind and kubectl.

cd example/kubernetes
./setup-local.sh

The script creates the kind cluster spring-actor-demo, builds the chat app (../../gradlew clean build -x test in example/chat), builds the image spring-actor-chat:local from Dockerfile.kubernetes, loads it into kind, and applies overlays/local. Then open http://localhost:8080.

Check the cluster:

kubectl get pods -n spring-actor

POD=$(kubectl get pods -n spring-actor -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl exec -n spring-actor $POD -- curl -s localhost:7626/cluster/members | jq   # three members, "Up"

kubectl logs -f -n spring-actor -l app=spring-actor

./port-forward-pods.sh forwards ports 8080, 8081 and 8082 to the three pods one by one, so you can open the chat on each. Remove everything with ./cleanup-local.sh.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
example/kubernetes/
├── setup-local.sh, cleanup-local.sh, port-forward-pods.sh
├── base/                  namespace, RBAC (pod reader), ConfigMap, Services, Deployment, monitors, NetworkPolicy
├── overlays/
│   ├── local/             used by setup-local.sh: 3 replicas, NodePort 30080 (kind maps it to localhost:8080)
│   ├── dev/, prod/        prod adds an HPA
│   ├── discovery-jdbc/    no RBAC: peers through PostgreSQL
│   └── discovery-redis/   no RBAC: peers through Redis
├── components/discovery/  shared by the two discovery overlays
├── monitoring/            ServiceMonitor, alert rules, Grafana dashboard
└── scripts/               deploy, rollout, debug, load, canary, blue-green, test-strategies, monitoring

docs.title: Cluster formation through the Kubernetes API
docs.text: The chat app's kubernetes profile clears the seed-node list (application-kubernetes.yml), and the ConfigMap in base/ sets Cluster Bootstrap under spring.actor.pekko.management.cluster.bootstrap with discovery-method: kubernetes-api. Each pod lists the pods with the label app=spring-actor (the RBAC Role in base/rbac.yaml allows that), contacts them on the management port 7626, and joins the existing cluster or forms a new one. All overlays use Pekko's default ports: remoting 25520, management 7626.

docs.title: Graceful shutdown
docs.text: Pods get terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45: a 10-second preStop sleep so the Services stop sending new requests, Spring Boot's graceful drain of the requests in flight, then up to 25 seconds (spring.actor.shutdown.timeout) for the actor system to leave the cluster.

docs.title: Without RBAC: JDBC or Redis discovery
docs.text:
When pods may not read the Kubernetes API, use an overlay that finds peers through a store the app already uses:

kubectl apply -k overlays/discovery-jdbc    # PostgreSQL at postgres:5432, Secret spring-actor-db
kubectl apply -k overlays/discovery-redis   # Redis at redis:6379

Each pod writes its own entry to the store, renews it every 5 seconds and deletes it on graceful shutdown. The components/discovery component removes the RBAC objects and the service account token, and sets readiness on Actuator health. The chat image does not contain actor-jdbc or actor-redis, so these overlays need your own image (images: in the overlay).

./gradlew :example:kubernetes:test renders every overlay (it needs kubectl, and skips otherwise) and checks that the ConfigMap, Deployment and Services agree on the ports, that the grace period covers the shutdown, and that the discovery overlays contain no RBAC and open only the expected ports.

docs.title: Rollouts
docs.text:
Strategy Command What happens Rolling update kubectl set image deployment/spring-actor spring-actor=spring-actor-chat:v2 -n spring-actor New pods join the cluster one at a time; old pods leave Canary scripts/canary.sh start <image>, then promote or abort A few new pods join the running cluster and get a share of traffic Blue-green scripts/blue-green.sh deploy <image> (waits for warm-up), activate (through the generation endpoint), verify, retire, rollback A second, separate cluster; the HTTP Service switches in one step

scripts/test-strategies.sh runs all three under load on the kind cluster and fails if any request failed. scripts/load.sh counts a request as ok only when the actor replied.

Rolling updates and canaries mix versions in one cluster, so messages and sharded state must stay readable by both versions. The Deployments guide explains how.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
With the Prometheus Operator installed (for example kube-prometheus-stack):

./scripts/monitoring.sh          # apply; `render` prints the manifests, `delete` removes them

It installs the ServiceMonitor for /actuator/prometheus, the actor-alerts PrometheusRule and the Actors Grafana dashboard. See Monitoring.

docs.text:
• Delete a pod (kubectl delete pod <name> -n spring-actor) and watch a new one join.
  • Scale to five pods: kubectl scale deployment spring-actor -n spring-actor --replicas=5.
  • Run scripts/test-strategies.sh and read the failure counts.

docs.title: Logging Example
docs.text:
Actor logs with context: static MDC values set when an actor spawns, per-message MDC values computed from each message, actor tags, a request id carried from HTTP through several actors, and Logback writing both plain text and JSON files.

  • Source: example/logging
  • Runs: one node, no cluster
  • Modules: actor-spring-boot-starter, Spring WebFlux, Logback, logstash-logback-encoder

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
• Static MDC: withMdc(MdcConfig.of(...)) on the spawn builder, the same on every log line of that actor
  • Per-message MDC: withMdc(msg -> ...) on the behavior builder, computed for each message
  • Tags: withTags(TagsConfig.of(...)), written to the pekkoTags MDC key
  • Request tracing: a WebFilter puts a request id in the MDC, services copy it into each message, and each actor puts it back in its MDC
  • Async and JSON appenders in logback.xml

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
./gradlew :example:logging:bootRun

The app listens on port 8080 and writes to the console, logs/application.log and logs/application-json.log (relative to the directory you start it from).

# Order: per-message MDC (orderId, userId, amount)
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/orders \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"userId": "CUST-123", "amount": 99.99}'

# Payment: static MDC (service, region, version) plus per-message MDC
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/payments \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"orderId": "ORD-123", "userId": "CUST-123", "amount": 99.99, "paymentMethod": "credit_card"}'

# Notification: tags and static MDC
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/notifications \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"userId": "USER-123", "type": "email", "message": "Your order has been processed"}'

# Checkout: order -> payment -> notification, all with the same request id
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/checkout \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-Request-Id: REQ-demo-1" \
  -d '{"userId": "CUST-123", "amount": 99.99, "paymentMethod": "credit_card"}'

Then filter the logs:

grep "REQ-demo-1" logs/application.log               # one request through every actor
grep "pekkoTags.*critical" logs/application.log       # actors tagged critical
tail -f logs/application-json.log | jq .              # JSON lines with MDC fields

docs.title: Static MDC and tags at spawn time
docs.text:
The services spawn one actor each in their constructor:

JavaKotlin 
Map<String, String> staticMdc = Map.of(
        "service", "payment-service",
        "region", "us-east-1",
        "version", "2.0");

this.paymentProcessor = actorSystem
        .actor(PaymentProcessorActor.class)
        .withId("payment-processor")
        .withMdc(MdcConfig.of(staticMdc))
        .withTags(TagsConfig.of("payment-service", "critical", "io-bound"))
        .withBlockingDispatcher()
        .withTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
        .spawnAndWait();

val paymentProcessor = actorSystem.actor<PaymentProcessorActor, _>()
    .withId("payment-processor")
    .withMdc(MdcConfig.of(mapOf("service" to "payment-service", "region" to "us-east-1", "version" to "2.0")))
    .withTags(TagsConfig.of("payment-service", "critical", "io-bound"))
    .withBlockingDispatcher()
    .withTimeout(5.seconds)
    .spawnAndWait()

All three actors simulate work with Thread.sleep, so all three are spawned with withBlockingDispatcher(): blocking on the default dispatcher would hold up every other actor.

docs.title: Per-message MDC
docs.text:
The behavior builder's withMdc takes a function from the message to a map. Its values are added to the static ones for that message's log lines:

JavaKotlin 
return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
        .withMdc(msg -> {
            if (msg instanceof ProcessOrder order) {
                Map<String, String> mdc = new HashMap<>();
                mdc.put("orderId", order.orderId);
                mdc.put("userId", order.userId);
                mdc.put("amount", String.valueOf(order.amount));
                if (order.requestId != null) {
                    mdc.put("requestId", order.requestId);
                }
                return mdc;
            }
            return Map.of();
        })
        .onMessage(ProcessOrder.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
            ctx.getLog().info("Starting order processing");
            // ...
        })
        .build();

actorBehavior<Command>(actorContext)
    .withMdc { msg ->
        when (msg) {
            is ProcessOrder -> buildMap {
                put("orderId", msg.orderId)
                put("userId", msg.userId)
                put("amount", msg.amount.toString())
                msg.requestId?.let { put("requestId", it) }
            }
            else -> emptyMap()
        }
    }
    .onMessage(ProcessOrder::class.java) { ctx, msg ->
        ctx.log.info("Starting order processing")
        // ...
    }
    .build()

Use ctx.getLog() inside handlers: those log lines carry the MDC values.

docs.title: Carrying the request id
docs.text: MdcWebFilter reads X-Request-Id (or creates a UUID) and X-User-Id, puts them in the MDC, and echoes X-Request-Id in the response. An actor runs on another thread, so the MDC does not follow the message by itself. The services read MDC.get("requestId") and put it in the command; the actor's per-message MDC puts it back.

docs.title: Logback
docs.text:
logback.xml writes the MDC keys in the console and file patterns, for example:

%d{ISO8601} %-5level [%thread] [%X{pekkoSource}] [%X{pekkoTags}] [reqId=%X{requestId}] [userId=%X{userId}] %logger{36} - %msg%n
Appender Output CONSOLE Plain text ASYNC_FILE logs/application.log, rolled daily, 30 days, 10 GB cap ASYNC_JSON logs/application-json.log with LogstashEncoder, MDC keys as JSON fields

The file appenders are AsyncAppenders with a queue of 1,024 and neverBlock=false: when the queue is full, the logging thread waits rather than dropping lines. Set neverBlock to true if you prefer to drop lines instead of slowing actors down.

docs.text:

  • Send 100 checkouts in a loop and follow one request id through application-json.log with jq.
