docs.title: Metrics Example
docs.text:
The simple example's HelloActor with actor metrics turned on and exposed to Prometheus through Spring Boot Actuator. Use it to see which meters an app gets and how restarts and stops show up in them.

  • Source: example/metrics-example
  • Runs: one node, no cluster
  • Modules: actor-spring-boot-starter, actor-metrics (with its optional Java agent attached), Spring WebFlux, Actuator, micrometer-registry-prometheus

The full list of meters, their tags, the Grafana dashboard and the alert rules are in the Monitoring guide. This page covers only the example.

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
• The dependencies and the Actuator setting that turn on actor metrics
  • Attaching the actor-metrics Java agent from Gradle (bootRun and test)
  • Message, failure, restart and mailbox meters moving as you call the actor

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
./gradlew :example:metrics-example:bootRun

bootRun builds the agent jar (:actor-metrics:agentJar) first and starts the JVM with -javaagent:...agent.jar. The app listens on port 8080.

Send some traffic, then read the meters:

for i in $(seq 1 20); do curl -s http://localhost:8080/hello > /dev/null; done
curl http://localhost:8080/hello/restart
curl http://localhost:8080/hello/stop

curl -s http://localhost:8080/actuator/prometheus | grep '^actor_'

Other endpoints:

Endpoint What it does GET /hello Asks hello-actor for a greeting (spawns it if needed) GET /hello/restart Makes the actor throw, so supervision restarts it GET /hello/stop Stops the actor GET /debug/actor-path Returns the actor's path, the value the opt-in actor.path tag uses GET /actuator/prometheus All meters in Prometheus format GET /actuator/metrics Meter names, for a quick look without Prometheus

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
dependencies {
    implementation(project(":actor-spring-boot-starter"))
    implementation(project(":actor-metrics"))

    implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-webflux")
    implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-actuator")
    implementation("io.micrometer:micrometer-registry-prometheus")
}

In your own app, use the published coordinates (io.github.seonwkim:actor-metrics). With a MeterRegistry bean on the classpath (Actuator creates one), the starter meters every actor it spawns. No code is needed. spring.actor.metrics.enabled=false turns it off.

docs.title: Expose the endpoint
docs.text:
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: prometheus, health, info, metrics

docs.title: Attach the agent (optional)
docs.text:
The starter records the main meters without any agent. The example also attaches the actor-metrics Java agent, which adds a few meters that no public hook exposes (see Monitoring). The Gradle wiring:

tasks.named<BootRun>("bootRun") {
    dependsOn(":actor-metrics:agentJar")
    val agentJar = project(":actor-metrics").tasks.named<Jar>("agentJar").get()
    jvmArgs = listOf("-javaagent:${agentJar.archiveFile.get().asFile.absolutePath}")
}

The test task gets the same -javaagent argument, so tests run with the agent too.

docs.title: The actor
docs.text: HelloActor, HelloService and HelloController are the same as in the simple example, plus the /debug/actor-path endpoint. The actor restarts on failure, up to 10 times a minute, so /hello/restart increases the restart counter.

  • Start a Prometheus and Grafana and import the dashboard from the repository's monitoring/ directory.
  • For metrics in a cluster, see the chat example and the Kubernetes example.

docs.title: Persistence Example
docs.text:
Three ways an actor can keep its state in a database with plain Spring Data JPA: save the current state, store every change as an event, or save snapshots now and then. Each is one actor per order id.

  • Source: example/persistence
  • Runs: one node, no cluster, H2 in memory
  • Modules: actor-spring-boot-starter, Spring MVC, Spring Data JPA, H2, Actuator

Hand-written patterns

This example writes the persistence code itself on top of JPA repositories. It does not use the starter's actor-persistence module. For the module's event-sourced actors with a journal, see Event sourcing.

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
• OrderActor: loads its order when it starts and saves it on every change (JPA entity with @Version)
  • EventLogOrderActor: appends each change to an order_events table and rebuilds its state by replaying the events when it starts
  • SnapshotOrderActor: saves the state as JSON every 10 changes or 60 seconds, and starts from the latest snapshot
  • Running actors that block on JDBC on the blocking dispatcher

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
./gradlew :example:persistence:bootRun

The app listens on port 8080. The H2 console is at http://localhost:8080/h2-console (JDBC URL jdbc:h2:mem:orderdb, user sa, empty password).

docs.title: Current state (/api/orders)
docs.text:
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080/api/orders/order-1?customerId=customer-1&amount=100.50"
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080/api/orders/order-1/items?productId=prod-1&quantity=2&price=50.25"
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080/api/orders/order-1/approve"
curl "http://localhost:8080/api/orders/order-1"

docs.title: Event log (/api/orders/eventlog)
docs.text:
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080/api/orders/eventlog/order-2?customerId=customer-2&amount=200.00"
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080/api/orders/eventlog/order-2/items?productId=prod-2&quantity=3&price=66.67"
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080/api/orders/eventlog/order-2/approve?approvedBy=admin"

docs.title: Snapshots (/api/orders/snapshot)
docs.text:
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080/api/orders/snapshot/order-3?customerId=customer-3&amount=150.00"
curl -X PUT "http://localhost:8080/api/orders/snapshot/order-3?amount=175.00"
curl "http://localhost:8080/api/orders/snapshot/order-3"
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080/api/orders/snapshot/order-3/save-snapshot"

docs.title: Blocking work goes on the blocking dispatcher
docs.text:
JPA calls block their thread until the database answers. The controller spawns these actors with withBlockingDispatcher(), so they never hold the default dispatcher's threads that every other actor shares:

JavaKotlin 
private <A extends SpringActorWithContext<C, ?>, C> CompletionStage<SpringActorHandle<C>> onBlockingDispatcher(
        Class<A> actorClass, String orderId) {
    return actorSystem
            .actor(actorClass)
            .withId(orderId)
            .withBlockingDispatcher()
            .getOrSpawn();
}

// Call from a suspend function or a coroutine.
suspend fun order(orderId: String): SpringActorHandle<OrderActor.Command> =
    actorSystem.actor<OrderActor, _>()
        .withId(orderId)
        .withBlockingDispatcher()
        .awaitGetOrSpawn()

Each endpoint then asks the actor with a 5-second timeout.

docs.title: Current state: OrderActor
docs.text:
The actor gets its repository by constructor injection, loads the order in withState, and saves after each change:

@Override
public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
    return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
            .withState(ctx -> {
                Order order = orderRepository.findByOrderId(actorContext.actorId()).orElse(null);
                return new OrderActorBehavior(ctx, actorContext, orderRepository, order);
            })
            .onMessage(CreateOrder.class, OrderActorBehavior::handleCreateOrder)
            .onMessage(AddItem.class, OrderActorBehavior::handleAddItem)
            .onMessage(GetOrder.class, OrderActorBehavior::handleGetOrder)
            .onMessage(ApproveOrder.class, OrderActorBehavior::handleApproveOrder)
            .build();
}

Because one actor handles all writes for an order, writes for the same order never race. @Version on Order still catches a write from outside the actor (OptimisticLockingFailureException).

docs.title: Event log: EventLogOrderActor
docs.text:
Each command appends a domain event (OrderCreatedEvent, OrderItemAddedEvent, OrderApprovedEvent, OrderCancelledEvent) as JSON with a sequence number. On start, the actor replays them:

private OrderState rebuildState(String orderId) {
    List<OrderEvent> events = eventRepository.findByOrderIdOrderBySequenceNumberAsc(orderId);
    OrderState state = new OrderState(orderId);
    for (OrderEvent event : events) {
        state.apply(deserializeEvent(event)); // the real code wraps this in try/catch
    }
    return state;
}

/history returns the stored events, the order's full audit trail.

docs.title: Snapshots: SnapshotOrderActor
docs.text:
On start, the actor reads the latest snapshot (or the order row). After each change it asks a SnapshotStrategy whether to save one:

SnapshotStrategy strategy = new HybridSnapshotStrategy(
        10,     // every 10 operations
        60000); // or every 60 seconds

After saving, it deletes snapshots older than an hour once there are more than five.

docs.title: Things to keep in mind
docs.text:
• The database is in memory: everything is gone when the app stops. build.gradle.kts also includes the PostgreSQL driver; point spring.datasource.* at PostgreSQL to keep the data.
  • Each actor here is a local actor. On a cluster, make them sharded actors so one node owns each order.

docs.title: Try next
docs.text:
• Restart the app with a file-based H2 URL (jdbc:h2:file:./orderdb) and check that each actor reloads its order.
  • Add a RejectOrder endpoint for OrderActor (the actor already handles it).
  • Compare with the starter's own event sourcing in Event sourcing.

docs.text:

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
One local actor behind a REST API. It is the smallest complete app: define an actor, get or spawn it, ask it a question, and watch it restart and stop.

Start here if you are new to the library.

  • Source: example/simple
  • Runs: one node, no cluster (spring.actor.provider: local)
  • Modules: actor-spring-boot-starter, Spring WebFlux

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
• An actor as a Spring @Component (SpringActor)
  • Commands with a typed reply (AskCommand<String>)
  • getOrSpawn to get the actor if it runs, or start it if not
  • ask with a timeout, turned into a Mono for WebFlux
  • A restart supervision strategy with a limit
  • Lifecycle signals: PreRestart and PostStop

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
From the repository root:

./gradlew :example:simple:bootRun

The app listens on port 8080. In another terminal:

curl http://localhost:8080/hello
# Hello from actor hello-actor

curl http://localhost:8080/hello/restart
# Triggering failure - actor will restart

curl http://localhost:8080/hello/stop
# Actor stopped - PostStop signal will be triggered

Watch the application log: /hello/restart logs "is being restarted due to failure" (the PreRestart handler), and /hello/stop logs "is stopping" (the PostStop handler). The next /hello after a stop spawns a new actor.

docs.title: Turn on actor support
docs.text:
The starter is on the classpath, so @SpringBootApplication is enough:

@SpringBootApplication
public class SpringPekkoApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(SpringPekkoApplication.class, args);
    }
}

application.yml runs a local actor system:

spring:
  actor:
    provider: local

docs.title: The actor: HelloActor
docs.text:
The actor is a Spring bean. Its commands share one interface. A command that expects an answer extends AskCommand<R>, where R is the reply type.

@Component
public class HelloActor implements SpringActor<HelloActor.Command> {

    public interface Command {}

    public static class SayHello extends AskCommand<String> implements Command {}

    public static class TriggerFailure extends AskCommand<String> implements Command {}

    @Override
    public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
        return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                .withState(ctx -> new HelloActorBehavior(ctx, actorContext))
                .onMessage(SayHello.class, HelloActorBehavior::onSayHello)
                .onMessage(TriggerFailure.class, HelloActorBehavior::onTriggerFailure)
                .onSignal(PreRestart.class, HelloActorBehavior::onPreRestart)
                .onSignal(PostStop.class, HelloActorBehavior::onPostStop)
                .withSupervisionStrategy(SupervisionStrategy.restart().withLimit(10, Duration.ofMinutes(1)))
                .build();
    }
}
  • withState creates the actor's state object when the actor starts (and again after each restart). Handlers are methods on that object.
  • withSupervisionStrategy(SupervisionStrategy.restart().withLimit(10, Duration.ofMinutes(1))) restarts the actor when a handler throws, up to 10 times a minute.

The handlers reply with msg.reply(...) and return the next behavior:

private SpringActorBehavior<Command> onSayHello(SayHello msg) {
    msg.reply("Hello from actor " + actorContext.actorId());
    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
}

private SpringActorBehavior<Command> onTriggerFailure(TriggerFailure msg) {
    msg.reply("Triggering failure - actor will restart");
    throw new RuntimeException("Intentional failure to demonstrate PreRestart signal");
}

onTriggerFailure replies first and then throws, so the caller gets an answer and the actor restarts.

docs.title: Talking to the actor: HelloService
docs.text:
@Service
public class HelloService {
    private final SpringActorSystem actorSystem;

    public HelloService(SpringActorSystem actorSystem) {
        this.actorSystem = actorSystem;
    }

    public Mono<String> hello() {
        return Mono.fromCompletionStage(
                actorSystem.getOrSpawn(HelloActor.class, "hello-actor")
                        .thenCompose(actor -> actor.ask(new HelloActor.SayHello())
                                .withTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3))
                                .execute()));
    }

    public Mono<String> stopActor() {
        return Mono.fromCompletionStage(
                actorSystem.getOrSpawn(HelloActor.class, "hello-actor").thenCompose(actor -> {
                    actor.stop();
                    return Mono.just("Actor stopped - PostStop signal will be triggered").toFuture();
                }));
    }
}
  • getOrSpawn(HelloActor.class, "hello-actor") returns the running actor with that id, or spawns it.
  • ask(...).withTimeout(...).execute() sends the command and returns a CompletionStage of the reply.
  • actor.stop() stops the actor; its PostStop handler runs.

HelloController maps /hello, /hello/restart and /hello/stop to these methods.

docs.title: Try next
docs.text:
• Call /hello/restart more than 10 times within a minute. After the limit, supervision stops the actor instead of restarting it.
  • Add a counter to HelloActorBehavior and return it in the reply. A restart resets it, because withState builds a new state object.
  • Spawn a second actor with another id and check that each has its own state.
  • Compare with the Kotlin example, the same app with suspend functions.

docs.title: Synchronization Example
docs.text:
A counter that many requests increment at the same time, on three nodes, built three ways: a database row lock, a Redis lock, and a sharded actor. A load script checks that each one ends at the right value.

  • Source: example/synchronization
  • Runs: three nodes on one machine, plus MySQL and Redis
  • Modules: actor-spring-boot-starter-cluster, Spring WebFlux, Spring Data JPA, Spring Data Redis Reactive

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
• Why an actor needs no lock: it handles one message at a time, so value++ in its handler is safe.
  • A sharded actor per counter id: one instance in the cluster, whichever node gets the request.
  • The cost of the alternatives: a SELECT ... FOR UPDATE per increment, or a Redis lock with retries.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
You need MySQL on localhost:3306 (user root, password root) and Redis on localhost:6379. The app creates the counter_db database and the counter table on start. For example, with Docker:

docker run -d --name counter-mysql -p 3306:3306 -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=root mysql:8
docker run -d --name counter-redis -p 6379:6379 redis:7

Start three nodes from the repository root:

sh cluster-start.sh synchronization io.github.seonwkim.example.SpringPekkoApplication 8080 2551 3

Then run the check. It needs Apache Bench (ab):

cd example/synchronization
./verify.sh

verify.sh sends 9,000 increments for one counter id, split over the three nodes with 10 concurrent requests each, once per method (db, redis, actor). Each increment responds only after it is applied, so when the requests are done it reads the counter from node 8080 and compares it with 9,000. Each run uses a new counter id (verify-<timestamp>; set COUNTER_ID to choose one), so it can run again without clearing the database and Redis.

Stop the nodes with sh cluster-stop.sh from the repository root.

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text:
Method Increment Read Database lock GET /counter/db/{counterId}/increment GET /counter/db/{counterId} Redis lock GET /counter/redis/{counterId}/increment GET /counter/redis/{counterId} Actor GET /counter/actor/{counterId}/increment GET /counter/actor/{counterId}

The app also includes springdoc, so Swagger UI is at http://localhost:8080/swagger-ui.html.

docs.title: The actor: CounterActor
docs.text:
One sharded entity per counter id. The value lives in the actor's state; no lock, no database.

@Component
public class CounterActor implements SpringShardedActor<CounterActor.Command> {

    public static final ShardedEntityType<Command> TYPE_KEY = ShardedEntityType.of(Command.class, "CounterActor");

    public interface Command extends JsonSerializable {}

    public static class Increment extends AskCommand<Long> implements Command {}

    public static class GetValue extends AskCommand<Long> implements Command {}

    @Override
    public ShardedEntityType<Command> entityType() {
        return TYPE_KEY;
    }

    @Override
    public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringShardedActorContext<Command> ctx) {
        return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, ctx)
                .withState(context -> new CounterActorBehavior(ctx.getEntityId()))
                .onMessage(Increment.class, CounterActorBehavior::onIncrement)
                .onMessage(GetValue.class, CounterActorBehavior::onGetValue)
                .build();
    }

    private static class CounterActorBehavior {
        private final String counterId;
        private long value = 0;

        CounterActorBehavior(String counterId) {
            this.counterId = counterId;
        }

        private SpringActorBehavior<Command> onIncrement(Increment msg) {
            value++;
            msg.reply(value);
            return SpringActorBehavior.same();
        }

        private SpringActorBehavior<Command> onGetValue(GetValue msg) {
            msg.reply(value);
            return SpringActorBehavior.same();
        }
    }
}

ActorCounterService sends both commands with ask, so an increment's HTTP response waits until the actor applied it:

JavaKotlin 
public Mono<Long> increment(String counterId) {
    var actorRef = springActorSystem.sharded(CounterActor.class).withId(counterId).get();
    return Mono.fromCompletionStage(actorRef.ask(new CounterActor.Increment())
            .withTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3))
            .execute());
}

public Mono<Long> getValue(String counterId) {
    var actorRef = springActorSystem.sharded(CounterActor.class).withId(counterId).get();
    CompletionStage<Long> response = actorRef.ask(new CounterActor.GetValue())
            .withTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3))
            .onTimeout(() -> 0L)
            .execute();
    return Mono.fromCompletionStage(response);
}

// Call from a suspend function or a coroutine.
suspend fun increment(counterId: String): Long =
    actorSystem.sharded<CounterActor, _>()
        .withId(counterId)
        .get()
        .ask(CounterActor.Increment())
        .withTimeout(3.seconds)
        .await()

suspend fun getValue(counterId: String): Long =
    actorSystem.sharded<CounterActor, _>()
        .withId(counterId)
        .get()
        .ask(CounterActor.GetValue())
        .withTimeout(3.seconds)
        .onTimeout { 0L }
        .await()

docs.title: The database lock: DbCounterService
docs.text:
Each increment opens a transaction and locks the row with a native query:

@Query(value = "SELECT * FROM counter WHERE counter_id = :counterId FOR UPDATE", nativeQuery = true)
Optional<Counter> findByIdWithLock(@Param("counterId") String counterId);

Concurrent increments of the same counter wait for each other inside the database, and each one holds a connection while it waits.

docs.title: The Redis lock: RedisCounterService
docs.text: Each increment takes a lock key with setIfAbsent (2-second expiry), runs INCR, and deletes the lock. When the lock is taken, it retries with backoff, up to 50 times. Every increment costs at least three Redis round trips, more under contention.

docs.title: Things to keep in mind
docs.text: • The actor counter lives in memory. If the node that hosts the entity stops, the count is lost. For a count that must survive, persist it: see State in a database or Event sourcing.

docs.title: Try next
docs.text:
• Raise NUM_REQUESTS and CONCURRENCY in verify.sh and compare how long each method takes.
  • Use many counter ids instead of one. The actor version spreads them over the nodes; the database version spreads them over rows.

docs.text:
• Sharded actors
  • Messaging: tell and ask
  • Cluster example

docs.title: Virtual Threads Example
docs.text:
Actors on Java 21 virtual threads, configured with typed spring.actor.* keys and no Pekko HOCON. An endpoint sends a message to an actor on a virtual-thread dispatcher, and the actor logs whether its thread is virtual.

  • Source: example/virtual-threads
  • Runs: one node, no cluster; needs Java 21 or later
  • Modules: actor-spring-boot-starter, Spring WebFlux, Actuator

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
• spring.actor.virtual-threads.enabled: runs the blocking dispatcher (withBlockingDispatcher()) on virtual threads
  • spring.actor.dispatchers.<name>.virtual: true: a named dispatcher on virtual threads
  • withDispatcherFromConfig("<name>") to spawn an actor on that dispatcher

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
./gradlew :example:virtual-threads:bootRun

curl http://localhost:8080/api/virtual

The response describes the dispatcher. The proof is in the application log:

Task 'virtual-thread-executor' - Thread: ..., IsVirtual: true, ThreadId: ...

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
spring:
  actor:
    provider: local
    virtual-threads:
      enabled: true            # withBlockingDispatcher() runs on virtual threads
    dispatchers:
      virtual-threads-dispatcher:
        virtual: true          # withDispatcherFromConfig("virtual-threads-dispatcher")
Property Values What it does spring.actor.virtual-threads.enabled auto (default), true, false Runs the blocking dispatcher on virtual threads. auto follows Spring Boot's spring.threads.virtual.enabled. spring.actor.dispatchers.<name>.virtual true / false Defines a dispatcher that runs each task on a new virtual thread spring.actor.dispatchers.<name>.executor an Executor bean name The alternative: a dispatcher on a Spring Executor bean. Set one of virtual and executor, not both.

The default dispatcher always stays on platform threads.

docs.title: The actor: VirtualThreadTestActor
docs.text:
@Component
public class VirtualThreadTestActor
        implements SpringActorWithContext<VirtualThreadTestActor.Command, SpringActorContext> {

    public interface Command {}

    public static class CheckThread implements Command {
        public final String taskName;

        public CheckThread(String taskName) {
            this.taskName = taskName;
        }
    }

    @Override
    public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
        return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                .onMessage(CheckThread.class, this::onCheckThread)
                .build();
    }

    private SpringActorBehavior<Command> onCheckThread(SpringBehaviorContext<Command> context, CheckThread command) {
        Thread currentThread = Thread.currentThread();
        context.getLog().info("Task '{}' - Thread: {}, IsVirtual: {}, ThreadId: {}",
                command.taskName, currentThread.getName(), currentThread.isVirtual(), currentThread.threadId());
        return SpringActorBehavior.same();
    }
}

docs.title: Spawning on the virtual-thread dispatcher
docs.text:
The controller spawns one actor, on the first request, and every request sends it a message:

JavaKotlin 
private final Mono<SpringActorHandle<VirtualThreadTestActor.Command>> actor;

public VirtualThreadTestController(SpringActorSystem actorSystem) {
    this.actor = Mono.fromCompletionStage(() -> actorSystem
                    .actor(VirtualThreadTestActor.class)
                    .withId("virtual-actor")
                    .withDispatcherFromConfig("virtual-threads-dispatcher")
                    .spawn())
            .cache();
}

@GetMapping("/virtual")
public Mono<Map<String, Object>> testVirtual() {
    return actor.map(handle -> {
        handle.tell(new VirtualThreadTestActor.CheckThread("virtual-thread-executor"));
        return Map.of("dispatcher", "virtual-threads-dispatcher");
    });
}

private val actor = Mono.fromCompletionStage {
    actorSystem.actor<VirtualThreadTestActor, _>()
        .withId("virtual-actor")
        .withDispatcherFromConfig("virtual-threads-dispatcher")
        .spawn()
}.cache()

@GetMapping("/virtual")
fun testVirtual(): Mono<Map<String, Any>> = actor.map { handle ->
    handle.tell(VirtualThreadTestActor.CheckThread("virtual-thread-executor"))
    mapOf("dispatcher" to "virtual-threads-dispatcher")
}

spawn() returns a CompletionStage, so the WebFlux request thread never blocks; cache() keeps the handle for later requests. spawnAndWait() would block the request thread until the actor runs. In a Kotlin suspend function, use awaitSpawn().

docs.title: Things to keep in mind
docs.text:
• A virtual thread that blocks inside a synchronized block or a native call pins its carrier thread. Prefer java.util.concurrent locks in code that blocks on virtual threads.
  • Virtual threads help actors that block (JDBC, HTTP clients). Actors that only compute gain nothing.

docs.title: Try next
docs.text:
• Spawn the actor with withBlockingDispatcher() instead and check that it also runs on a virtual thread (because spring.actor.virtual-threads.enabled is true).
  • Set spring.actor.virtual-threads.enabled: false and repeat: the blocking dispatcher now logs IsVirtual: false.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Dispatchers: default, blocking, named and virtual-thread dispatchers
  • Configuration: every spring.actor.* property

docs.title: AI Agents
docs.text:
This guide shows how the starter's pieces fit together for AI agents: one supervised sharded actor per agent that keeps the conversation, pipeToSelf for model calls, a per-node rate limiter, a human approval step with ask and a timeout, and snapshots that survive a restart.

All Java code on this page is included from the runnable example in example/agent. The Kotlin tabs show the same code in Kotlin, written with the actor-kotlin module; they are not part of the example. The example uses a fake model, so it needs no API key and no network:

./gradlew :example:agent:bootRun   # runs one demo conversation and logs it
./gradlew :example:agent:test      # the tests named at the end of this page

docs.title: Why actors fit agents
docs.text:
An agent is a long conversation with state, slow external calls, and side effects. Actors give you:

  • One owner per conversation. An agent's actor handles one message at a time, so its history needs no locks, even with thousands of agents on one node.
  • Location transparency. With sharding, the cluster keeps exactly one instance of each agent id and routes messages to it, wherever it lives.
  • No blocked threads. A model call can take seconds. The actor sends the call, keeps answering other messages, and handles the reply as a new message.
  • Supervision. If the agent's code throws, a supervisor restarts it from its last snapshot.

docs.title: The model behind an interface
docs.text:
The agent only knows this interface. The example ships a scripted fake; a real provider is another bean that implements it.

JavaKotlin 
/**
 * The only thing an agent knows about the model. Swap the fake for a real provider by adding
 * another bean that implements this interface; the agent code does not change.
 */
public interface LlmClient {

    /**
     * Sends the conversation so far and returns the model's next step. Must not block the
     * caller: the agent pipes the result back to itself.
     */
    CompletionStage<LlmReply> complete(List<ChatMessage> conversation);
}

/**
 * The only thing an agent knows about the model. Swap the fake for a real provider by adding
 * another bean that implements this interface; the agent code does not change.
 */
interface LlmClient {
    /**
     * Sends the conversation so far and returns the model's next step. Must not block the
     * caller: the agent pipes the result back to itself.
     */
    fun complete(conversation: List<ChatMessage>): CompletionStage<LlmReply>
}

The fake model used by the example:

JavaKotlin 
/**
 * A scripted model, so the example runs without an API key or network.
 *
 * <ul>
 *   <li>"weather in <city>" asks for the {@code weather} tool;
 *   <li>"refund <order>" asks for the {@code refund} tool, which needs a human approval;
 *   <li>"my name is <name>" is remembered, and "what is my name?" answers from the conversation;
 *   <li>a tool result is turned into the final answer;
 *   <li>anything else is echoed.
 * </ul>
 */
@Component
public class FakeLlmClient implements LlmClient {

    private final AgentProperties properties;

    public FakeLlmClient(AgentProperties properties) {
        this.properties = properties;
    }

    @Override
    public CompletionStage<LlmReply> complete(List<ChatMessage> conversation) {
        long latencyMillis = properties.getFakeLlmLatency().toMillis();
        return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(
                () -> reply(conversation), CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(latencyMillis, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS));
    }

    static LlmReply reply(List<ChatMessage> conversation) {
        ChatMessage last = conversation.get(conversation.size() - 1);
        if (last.role() == ChatMessage.Role.TOOL_RESULT) {
            return LlmReply.answer("Tool " + last.toolName() + " says: " + last.content());
        }
        String text = last.content().trim();
        String lower = text.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT);
        int weather = lower.indexOf("weather in ");
        if (weather >= 0) {
            String city = text.substring(weather + "weather in ".length()).replaceAll("[?.!]+$", "");
            return LlmReply.callTool("weather", city);
        }
        if (lower.startsWith("refund ")) {
            return LlmReply.callTool("refund", text.substring("refund ".length()));
        }
        if (lower.startsWith("what is my name")) {
            for (int i = conversation.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
                ChatMessage message = conversation.get(i);
                if (message.role() == ChatMessage.Role.USER
                        && message.content().toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT).startsWith("my name is ")) {
                    return LlmReply.answer("Your name is " + message.content().substring("my name is ".length()));
                }
            }
            return LlmReply.answer("You did not tell me your name.");
        }
        if (lower.startsWith("my name is ")) {
            return LlmReply.answer("Nice to meet you, " + text.substring("my name is ".length()));
        }
        return LlmReply.answer("You said: " + text);
    }
}

/**
 * A scripted model, so the example runs without an API key or network.
 *
 * - "weather in <city>" asks for the `weather` tool;
 * - "refund <order>" asks for the `refund` tool, which needs a human approval;
 * - "my name is <name>" is remembered, and "what is my name?" answers from the conversation;
 * - a tool result is turned into the final answer;
 * - anything else is echoed.
 */
@Component
class FakeLlmClient(private val properties: AgentProperties) : LlmClient {

    override fun complete(conversation: List<ChatMessage>): CompletionStage<LlmReply> =
        CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(
            { reply(conversation) },
            CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(properties.fakeLlmLatency.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS),
        )

    companion object {
        fun reply(conversation: List<ChatMessage>): LlmReply {
            val last = conversation.last()
            if (last.role == ChatMessage.Role.TOOL_RESULT) {
                return LlmReply.answer("Tool ${last.toolName} says: ${last.content}")
            }
            val text = last.content.trim()
            val lower = text.lowercase()
            val weather = lower.indexOf("weather in ")
            return when {
                weather >= 0 -> {
                    val city = text.substring(weather + "weather in ".length).replace(Regex("[?.!]+$"), "")
                    LlmReply.callTool("weather", city)
                }
                lower.startsWith("refund ") -> LlmReply.callTool("refund", text.substring("refund ".length))
                lower.startsWith("what is my name") -> {
                    val name = conversation.lastOrNull {
                        it.role == ChatMessage.Role.USER && it.content.lowercase().startsWith("my name is ")
                    }
                    if (name != null) LlmReply.answer("Your name is " + name.content.substring("my name is ".length))
                    else LlmReply.answer("You did not tell me your name.")
                }
                lower.startsWith("my name is ") -> LlmReply.answer("Nice to meet you, " + text.substring("my name is ".length))
                else -> LlmReply.answer("You said: $text")
            }
        }
    }
}

Tools are beans too. A tool that changes the world asks for a human approval first:

JavaKotlin 
/** A function the model may ask the agent to run. */
public interface Tool {

    String name();

    /** Tools that change the world wait for a human to approve the call. */
    default boolean requiresApproval() {
        return false;
    }

    String invoke(String argument);
}

/** A function the model may ask the agent to run. */
interface Tool {
    fun name(): String

    /** Tools that change the world wait for a human to approve the call. */
    fun requiresApproval(): Boolean = false

    fun invoke(argument: String): String
}

docs.title: One sharded actor per agent
docs.text:
Each agent id is a sharded entity. Its behavior is the agent's logic, AgentBrain, under a restart supervisor.

JavaKotlin 
/**
 * One sharded entity per agent id: the cluster keeps exactly one instance of each agent, on
 * some node, and routes every message for that id to it.
 *
 * <p>The agent's logic is {@link AgentBrain}, run under a restart supervisor. If it crashes, the
 * supervisor restarts it and it reloads its conversation from the snapshot store.
 */
@Component
public class AgentActor implements SpringShardedActor<AgentActor.Command> {

    public static final ShardedEntityType<Command> TYPE_KEY = ShardedEntityType.of(Command.class, "Agent");

    /** Commands may cross nodes, so they are JSON serializable. */
    public interface Command extends JsonSerializable {}

    /** A user message. The reply is the agent's final answer for this turn. */
    public static final class Chat extends AskCommand<AgentAnswer> implements Command {
        public final String text;

        @JsonCreator
        public Chat(@JsonProperty("text") String text) {
            this.text = text;
        }
    }

    /** Reads the agent's state. Answered at once, even while an LLM call is pending. */
    public static final class GetConversation extends AskCommand<ConversationView> implements Command {}

    /** Makes the agent throw, to show supervision. */
    public static final class SimulateCrash implements Command {
        @JsonCreator
        public SimulateCrash() {}
    }

    private final AgentBrain.Dependencies dependencies;

    public AgentActor(
            AgentRuntime runtime,
            LlmClient llm,
            ToolRegistry tools,
            AgentSnapshotStore snapshots,
            AgentProperties properties) {
        this.dependencies = new AgentBrain.Dependencies(
                llm,
                tools,
                snapshots,
                runtime.rateLimiter(),
                runtime.approvals(),
                properties.getApprovalTimeout(),
                properties.getMaxToolSteps());
    }

    @Override
    public ShardedEntityType<Command> entityType() {
        return TYPE_KEY;
    }

    @Override
    public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringShardedActorContext<Command> ctx) {
        return AgentBrain.behavior(SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, ctx), ctx.getEntityId(), dependencies);
    }
}

/**
 * One sharded entity per agent id: the cluster keeps exactly one instance of each agent, on
 * some node, and routes every message for that id to it.
 *
 * The agent's logic is [AgentBrain], run under a restart supervisor. If it crashes, the
 * supervisor restarts it and it reloads its conversation from the snapshot store.
 */
@Component
class AgentActor(
    runtime: AgentRuntime,
    llm: LlmClient,
    tools: ToolRegistry,
    snapshots: AgentSnapshotStore,
    properties: AgentProperties,
) : SpringShardedActor<AgentActor.Command> {

    companion object {
        val TYPE_KEY: ShardedEntityType<Command> = ShardedEntityType.of(Command::class.java, "Agent")
    }

    /** Commands may cross nodes, so they are JSON serializable. */
    interface Command : JsonSerializable

    /** A user message. The reply is the agent's final answer for this turn. */
    class Chat @JsonCreator constructor(@JsonProperty("text") val text: String) : AskCommand<AgentAnswer>(), Command

    /** Reads the agent's state. Answered at once, even while an LLM call is pending. */
    class GetConversation : AskCommand<ConversationView>(), Command

    /** Makes the agent throw, to show supervision. */
    class SimulateCrash @JsonCreator constructor() : Command

    private val dependencies = AgentBrain.Dependencies(
        llm,
        tools,
        snapshots,
        runtime.rateLimiter,
        runtime.approvals,
        properties.approvalTimeout,
        properties.maxToolSteps,
    )

    override fun entityType(): ShardedEntityType<Command> = TYPE_KEY

    override fun create(ctx: SpringShardedActorContext<Command>): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
        AgentBrain.behavior(actorBehavior<Command>(ctx), ctx.entityId, dependencies)
}

Callers address agents by id and never need to know which node hosts them:

JavaKotlin 
/** Talks to agents by id. The agent may live on any node of the cluster. */
@Service
public class AgentService {

    private final SpringActorSystem actorSystem;

    public AgentService(SpringActorSystem actorSystem) {
        this.actorSystem = actorSystem;
    }

    public CompletionStage<AgentAnswer> chat(String agentId, String text, Duration timeout) {
        return agent(agentId)
                .ask(new AgentActor.Chat(text))
                .withTimeout(timeout)
                .execute();
    }

    public CompletionStage<ConversationView> conversation(String agentId, Duration timeout) {
        return agent(agentId)
                .ask(new AgentActor.GetConversation())
                .withTimeout(timeout)
                .execute();
    }

    public void simulateCrash(String agentId) {
        agent(agentId).tell(new AgentActor.SimulateCrash());
    }

    private SpringShardedActorHandle<AgentActor.Command> agent(String agentId) {
        return actorSystem.sharded(AgentActor.class).withId(agentId).get();
    }
}

/** Talks to agents by id. The agent may live on any node of the cluster. */
@Service
class AgentService(private val actorSystem: SpringActorSystem) {

    suspend fun chat(agentId: String, text: String, timeout: Duration): AgentAnswer =
        agent(agentId).ask(AgentActor.Chat(text)).withTimeout(timeout).await()

    suspend fun conversation(agentId: String, timeout: Duration): ConversationView =
        agent(agentId).ask(AgentActor.GetConversation()).withTimeout(timeout).await()

    fun simulateCrash(agentId: String) {
        agent(agentId).tell(AgentActor.SimulateCrash())
    }

    private fun agent(agentId: String): SpringShardedActorHandle<AgentActor.Command> =
        actorSystem.sharded<AgentActor, _>().withId(agentId).get()
}

Single node by default

The example sets spring.actor.cluster.join-self: true, so one node forms its own cluster. For more nodes, remove it and list spring.actor.cluster.seed-nodes as in the Sharded Actors guide.

docs.title: The agent loop without blocking
docs.text:
A turn is: user message, rate-limit permit, model call, then either a final answer or a tool call followed by another model call. The model call returns a CompletionStage; pipeToSelf turns its result into a message, so the actor never waits on it.

JavaKotlin 
    private void requestPermit() {
        status = Status.PERMIT;
        deps.rateLimiter().tell(RateLimiterActor.Acquire.replyingTo(permits));
    }

    private SpringActorBehavior<AgentActor.Command> onPermit(PermitGranted granted) {
        if (status != Status.PERMIT) {
            return SpringActorBehavior.same();
        }
        status = Status.LLM;
        ctx.getLog().debug("Agent {} calls the LLM", agentId);
        // The future completes on another thread; pipeToSelf turns it into a message, so
        // the actor never waits and never touches its state from that thread.
        ctx.pipeToSelf(deps.llm().complete(List.copyOf(conversation)), LlmResponded::new);
        return SpringActorBehavior.same();
    }

    private SpringActorBehavior<AgentActor.Command> onLlmResponded(LlmResponded responded) {
        if (status != Status.LLM) {
            return SpringActorBehavior.same(); // a reply for an earlier incarnation
        }
        if (responded.error() != null) {
            finishTurn("Sorry, the model call failed: " + responded.error().getMessage());
            return SpringActorBehavior.same();
        }
        LlmReply reply = responded.reply();
        if (!reply.isToolCall()) {
            finishTurn(reply.text());
            return SpringActorBehavior.same();
        }
        if (++toolSteps > deps.maxToolSteps()) {
            finishTurn("Stopped after " + deps.maxToolSteps() + " tool calls.");
            return SpringActorBehavior.same();
        }
        append(ChatMessage.toolCall(reply.toolName(), reply.toolArgument()));
        Optional<Tool> tool = deps.tools().find(reply.toolName());
        if (tool.isEmpty()) {
            toolResult(reply, "unknown tool");
        } else if (tool.get().requiresApproval()) {
            askForApproval(reply);
        } else {
            runTool(tool.get(), reply);
        }
        return SpringActorBehavior.same();
    }

private fun requestPermit() {
    status = Status.PERMIT
    deps.rateLimiter.tell(RateLimiterActor.Acquire.replyingTo(permits))
}

private fun onPermit(): SpringActorBehavior<AgentActor.Command> {
    if (status != Status.PERMIT) {
        return SpringActorBehavior.same()
    }
    status = Status.LLM
    ctx.log.debug("Agent {} calls the LLM", agentId)
    // The future completes on another thread; pipeToSelf turns it into a message, so
    // the actor never waits and never touches its state from that thread.
    ctx.pipeToSelf(deps.llm.complete(conversation.toList())) { reply, error -> LlmResponded(reply, error) }
    return SpringActorBehavior.same()
}

private fun onLlmResponded(responded: LlmResponded): SpringActorBehavior<AgentActor.Command> {
    if (status != Status.LLM) {
        return SpringActorBehavior.same() // a reply for an earlier incarnation
    }
    val reply = responded.reply
    if (responded.error != null || reply == null) {
        finishTurn("Sorry, the model call failed: ${responded.error?.message}")
        return SpringActorBehavior.same()
    }
    val toolName = reply.toolName
    val toolArgument = reply.toolArgument
    if (toolName == null || toolArgument == null) {
        finishTurn(reply.text.orEmpty())
        return SpringActorBehavior.same()
    }
    if (++toolSteps > deps.maxToolSteps) {
        finishTurn("Stopped after ${deps.maxToolSteps} tool calls.")
        return SpringActorBehavior.same()
    }
    append(ChatMessage.toolCall(toolName, toolArgument))
    val tool = deps.tools.find(toolName).orElse(null)
    when {
        tool == null -> toolResult(reply, "unknown tool")
        tool.requiresApproval() -> askForApproval(reply)
        else -> runTool(tool, reply)
    }
    return SpringActorBehavior.same()
}

While a call is pending the agent still answers GetConversation at once, and a new Chat waits in a queue until the current turn ends.

docs.title: A rate limiter per node
docs.text:
Model providers limit calls per second. Each node spawns one rate limiter actor and every agent on that node asks it for a permit before each call. It keeps a sliding one-second window, so no one-second span ever holds more than agent.calls-per-second calls.

JavaKotlin 
/**
 * One per node: hands out permits for LLM calls, at most {@code agent.calls-per-second} in any
 * one-second window. Requests over the limit wait in a queue; a timer wakes the actor when the
 * oldest permit leaves the window.
 *
 * <p>The starter has no rate limiter, so this is a plain actor with a timer from its behavior context.
 */
@Component
public class RateLimiterActor implements SpringActor<RateLimiterActor.Command> {

    public interface Command {}

    /** Ask for one permit. The reply comes when the call may start. */
    public static final class Acquire extends AskCommand<Permit> implements Command {

        @Nullable private final SpringActorRef<Permit> adapter;

        public Acquire() {
            this(null);
        }

        private Acquire(@Nullable SpringActorRef<Permit> adapter) {
            this.adapter = adapter;
        }

        /** For actors that want the permit as a message instead of a future. */
        public static Acquire replyingTo(SpringActorRef<Permit> replyTo) {
            return new Acquire(replyTo);
        }

        void grant(Permit permit) {
            if (adapter != null) {
                adapter.tell(permit);
            } else {
                reply(permit);
            }
        }
    }

    /** @param grantedAtNanos {@link System#nanoTime()} when the permit was granted */
    public record Permit(long grantedAtNanos) {}

    private enum WakeUp implements Command {
        INSTANCE
    }

    private static final Duration WINDOW = Duration.ofSeconds(1);

    private final int callsPerSecond;

    public RateLimiterActor(AgentProperties properties) {
        this.callsPerSecond = properties.getCallsPerSecond();
    }

    @Override
    public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
        return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                .withState(ctx -> new SlidingWindow(ctx, callsPerSecond, WINDOW.toNanos()))
                .onMessage(Acquire.class, SlidingWindow::onAcquire)
                .onMessage(WakeUp.class, (window, wakeUp) -> window.drain())
                .build();
    }

    private static final class SlidingWindow {
        private final SpringBehaviorContext<Command> ctx;
        private final int limit;
        private final long windowNanos;
        private final Deque<Long> granted = new ArrayDeque<>();
        private final Deque<Acquire> waiting = new ArrayDeque<>();

        SlidingWindow(SpringBehaviorContext<Command> ctx, int limit, long windowNanos) {
            this.ctx = ctx;
            this.limit = limit;
            this.windowNanos = windowNanos;
        }

        SpringActorBehavior<Command> onAcquire(Acquire acquire) {
            waiting.addLast(acquire);
            return drain();
        }

        SpringActorBehavior<Command> drain() {
            long now = System.nanoTime();
            while (!granted.isEmpty() && now - granted.peekFirst() >= windowNanos) {
                granted.removeFirst();
            }
            while (!waiting.isEmpty() && granted.size() < limit) {
                granted.addLast(now);
                waiting.removeFirst().grant(new Permit(now));
            }
            if (!waiting.isEmpty()) {
                long untilFree = windowNanos - (now - granted.peekFirst());
                ctx.startSingleTimer(WakeUp.INSTANCE, WakeUp.INSTANCE, Duration.ofNanos(untilFree));
            }
            return SpringActorBehavior.same();
        }
    }
}

/**
 * One per node: hands out permits for LLM calls, at most `agent.calls-per-second` in any
 * one-second window. Requests over the limit wait in a queue; a timer wakes the actor when the
 * oldest permit leaves the window.
 *
 * The starter has no rate limiter, so this is a plain actor with a timer from its behavior context.
 */
@Component
class RateLimiterActor(properties: AgentProperties) : SpringActor<RateLimiterActor.Command> {

    interface Command

    /** Ask for one permit. The reply comes when the call may start. */
    class Acquire private constructor(private val adapter: SpringActorRef<Permit>?) : AskCommand<Permit>(), Command {
        constructor() : this(null)

        internal fun grant(permit: Permit) {
            if (adapter != null) adapter.tell(permit) else reply(permit)
        }

        companion object {
            /** For actors that want the permit as a message instead of a future. */
            fun replyingTo(replyTo: SpringActorRef<Permit>) = Acquire(replyTo)
        }
    }

    /** @param grantedAtNanos [System.nanoTime] when the permit was granted */
    data class Permit(val grantedAtNanos: Long)

    private data object WakeUp : Command

    private val callsPerSecond = properties.callsPerSecond

    override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
        actorBehavior<Command>(actorContext)
            .withState { ctx -> SlidingWindow(ctx, callsPerSecond, 1.seconds.inWholeNanoseconds) }
            .onMessage(Acquire::class.java) { window, acquire -> window.onAcquire(acquire) }
            .onMessage(WakeUp::class.java) { window, _ -> window.drain() }
            .build()

    private class SlidingWindow(
        private val ctx: SpringBehaviorContext<Command>,
        private val limit: Int,
        private val windowNanos: Long,
    ) {
        private val granted = ArrayDeque<Long>()
        private val waiting = ArrayDeque<Acquire>()

        fun onAcquire(acquire: Acquire): SpringActorBehavior<Command> {
            waiting.addLast(acquire)
            return drain()
        }

        fun drain(): SpringActorBehavior<Command> {
            val now = System.nanoTime()
            while (granted.isNotEmpty() && now - granted.first() >= windowNanos) {
                granted.removeFirst()
            }
            while (waiting.isNotEmpty() && granted.size < limit) {
                granted.addLast(now)
                waiting.removeFirst().grant(Permit(now))
            }
            if (waiting.isNotEmpty()) {
                val untilFree = windowNanos - (now - granted.first())
                ctx.startSingleTimer(WakeUp, WakeUp, Duration.ofNanos(untilFree))
            }
            return SpringActorBehavior.same()
        }
    }
}

The node-local actors are spawned once, when Spring starts:

JavaKotlin 
/**
 * Node-local actors that every agent on this node shares: the LLM rate limiter and the approval
 * gateway. Each node spawns its own, so the rate limit is per node.
 */
@Component
public class AgentRuntime {

    private final SpringActorHandle<RateLimiterActor.Command> rateLimiter;
    private final SpringActorHandle<ApprovalActor.Command> approvals;

    // The actor beans are parameters so Spring registers them before they are spawned here.
    public AgentRuntime(SpringActorSystem actorSystem, RateLimiterActor rateLimiterActor, ApprovalActor approvalActor) {
        this.rateLimiter = actorSystem
                .actor(RateLimiterActor.class)
                .withId("llm-rate-limiter")
                .spawnAndWait();
        this.approvals =
                actorSystem.actor(ApprovalActor.class).withId("approvals").spawnAndWait();
    }

/**
 * Node-local actors that every agent on this node shares: the LLM rate limiter and the approval
 * gateway. Each node spawns its own, so the rate limit is per node.
 */
@Component
class AgentRuntime(
    actorSystem: SpringActorSystem,
    // The actor beans are parameters so Spring registers them before they are spawned here.
    rateLimiterActor: RateLimiterActor,
    approvalActor: ApprovalActor,
) {
    val rateLimiter: SpringActorHandle<RateLimiterActor.Command> =
        actorSystem.actor<RateLimiterActor, _>().withId("llm-rate-limiter").spawnAndWait()
    val approvals: SpringActorHandle<ApprovalActor.Command> =
        actorSystem.actor<ApprovalActor, _>().withId("approvals").spawnAndWait()
}

Per node, not per cluster

With three nodes the cluster can make three times agent.calls-per-second calls. For a cluster-wide limit, run the limiter as a cluster singleton (asClusterSingleton()) instead.

docs.title: A human approval step
docs.text:
When the model asks for a tool that needs approval, the agent asks the node's approval gateway with a timeout. The gateway holds the request until a human answers; if nobody answers in time, the ask fails and the agent tells the model the tool was not run.

JavaKotlin 
    private void askForApproval(LlmReply call) {
        status = Status.APPROVAL;
        PendingApproval request =
                new PendingApproval(agentId + "-" + UUID.randomUUID(), agentId, call.toolName(), call.toolArgument());
        Duration timeout = deps.approvalTimeout();
        ctx.pipeToSelf(
                deps.approvals()
                        .ask(new ApprovalActor.RequestApproval(request, timeout))
                        .withTimeout(timeout)
                        .execute(),
                (ApprovalDecision decision, Throwable error) -> {
                    if (error != null) {
                        return new ApprovalResolved(call, false, "no human answer within " + timeout);
                    }
                    return new ApprovalResolved(
                            call, decision.approved(), decision.approved() ? "approved" : "rejected by a human");
                });
    }

    private SpringActorBehavior<AgentActor.Command> onApprovalResolved(ApprovalResolved resolved) {
        if (status != Status.APPROVAL) {
            return SpringActorBehavior.same();
        }
        LlmReply call = resolved.call();
        Optional<Tool> tool = deps.tools().find(call.toolName());
        if (resolved.approved() && tool.isPresent()) {
            runTool(tool.get(), call);
        } else {
            toolResult(call, "not run: " + resolved.reason());
        }
        return SpringActorBehavior.same();
    }

private fun askForApproval(call: LlmReply) {
    status = Status.APPROVAL
    val request = PendingApproval("$agentId-${UUID.randomUUID()}", agentId, call.toolName!!, call.toolArgument!!)
    val timeout = deps.approvalTimeout
    ctx.pipeToSelf(
        deps.approvals
            .ask(ApprovalActor.RequestApproval(request, timeout))
            .withTimeout(timeout)
            .execute(),
    ) { decision, error ->
        if (error != null || decision == null) {
            ApprovalResolved(call, false, "no human answer within $timeout")
        } else {
            ApprovalResolved(call, decision.approved, if (decision.approved) "approved" else "rejected by a human")
        }
    }
}

private fun onApprovalResolved(resolved: ApprovalResolved): SpringActorBehavior<AgentActor.Command> {
    if (status != Status.APPROVAL) {
        return SpringActorBehavior.same()
    }
    val call = resolved.call
    val tool = deps.tools.find(call.toolName!!).orElse(null)
    if (resolved.approved && tool != null) {
        runTool(tool, call)
    } else {
        toolResult(call, "not run: ${resolved.reason}")
    }
    return SpringActorBehavior.same()
}

The human side, for a controller, a chat bot or a test:

JavaKotlin 
/** The human side of the approval step, for a controller, a Slack bot or a test. */
@Service
public class ApprovalService {

    private static final Duration TIMEOUT = Duration.ofSeconds(3);

    private final AgentRuntime runtime;

    public ApprovalService(AgentRuntime runtime) {
        this.runtime = runtime;
    }

    public CompletionStage<List<PendingApproval>> pending() {
        return runtime.approvals()
                .ask(new ApprovalActor.ListPending())
                .withTimeout(TIMEOUT)
                .execute();
    }

    /** Completes with false if the request is unknown or its timeout has passed. */
    public CompletionStage<Boolean> decide(String requestId, boolean approved) {
        return runtime.approvals()
                .ask(new ApprovalActor.Decide(requestId, approved))
                .withTimeout(TIMEOUT)
                .execute();
    }
}

/** The human side of the approval step, for a controller, a Slack bot or a test. */
@Service
class ApprovalService(private val runtime: AgentRuntime) {

    suspend fun pending(): List<PendingApproval> =
        runtime.approvals.ask(ApprovalActor.ListPending()).withTimeout(TIMEOUT).await()

    /** Returns false if the request is unknown or its timeout has passed. */
    suspend fun decide(requestId: String, approved: Boolean): Boolean =
        runtime.approvals.ask(ApprovalActor.Decide(requestId, approved)).withTimeout(TIMEOUT).await()

    private companion object {
        val TIMEOUT: Duration = Duration.ofSeconds(3)
    }
}

docs.title: Supervision and restarts
docs.text:
The agent's logic runs under a restart supervisor (withSupervisionStrategy). A restart creates the state again with withState, and the state loads the last snapshot:

JavaKotlin 
    /**
     * Restart on failure, at most 10 times a minute. A restart creates the state again, so the
     * brain reloads its conversation from the last snapshot. After the limit the entity stops,
     * and sharding starts a fresh one on the next message.
     */
    public static SpringActorBehavior<AgentActor.Command> behavior(
            SpringActorBehavior.Builder<AgentActor.Command, SpringBehaviorContext<AgentActor.Command>> builder,
            String agentId,
            Dependencies dependencies) {
        return builder.withSupervisionStrategy(SupervisionStrategy.restart().withLimit(10, Duration.ofMinutes(1)))
                .withState(ctx -> new AgentBrain(ctx, agentId, dependencies))
                .onMessage(AgentActor.Chat.class, AgentBrain::onChat)
                .onMessage(AgentActor.GetConversation.class, AgentBrain::onGetConversation)
                .onMessage(AgentActor.SimulateCrash.class, AgentBrain::onSimulateCrash)
                .onMessage(PermitGranted.class, AgentBrain::onPermit)
                .onMessage(LlmResponded.class, AgentBrain::onLlmResponded)
                .onMessage(ApprovalResolved.class, AgentBrain::onApprovalResolved)
                .build();
    }

    private AgentBrain(SpringBehaviorContext<AgentActor.Command> ctx, String agentId, Dependencies dependencies) {
        this.ctx = ctx;
        this.agentId = agentId;
        this.deps = dependencies;
        this.permits = ctx.messageAdapter(RateLimiterActor.Permit.class, PermitGranted::new);
        dependencies.snapshots().load(agentId).ifPresent(snapshot -> conversation.addAll(snapshot.conversation()));
    }

companion object {
    /**
     * Restart on failure, at most 10 times a minute. A restart creates the state again, so the
     * brain reloads its conversation from the last snapshot. After the limit the entity stops,
     * and sharding starts a fresh one on the next message.
     */
    fun behavior(
        builder: SpringActorBehavior.Builder<AgentActor.Command, SpringBehaviorContext<AgentActor.Command>>,
        agentId: String,
        dependencies: Dependencies,
    ): SpringActorBehavior<AgentActor.Command> =
        builder.withSupervisionStrategy(SupervisionStrategy.restart().withLimit(10, 1.minutes.toJavaDuration()))
            .withState { ctx -> AgentBrain(ctx, agentId, dependencies) }
            .onMessage(AgentActor.Chat::class.java) { brain, msg -> brain.onChat(msg) }
            .onMessage(AgentActor.GetConversation::class.java) { brain, msg -> brain.onGetConversation(msg) }
            .onMessage(AgentActor.SimulateCrash::class.java) { brain, _ -> brain.onSimulateCrash() }
            .onMessage(PermitGranted::class.java) { brain, _ -> brain.onPermit() }
            .onMessage(LlmResponded::class.java) { brain, msg -> brain.onLlmResponded(msg) }
            .onMessage(ApprovalResolved::class.java) { brain, msg -> brain.onApprovalResolved(msg) }
            .build()
}

private val permits: SpringActorRef<RateLimiterActor.Permit> =
    ctx.messageAdapter(RateLimiterActor.Permit::class.java) { PermitGranted(it) }
private val conversation = mutableListOf<ChatMessage>()

init {
    deps.snapshots.load(agentId).ifPresent { conversation.addAll(it.conversation) }
}

Every change to the conversation is saved before the agent moves on, so a new actor system finds the agent where it left off:

JavaKotlin 
    /** Every change to the conversation is written before the agent moves on. */
    private void append(ChatMessage message) {
        conversation.add(message);
        deps.snapshots().save(new AgentSnapshot(agentId, List.copyOf(conversation)));
    }

/** Every change to the conversation is written before the agent moves on. */
private fun append(message: ChatMessage) {
    conversation.add(message)
    deps.snapshots.save(AgentSnapshot(agentId, conversation.toList()))
}

The store is an interface. The example writes one JSON file per agent; for a database, implement it with a JPA entity and repository like ActorSnapshot and ActorSnapshotRepository in the persistence example (see also State in a Database).

JavaKotlin 
/**
 * Saves and loads agent snapshots. The example writes JSON files; a JPA implementation with an
 * {@code ActorSnapshot} entity and repository, as in example/persistence, plugs in the same way.
 */
public interface AgentSnapshotStore {

    Optional<AgentSnapshot> load(String agentId);

    void save(AgentSnapshot snapshot);
}

/**
 * Saves and loads agent snapshots. The example writes JSON files; a JPA implementation with an
 * `ActorSnapshot` entity and repository, as in example/persistence, plugs in the same way.
 */
interface AgentSnapshotStore {
    fun load(agentId: String): Optional<AgentSnapshot>

    fun save(snapshot: AgentSnapshot)
}

docs.text: Test Shows AgentConversationTest user message, model reply, tool call, tool result, final answer ConcurrentAgentsTest 100 agents at once, each with its own id and its own history RateLimiterTest no one-second window holds more permits than the limit SlowLlmTest the agent answers other messages while a model call is pending SupervisionTest a crashed agent restarts and reloads its conversation ActorSystemRestartTest the conversation survives a restart of the whole actor system HumanApprovalTest approve, reject, and a timeout when nobody answers

docs.title: What the starter does not provide yet
docs.text:
The example builds these itself:

  • Rate limiting. There is no rate limiter in the starter; the example's is an actor.

docs.title: Kotlin
docs.text: The actor-kotlin module adds a thin Kotlin layer over the Java API: a behavior { } DSL for actor behaviors, suspend functions instead of CompletionStage, reified type parameters instead of Class arguments, and kotlin.time.Duration timeouts. Each function calls the Java API, so everything in the other guides applies unchanged.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Add actor-kotlin next to the starter. It brings kotlinx-coroutines-core; Spring Boot manages its version.

dependencies {
    implementation("io.github.seonwkim:actor-spring-boot-starter:1.0.0")
    implementation("io.github.seonwkim:actor-kotlin:1.0.0")
}

The module is compiled with Kotlin 1.9.25, the version Spring Boot 3.5 manages, so applications on that version or later can use it.

docs.title: Null safety
docs.text:
actor-api declares its nullability: values are non-null unless marked @Nullable (for example AskCommand.getReplyTo()). Kotlin turns those annotations into Kotlin types with the -Xjsr305=strict compiler flag, which projects generated by start.spring.io already set:

kotlin {
    compilerOptions {
        freeCompilerArgs.addAll("-Xjsr305=strict")
    }
}

Without the flag, Kotlin only warns, and the API's types are platform types (String!).

docs.title: Defining an actor
docs.text:
behavior<Command>(actorContext) { ... } builds the behavior with SpringActorBehavior.builder. Commands are often a sealed interface:

@Component
class HelloActor : SpringActor<HelloActor.Command> {
    sealed interface Command

    class SayHello : AskCommand<String>(), Command

    data class LogVisit(val name: String) : Command

    override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
        behavior<Command>(actorContext) {
            onMessage<SayHello> { msg ->
                msg.reply("Hello from actor ${actorContext.actorId()}")
                same()
            }
            onMessage<LogVisit> { msg ->
                log.info("{} visited", msg.name)   // the behavior context is `this`
                same()
            }
        }
}

Inside the block:

DSL Java builder onMessage<M> { msg -> next } .onMessage(M.class, (ctx, msg) -> next) onSignal<PostStop> { signal -> next } .onSignal(PostStop.class, (ctx, signal) -> next) withSupervisionStrategy(strategy) .withSupervisionStrategy(strategy) withMdc { msg -> mapOf(...) } .withMdc(msg -> Map.of(...)) same(), stopped(), unhandled() SpringActorBehavior.same(), .stopped(), .unhandled()

A handler runs with the behavior context as this, so self, log, pipeToSelf(...), watch(...) and the timers need no ctx. prefix. It returns the next behavior: same(), stopped(), unhandled(), or another behavior { } to switch behaviors.

docs.title: State
docs.text:
To keep state in an object, pass a state factory (withState). It runs when the actor starts and again on each restart, and the handlers then run with the state object as this:

override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
    behavior<Command, Counter>(actorContext, state = { ctx -> Counter(ctx) }) {
        onMessage<Add> { msg -> onAdd(msg) }
        onMessage<Get> { msg -> onGet(msg) }
    }

behavior<Command, _> works too: Kotlin infers the state type from the factory.

actorBehavior<Command>(actorContext) returns the Java builder itself, for code that prefers the chained .onMessage(Type::class.java) { ctx, msg -> ... }.build() style.

docs.title: Spawning and finding actors
docs.text:
The reified helpers take the actor type as a type argument. Kotlin can't infer the command type from the actor type by itself, so pass _ for it:

// actorSystem.actor(HelloActor::class.java)
val builder = actorSystem.actor<HelloActor, _>()

// Suspends until the actor runs
val hello: SpringActorHandle<HelloActor.Command> =
    actorSystem.actor<HelloActor, _>().withId("hello").withTimeout(5.seconds).awaitSpawn()

val running = actorSystem.awaitGetOrSpawn<HelloActor, _>("hello") // spawn when none runs
val maybe = actorSystem.awaitGet<HelloActor, _>("hello")          // null when none runs
val exists = actorSystem.awaitExists<HelloActor, _>("hello")

// Sharded actors (cluster mode)
val counter = actorSystem.sharded<CounterActor, _>().withId("counter-1").get()
Kotlin Java API it calls actor<A, _>() actor(A.class) sharded<A, _>() sharded(A.class) awaitGetOrSpawn<A, _>(id), awaitGet<A, _>(id), awaitExists<A, _>(id) getOrSpawn, find (as a nullable), exists with A.class builder.awaitSpawn(), builder.awaitGetOrSpawn() spawn(), getOrSpawn() on the spawn builder behavior<C>(actorContext) { }, behavior<C, S>(actorContext, state = { ctx -> S(ctx) }) { } SpringActorBehavior.builder(C.class, actorContext), then withState, the handlers and build() actorBehavior<C>(actorContext) SpringActorBehavior.builder(C.class, actorContext) handle.child<A, _>(), handle.child<A, _>(id) child(A.class), child(A.class, id) awaitSpawn(), awaitGetOrSpawn(), awaitExists() on a child builder; awaitGet(), awaitExists() on a child reference spawn(), getOrSpawn(), get(), exists() withTimeout(5.seconds), withLimit(10, 1.minutes), startSingleTimer(key, msg, 30.seconds), startTimerAtFixedRate(key, msg, 10.seconds) the same methods with a java.time.Duration unwrap<X>() on the actor system, a ref or a behavior context unwrap(X.class)

docs.title: Child actors
docs.text:
handle.child<A, _>() is the child builder and handle.child<A, _>(id) the lookup reference of Child actors. Outside the parent, the await* functions suspend until the operation completes. A child lookup returns null when the child doesn't run:

// In a suspend function, with the parent's handle
val worker = dispatcher.child<WorkerActor, _>()
    .withId("worker-1")
    .withSupervisionStrategy(SupervisionStrategy.restart().withLimit(10, 1.minutes))
    .withTimeout(5.seconds)
    .awaitGetOrSpawn()

val found: SpringActorHandle<WorkerActor.Command>? = dispatcher.child<WorkerActor, _>("worker-1").awaitGet()
val running: Boolean = dispatcher.child<WorkerActor, _>("worker-1").awaitExists()

Inside the parent's own handlers, don't wait: pass spawn() or getOrSpawn() to pipeToSelf, as in Spawning children from inside the parent.

docs.title: Durations
docs.text:
These methods also take a kotlin.time.Duration: withTimeout on the spawn, sharded, child and ask builders and on the child reference, SupervisionStrategy.restart().withLimit, and the timers on the behavior context:

ctx.startSingleTimer("idle", IdleTimeout, 30.minutes)
ctx.startTimerAtFixedRate("flush", Flush, 10.seconds)

docs.title: Asking
docs.text:
awaitAsk sends an AskCommand and suspends until the reply arrives. Without a timeout, the handle's default timeout (3 seconds) applies.

val greeting: String = hello.awaitAsk(HelloActor.SayHello(), timeout = 2.seconds)

When no reply arrives in time, awaitAsk throws java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException. For a fallback value instead, use the ask builder and finish it with await():

val greeting = hello.ask(HelloActor.SayHello())
    .withTimeout(2.seconds)
    .onTimeout { "no answer" }
    .await()

awaitAsk works the same on a sharded actor handle. Cancelling the coroutine stops the wait; the command has already been sent.

docs.title: In a WebFlux controller
docs.text:
With kotlinx-coroutines-reactor and kotlin-reflect on the classpath, WebFlux runs suspend handler functions:

@RestController
class HelloController(private val actorSystem: SpringActorSystem) {
    @GetMapping("/hello")
    suspend fun hello(): String =
        actorSystem.awaitGetOrSpawn<HelloActor, _>("hello-actor")
            .awaitAsk(HelloActor.SayHello(), timeout = 3.seconds)
}

The full application is in example/kotlin: the simple example, written in Kotlin. The Kotlin example page walks through it.
