docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
The actor-test module has three tools for tests:

  • @ActorTest: a test slice that starts the actor system and your actor beans, and nothing else.
  • ActorCluster: several nodes of your application in one JVM, each on a port it binds itself, for cluster tests.
  • Contract suites: the tests every PeerRegistry and LeaseStore must pass, to run against your own store, plus in-memory fakes of both.

Add it as a test dependency:

GradleMaven 
testImplementation 'io.github.seonwkim:actor-test:1.0.0'

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.seonwkim</groupId>
    <artifactId>actor-test</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0</version>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>

actor-test has no Pekko types in its API. It brings JUnit 5 and Spring Boot's test support, not the starter: your application already has that.

docs.title: Test actors with @ActorTest
docs.text:
@ActorTest works like Spring Boot's @DataJpaTest or @WebMvcTest. It finds your @SpringBootApplication, turns its auto-configuration off and keeps only actor beans from the component scan. You get the SpringActorSystem and every SpringActor and SpringShardedActor bean, without a web server, a DataSource or your services. Only configuration properties, Jackson and Spring's task executor are auto-configured, because the actor system uses them when they are there.

JavaKotlin 
@ActorTest
class GreeterActorTest {

    @Autowired
    SpringActorSystem actorSystem;

    @Test
    void greets() throws Exception {
        String reply = actorSystem.actor(GreeterActor.class)
                .withId("greeter")
                .spawnAndWait()
                .ask(new GreeterActor.Greet("Ada"))
                .execute()
                .toCompletableFuture()
                .get();

        assertThat(reply).isEqualTo("hello Ada");
    }
}

@ActorTest
class GreeterActorTest {

    @Autowired
    lateinit var actorSystem: SpringActorSystem

    @Test
    fun greets() = runBlocking<Unit> {
        val reply: String = actorSystem.actor<GreeterActor, _>()
            .withId("greeter")
            .awaitSpawn()
            .awaitAsk(GreeterActor.Greet("Ada"))

        assertThat(reply).isEqualTo("hello Ada")
    }
}

In Kotlin, runBlocking (from kotlinx-coroutines-core, which actor-kotlin brings) runs the suspend calls in the test. Name actors to start only those, and add properties:

JavaKotlin 
@ActorTest(actors = GreeterActor.class, properties = "spring.actor.name=greeter-test")

@ActorTest(actors = [GreeterActor::class], properties = ["spring.actor.name=greeter-test"])

An actor that needs another bean gets it with @Import(MyService.class) or @MockitoBean. includeFilters, excludeFilters and excludeAutoConfiguration work as on Spring Boot's own slices.

The actor system is the one your application's auto-configuration starts: the slice imports the same actor auto-configurations, so spring.actor.* properties from application.yml apply.

docs.title: Cluster tests with ActorCluster
docs.text:
ActorCluster starts several Spring contexts of your application in one JVM. Each node binds port 0, so the operating system gives it a free port as it binds and no other test or process can take that port in between. Node 1 joins itself (spring.actor.cluster.join-self) and forms the cluster at once; the others join it at the address it bound. start() returns when every node sees every node up. With Pekko Management on the classpath, each node's management server binds port 0 too.

With JUnit 5, register ActorClusterExtension. On an instance field it starts a cluster for each test; on a static field (in Kotlin, a @JvmField in a companion object), one for the whole class.

JavaKotlin 
class ShardedCounterClusterTest {

    @RegisterExtension
    final ActorClusterExtension cluster = new ActorClusterExtension(
            ActorCluster.builder(MyApplication.class)
                    .nodes(3)
                    .roles(1, "frontend")
                    .properties("app.feature.enabled=true"));

    @Test
    void anEntityKeepsItsStateWhenANodeLeaves() {
        SpringActorSystem first = cluster.node(1).getBean(SpringActorSystem.class);
        // ... message a sharded entity from node 1

        cluster.cluster().stop(2);
        cluster.cluster().awaitMembersUp(2);
        // ... the entity answers from another node
    }
}

class ShardedCounterClusterTest {

    @JvmField
    @RegisterExtension
    val cluster = ActorClusterExtension(
        ActorCluster.builder(MyApplication::class.java)
            .nodes(3)
            .roles(1, "frontend")
            .properties("app.feature.enabled=true"))

    @Test
    fun anEntityKeepsItsStateWhenANodeLeaves() {
        val first = cluster.node(1).getBean(SpringActorSystem::class.java)
        // ... message a sharded entity from node 1

        cluster.cluster().stop(2)
        cluster.cluster().awaitMembersUp(2)
        // ... the entity answers from another node
    }
}

Without JUnit, use it directly; it is AutoCloseable:

JavaKotlin 
try (ActorCluster cluster = ActorCluster.builder(MyApplication.class).nodes(3).start()) {
    // ...
}

ActorCluster.builder(MyApplication::class.java).nodes(3).start().use { cluster ->
    // ...
}
Builder method What it sets nodes(int) Number of nodes, 3 by default systemName(String) The actor system name of every node properties(String...) key=value properties for every node nodeProperties(int, String...) Properties for one node, numbered from 1 roles(int, String...) Cluster roles of one node timeout(Duration) How long to wait for members to be up, 30 seconds by default classLoader(int, ClassLoader) The class loader one node, numbered from 1, loads your classes through. Use it to run two versions of a class side by side

The properties are passed as command-line arguments, so they override your application.yml. The cluster tracks membership through the starter's cluster events: upMembers(node) is the number of members a node sees up, and awaitMembersUp(count) waits until every running node sees that many.

docs.title: Two versions of a message in one cluster
docs.text:
To check that a message change survives a rolling update, run one node on the next version of the message class. Compile the new version into its own folder (for example with javax.tools.JavaCompiler in the test), and give that node a class loader that loads the class from there and every other class from your application:

JavaKotlin 
ClassLoader v2 = new ClassLoader(getClass().getClassLoader()) {
    @Override
    protected Class<?> loadClass(String name, boolean resolve) throws ClassNotFoundException {
        if (!name.equals(SayHello.class.getName())) {
            return super.loadClass(name, resolve);
        }
        synchronized (getClassLoadingLock(name)) {
            Class<?> loaded = findLoadedClass(name);
            if (loaded == null) {
                byte[] bytes = readClassFile(v2Classes, name); // your helper: the .class file's bytes
                loaded = defineClass(name, bytes, 0, bytes.length);
            }
            return loaded;
        }
    }
};

try (ActorCluster cluster = ActorCluster.builder(MyApplication.class)
        .nodes(2)
        .classLoader(2, v2)
        .start()) {
    // Node 1 sends the old SayHello to an entity on node 2, and node 2 sends the new one
    // (created through v2.loadClass(...)) to an entity on node 1.
}

val v2 = object : ClassLoader(javaClass.classLoader) {
    override fun loadClass(name: String, resolve: Boolean): Class<*> {
        if (name != SayHello::class.java.name) {
            return super.loadClass(name, resolve)
        }
        synchronized(getClassLoadingLock(name)) {
            return findLoadedClass(name) ?: readClassFile(v2Classes, name) // your helper: the .class file's bytes
                .let { bytes -> defineClass(name, bytes, 0, bytes.size) }
        }
    }
}

ActorCluster.builder(MyApplication::class.java)
    .nodes(2)
    .classLoader(2, v2)
    .start()
    .use { cluster ->
        // Node 1 sends the old SayHello to an entity on node 2, and node 2 sends the new one
        // (created through v2.loadClass(...)) to an entity on node 1.
    }

Put the entities on a given node with a role (roles(1, "v1") and role() on the sharded actor), so each message really crosses between the versions. The starter's own build runs this test (MixedVersionMessageTest in actor-cluster).

docs.title: Contract suites for your own store
docs.text:
A PeerRegistry or LeaseStore of your own (Cluster Formation, Split Brain and Leases) must behave like the built-in ones: for example, of twenty nodes that try to take a lease at once, exactly one wins. actor-test publishes the tests the built-in JDBC and Redis stores pass. Extend the suite and return your store:

JavaKotlinJavaKotlin 
class MyLeaseStoreContractTest extends LeaseStoreContract {

    private final MyLeaseStore store = new MyLeaseStore(testDatabase());

    @Override
    protected LeaseStore store() {
        return store;
    }
}

class MyLeaseStoreContractTest : LeaseStoreContract() {

    private val store = MyLeaseStore(testDatabase())

    override fun store(): LeaseStore = store
}

class MyPeerRegistryContractTest extends PeerRegistryContract {

    @Override
    protected PeerRegistry registry() {
        return new MyPeerRegistry(testDatabase());
    }
}

class MyPeerRegistryContractTest : PeerRegistryContract() {

    override fun registry(): PeerRegistry = MyPeerRegistry(testDatabase())
}

Each test uses its own lease or service name, so one store may serve every test. Some tests wait for a ttl of one to two seconds to pass, because stores may keep time in whole seconds.

InMemoryPeerRegistry and InMemoryLeaseStore pass the same suites. Declare one as a bean to run cluster tests with discovery.method: custom or lease.store: custom without a database; nodes in one JVM can share one instance.

docs.title: Cluster Formation
docs.text:
A node joins a cluster in one of two ways, set by spring.actor.cluster.join:

join How the node finds the cluster Use it when seed-nodes (default) The addresses in spring.actor.cluster.seed-nodes Nodes have fixed addresses discovery Peers found through spring.actor.cluster.discovery.method, then Pekko Cluster Bootstrap forms or joins the cluster Nodes come and go with changing addresses (Kubernetes, autoscaling groups)

docs.title: Joining through a store you already run
docs.text:
With discovery.method set to jdbc or redis, each node writes its own entry to a table or a Redis key, and reads the others' entries to find its peers. This needs no Kubernetes API access (no RBAC) and no DNS setup: only the store the application already uses, and network access between the nodes.

What each node does:

  1. At startup it registers itself (its management host and the port its management server bound) and starts Cluster Bootstrap.
  2. Every heartbeat-interval (default 5s) it renews its entry.
  3. Bootstrap lists the entries renewed within ttl (default 30s), contacts those nodes on their management port, and either joins the cluster they are in or, if there is none yet, the node with the lowest address forms it.
  4. On a graceful shutdown it deletes its entry first, so new nodes no longer contact it. A node that crashes stops renewing, and its entry is ignored once it is older than the ttl.

Times come from the store's clock (the database's CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, Redis TIME), so the nodes' clocks need not agree.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
Discovery uses Pekko Cluster Bootstrap and the management HTTP server, plus the module of your store:

GradleMaven 
implementation("io.github.seonwkim:actor-spring-boot-starter-cluster:$version")
implementation("org.apache.pekko:pekko-management-cluster-bootstrap_3:1.1.1")
implementation("org.apache.pekko:pekko-management-cluster-http_3:1.1.1")
implementation("io.github.seonwkim:actor-jdbc:$version")   // or actor-redis

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.seonwkim</groupId>
    <artifactId>actor-jdbc</artifactId> <!-- or actor-redis -->
    <version>${actor.version}</version>
</dependency>

actor-jdbc uses the application's DataSource, and actor-redis its RedisConnectionFactory (spring-boot-starter-data-redis).

docs.title: JDBC
docs.text:
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/orders
  actor:
    name: orders
    provider: cluster
    cluster:
      join: discovery
      discovery:
        method: jdbc
    jdbc:
      initialize-schema: always   # default: embedded (only H2, HSQLDB, Derby)
    pekko:
      management:
        http:
          port: 7626

The entries live in the actor_peer table. spring.actor.jdbc.initialize-schema decides when the starter creates it: embedded (the default) only in an embedded database, always, or never. With never, create it yourself, for example in a Flyway or Liquibase migration, from the schema file for your database in the actor-jdbc jar: io/github/seonwkim/actor/jdbc/schema-{h2,postgresql,mysql,mariadb}.sql.

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS actor_peer (
    service_name VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    node_id VARCHAR(500) NOT NULL,
    host VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    port INT NOT NULL,
    last_seen TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (service_name, node_id)
);

A node that crashes leaves its row behind; it is ignored once it is older than the ttl, and you can delete old rows at any time.

docs.title: Redis
docs.text:
spring:
  data:
    redis:
      host: redis
  actor:
    name: orders
    provider: cluster
    cluster:
      join: discovery
      discovery:
        method: redis

Each node is a hash under actor:peer:<service>:<node address> that expires after the ttl, so a crashed node's entry removes itself. The starter reads the keys with SCAN, which sees one server: use a single Redis or a primary with replicas (Sentinel), not Redis Cluster.

docs.title: Your own store
docs.text:
Implement io.github.seonwkim.actor.spi.PeerRegistry (in actor-api, no Pekko types) and declare it as a bean. Set discovery.method: custom. A PeerRegistry bean of your own also replaces the jdbc and redis stores.

JavaKotlin 
@Bean
PeerRegistry peerRegistry(MyStore store) {
    return new PeerRegistry() {
        public void register(Peer peer) { store.upsert(peer); }       // also marks it seen now
        public void deregister(Peer peer) { store.delete(peer); }
        public List<Peer> peers(String service, Duration ttl) { return store.seenWithin(service, ttl); }
    };
}

@Bean
fun peerRegistry(store: MyStore): PeerRegistry = object : PeerRegistry {
    override fun register(peer: Peer) = store.upsert(peer)            // also marks it seen now
    override fun deregister(peer: Peer) = store.delete(peer)
    override fun peers(service: String, ttl: Duration): List<Peer> = store.seenWithin(service, ttl)
}

MyStore stands for your own storage code. A Peer is the service name, the node id, and the management host and port. heartbeat(peer) runs every heartbeat-interval and calls register unless you override it.

Methods may block: the starter calls them on the blocking dispatcher. The starter owns the timers and the shutdown hook; a store only stores and reads entries. Run PeerRegistryContract from actor-test against your store to check it behaves like the built-in ones (see Testing).

docs.title: Other discovery methods
docs.text:
discovery.method also accepts Pekko's own methods. Each needs its library and its Pekko settings:

method Pekko method Library kubernetes-api kubernetes-api pekko-discovery-kubernetes-api_3 (the pods' service account needs RBAC to list pods) dns pekko-dns built in config config built in; peers under spring.actor.pekko.discovery.config.services

docs.title: Properties
docs.text: Key Default Meaning spring.actor.cluster.join seed-nodes seed-nodes or discovery spring.actor.cluster.seed-nodes none Addresses to join, as pekko://<name>@<host>:<port> spring.actor.cluster.discovery.method none jdbc, redis, custom, kubernetes-api, dns or config spring.actor.cluster.discovery.heartbeat-interval 5s How often a node renews its entry spring.actor.cluster.discovery.ttl 30s Entries older than this are ignored spring.actor.cluster.join-self false Form a one-node cluster without seed nodes, for local runs and tests spring.actor.cluster.roles none Roles of this node, for sharded actors and singletons spring.actor.jdbc.initialize-schema embedded When to create actor_peer and actor_lease: embedded, always, never

docs.title: What the nodes need
docs.text:
• Management port (Pekko's default 7626, spring.actor.pekko.management.http.port): Bootstrap contacts peers there. spring.actor.pekko.management.http.hostname must be an address other nodes can reach (the default is the machine's address). With jdbc or redis discovery the port may be 0: the node registers the port it bound.
  • Remoting port (spring.actor.remote.port, default 25520) between all nodes.
  • The store (database or Redis) from every node.
  • The nodes of one cluster use the same spring.actor.name: it is the service name their entries are stored under.

The Kubernetes example has ready-made overlays for both stores, with the NetworkPolicies: see example/kubernetes/overlays/discovery-jdbc and discovery-redis and the "Without RBAC" section of its README.

Bootstrap waits for pekko.management.cluster.bootstrap.contact-point-discovery.required-contact-point-nr (default 2) peers before it forms a new cluster. Set it to 1 for a single replica.

With join: discovery, the split brain resolver defaults to keep-majority. To choose another strategy, or to keep singletons and shards on one node with a lease, see Split Brain and Leases.

docs.title: Securing the discovery store
docs.text:
With jdbc or redis discovery, the store decides which hosts a new node contacts and joins: Bootstrap trusts every entry it reads. Leases in the same store (Split Brain and Leases) decide which node may run a singleton or a shard, or stays up after a split. So whoever can write actor_peer, actor_lease or the actor:peer: and actor:lease: keys can point new nodes at a host they control, or take a lease. Treat the store as part of the cluster's trust boundary: only the nodes write to it.

Remoting (25520) accepts any connection unless you set up Pekko's TLS transport (spring.actor.pekko.remote.artery.transport: tls-tcp and its ssl settings), and the management port (7626) has no authentication. So the store's permissions and the network rules (only the cluster's nodes reach these ports) are the controls.

Redis. Give the nodes a dedicated ACL user that can touch only the starter's keys and run only the commands the stores use:

ACL SETUSER actor-store on >change-me resetkeys ~actor:peer:* ~actor:lease:* resetchannels -@all +@connection +time +scan +hgetall +get +set +del +eval +evalsha +hset +pexpire
  • HSET, PEXPIRE, GET and DEL also run inside the stores' Lua scripts, and Redis checks a script's commands against the same ACL.
  • Turn on TLS (spring.data.redis.ssl.enabled: true) and auth (spring.data.redis.username, password).
  • Don't share the Redis database with untrusted writers. SCAN lists key names of the whole database, whatever the user's key patterns.

JDBC. Give the nodes a database user with rights only on the two tables, and create the tables from your migrations with another user (spring.actor.jdbc.initialize-schema: never):

-- PostgreSQL
CREATE ROLE actor_store LOGIN PASSWORD 'change-me';
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON actor_peer, actor_lease TO actor_store;

-- MySQL / MariaDB (orders is the schema)
CREATE USER 'actor_store'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY 'change-me';
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON orders.actor_peer TO 'actor_store'@'%';
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON orders.actor_lease TO 'actor_store'@'%';

No user that untrusted code can reach (another service, a reporting tool, an admin console) should be able to write these tables.

The built-in stores use the application's DataSource and RedisConnectionFactory, so these rights are the rights of the user the application connects as. If the application needs more rights on the same server, give the stores their own connection: declare PeerRegistry and LeaseStore beans built on a separate DataSource or RedisConnectionFactory (new JdbcPeerRegistry(dataSource), new JdbcLeaseStore(dataSource), new RedisPeerRegistry(connectionFactory, ttl), new RedisLeaseStore(connectionFactory)) and set discovery.method: custom and lease.store: custom (see Your own store).

docs.title: Replicated Data
docs.text:
Replicated data is a map, a counter or a set that every node of the cluster keeps a copy of. Any node reads and writes its own copy without a round trip, and the copies converge: changes made on different nodes at the same time are merged, never lost. These are Pekko Distributed Data's CRDTs (conflict-free replicated data types) behind a small API with no Pekko types.

Use it for small, shared, often-read state: feature flags, who is online, rate-limit counters, a cache of settings. It is not a database: the data lives in memory and is gone when every node stops.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Replicated data needs the cluster starter and cluster mode:

spring:
  actor:
    provider: cluster

The starter then provides a ReplicatedData bean. Each node starts Pekko's replicator when its actor system starts.

docs.title: Maps, counters and sets
docs.text:
ReplicatedData hands out a handle per name. Declare the handles you use as beans and inject them where you need them:

JavaKotlin 
@Configuration
class ReplicatedDataConfig {

    @Bean
    ReplicatedMap<String, Cart> carts(ReplicatedData data) {
        return data.map("carts");
    }

    @Bean
    ReplicatedCounter visits(ReplicatedData data) {
        return data.counter("visits");
    }

    @Bean
    ReplicatedSet<String> onlineUsers(ReplicatedData data) {
        return data.set("online-users");
    }
}

@Configuration
class ReplicatedDataConfig {

    @Bean
    fun carts(data: ReplicatedData): ReplicatedMap<String, Cart> = data.map("carts")

    @Bean
    fun visits(data: ReplicatedData): ReplicatedCounter = data.counter("visits")

    @Bean
    fun onlineUsers(data: ReplicatedData): ReplicatedSet<String> = data.set("online-users")
}

Or inject ReplicatedData and ask for a handle when the name is only known at run time, such as one counter per tenant: data.counter("requests-" + tenantId). A handle is a cheap view: two handles with the same name and kind read and write the same data. Use each name for one kind only.

Every read and write returns a CompletionStage:

JavaKotlin 
@Service
class CartService {
    private final ReplicatedMap<String, Cart> carts;

    CartService(ReplicatedMap<String, Cart> carts) {
        this.carts = carts;
    }

    CompletionStage<Void> save(String user, Cart cart) {
        return carts.put(user, cart);
    }

    CompletionStage<Optional<Cart>> find(String user) {
        return carts.get(user);
    }
}

@Service
class CartService(private val carts: ReplicatedMap<String, Cart>) {

    // await() is kotlinx.coroutines.future.await (kotlinx-coroutines-core, which actor-kotlin brings)
    suspend fun save(user: String, cart: Cart) {
        carts.put(user, cart).await()
    }

    suspend fun find(user: String): Cart? = carts.get(user).await().orElse(null)
}
Type Reads Writes When two nodes write at once ReplicatedMap<K, V> entries(), get(key) put(key, value), remove(key) The later write to a key wins, by wall clock ReplicatedCounter value() increment(delta), decrement(delta) Both changes count ReplicatedSet<E> elements() add(element), remove(element) An add wins over a concurrent remove

A map, counter or set nobody has written yet reads as empty (or zero).

docs.title: Consistency
docs.text:
Each read and write takes an optional Consistency: how many nodes to wait for.

Consistency Waits for Use it when local() (default) This node only Fast reads and writes; other nodes see the change shortly after, in the background majority(timeout) More than half of the nodes A write followed by a read on another node must see it all(timeout) Every node Rarely: one unreachable node makes it fail JavaKotlin 
Consistency majority = Consistency.majority(Duration.ofSeconds(3));

carts.put("alice", cart, majority);   // on node A
carts.get("alice", majority);         // on node B: sees the write

val majority = Consistency.majority(Duration.ofSeconds(3))

carts.put("alice", cart, majority)   // on node A
carts.get("alice", majority)         // on node B: sees the write

A majority write followed by a majority read always sees the write, because the two majorities share at least one node. If the nodes don't answer within the timeout, the stage completes with ReplicationTimeoutException. A write that times out is still applied on this node and spreads to the others later; it is not rolled back.

docs.title: What can be stored
docs.text:
Keys, values and set elements travel between nodes, so they must be serializable: String, Integer, Long, or a type that implements JsonSerializable or CborSerializable, the same as actor messages. Values that implement JsonSerializable use your application's ObjectMapper.

JavaKotlin 
public record Cart(List<String> items, int quantity) implements JsonSerializable {}

data class Cart(val items: List<String>, val quantity: Int) : JsonSerializable

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Small data. Each node holds every entry, a new node receives all of them, and a change can send a whole map or set to the other nodes. Keep each one to thousands of entries, not millions; split big data over several names.
  • In memory. The data survives a node restart while other nodes keep it, and is lost when all nodes stop. Keep the source of truth in a database.
  • Clock skew. A map decides concurrent writes to the same key by wall clock, so keep the nodes' clocks in sync (NTP).

docs.title: Tuning
docs.text:
Pekko's settings under pekko.cluster.distributed-data apply through the raw override, for example a shorter gossip interval:

spring:
  actor:
    pekko:
      cluster:
        distributed-data:
          gossip-interval: 1s

docs.text:

  • Sharded Actors: one owner per key, for state that must not merge
  • Cluster Formation: forming the cluster the data is replicated over

docs.title: Sharded Actors
docs.text:
A sharded actor is an actor type whose instances, called entities, are spread over the nodes of a cluster. Each entity has an id. The cluster runs at most one entity per id at a time, starts it on its first message, and moves it when nodes join or leave. You send a message to an id from any node, and it reaches the entity wherever it runs.

Use sharding when you have many things that each need their own actor: users, orders, devices, chat rooms. It spreads them over the nodes, so you scale out by adding nodes.

For one actor for the whole cluster, use a cluster singleton instead. For actors that live on one node only, use regular actors (Actors).

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Sharded actors need the cluster starter:

GradleMaven 
implementation("io.github.seonwkim:actor-spring-boot-starter-cluster:$version")

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.seonwkim</groupId>
    <artifactId>actor-spring-boot-starter-cluster</artifactId>
    <version>${actor.version}</version>
</dependency>

Then run the actor system in cluster mode. This is the configuration of the cluster example, three nodes on one machine:

spring:
  actor:
    name: spring-pekko-example
    provider: cluster
    remote:
      hostname: 127.0.0.1
      port: 2551
    cluster:
      seed-nodes:
        - pekko://spring-pekko-example@127.0.0.1:2551
        - pekko://spring-pekko-example@127.0.0.1:2552
        - pekko://spring-pekko-example@127.0.0.1:2553
      downing:
        strategy: keep-majority

Each node uses its own remote.port (2551, 2552, 2553) and the same spring.actor.name. See Cluster Formation for joining without fixed addresses, and Split Brain and Leases for the downing strategy.

docs.title: Write a sharded actor
docs.text:
Implement SpringShardedActor and annotate the class with @Component. The starter registers every sharded actor bean with the cluster when the actor system starts.

JavaKotlin 
@Component
public class HelloActor implements SpringShardedActor<HelloActor.Command> {

    public static final ShardedEntityType<Command> TYPE_KEY =
            ShardedEntityType.of(Command.class, "HelloActor");

    public interface Command extends JsonSerializable {}

    public static class SayHello extends AskCommand<String> implements Command {
        public final String message;

        public SayHello(String message) {
            this.message = message;
        }
    }

    @Override
    public ShardedEntityType<Command> entityType() {
        return TYPE_KEY;
    }

    @Override
    public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringShardedActorContext<Command> ctx) {
        String entityId = ctx.getEntityId();
        return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, ctx)
                .onMessage(SayHello.class, (behaviorCtx, msg) -> {
                    String reply = "Received from entity [" + entityId + "] on node ["
                            + behaviorCtx.nodeAddress() + "]";
                    behaviorCtx.getLog().info(reply);
                    msg.reply(reply);
                    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                })
                .build();
    }
}

@Component
class HelloActor : SpringShardedActor<HelloActor.Command> {

    companion object {
        val TYPE_KEY: ShardedEntityType<Command> = ShardedEntityType.of(Command::class.java, "HelloActor")
    }

    sealed interface Command : JsonSerializable

    class SayHello(val message: String) : AskCommand<String>(), Command

    override fun entityType(): ShardedEntityType<Command> = TYPE_KEY

    override fun create(ctx: SpringShardedActorContext<Command>): SpringActorBehavior<Command> {
        val entityId = ctx.entityId
        return actorBehavior<Command>(ctx)
            .onMessage(SayHello::class.java) { behaviorCtx, msg ->
                val reply = "Received from entity [$entityId] on node [${behaviorCtx.nodeAddress()}]"
                behaviorCtx.log.info(reply)
                msg.reply(reply)
                SpringActorBehavior.same()
            }
            .build()
    }
}

What differs from a regular actor:

Part What it does ShardedEntityType.of(Command.class, "HelloActor") Names the entity type and its message type. Nodes reach the same entities when they use the same name, so keep it stable across deployments. entityType() Returns that type. create(SpringShardedActorContext<T>) Builds the behavior of one entity, on the node that hosts it. ctx.getEntityId() is the entity's id (also ctx.actorId()), and the same SpringActorBehavior builder works as for a regular actor, withState included. sharding() Optional: how ids map to shards. Default ShardingStrategy.defaults(), 100 shards. role() Optional: the cluster role whose nodes host the entities. Default: every node.

Messages cross the network, so the command interface extends JsonSerializable (or CborSerializable), and so do the replies when they are not String or a number.

docs.title: Send messages
docs.text:
actorSystem.sharded(HelloActor.class).withId(id).get() returns a handle to the entity with that id. Getting a handle does not start the entity and costs nearly nothing: the entity starts on its first message.

JavaKotlin 
@Service
public class HelloService {

    private final SpringActorSystem actorSystem;

    public HelloService(SpringActorSystem actorSystem) {
        this.actorSystem = actorSystem;
    }

    public Mono<String> hello(String message, String entityId) {
        SpringShardedActorHandle<HelloActor.Command> entity =
                actorSystem.sharded(HelloActor.class).withId(entityId).get();

        CompletionStage<String> reply = entity
                .ask(new HelloActor.SayHello(message))
                .withTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3))
                .onTimeout(() -> "Request timed out for entity: " + entityId)
                .execute();

        return Mono.fromCompletionStage(reply);
    }
}

@Service
class HelloService(private val actorSystem: SpringActorSystem) {

    suspend fun hello(message: String, entityId: String): String {
        val entity = actorSystem.sharded<HelloActor, _>().withId(entityId).get()
        return entity.ask(HelloActor.SayHello(message))
            .withTimeout(3.seconds)
            .onTimeout { "Request timed out for entity: $entityId" }
            .await()
    }
}

The handle has tell, ask, entityId() and entityType(). withTimeout on the builder sets the default ask timeout of the handle (3 seconds otherwise).

There is no spawn, exists or stop for an entity, and no need to cache handles: get one per request.

Regular actor Sharded entity Created By you, with spawn() or getOrSpawn() By the cluster, on its first message Where it runs The node that spawned it One node of the cluster, chosen by its shard How many per id One per node One per cluster Handle From spawn, get or getOrSpawn From sharded(...).withId(id).get(), any time Messages Any Java object Serializable (JsonSerializable, CborSerializable)

docs.title: Shards and ids
docs.text:
Entities are grouped into shards: a hash of the entity id picks the shard, and the cluster places whole shards on nodes. When a node joins or leaves, shards move, and their entities start again on their new node on the next message.

JavaKotlin 
@Override
public ShardingStrategy sharding() {
    return ShardingStrategy.hashed(300);
}

override fun sharding(): ShardingStrategy = ShardingStrategy.hashed(300)
  • Use about ten times the largest number of nodes you expect. The default is 100.
  • Every node must use the same strategy for an entity type, and it must stay the same across deployments: a different number of shards sends the same id to a different shard.
  • Pick ids with many distinct values, such as user ids or order numbers, so the entities spread evenly.

docs.title: Run entities on some nodes only
docs.text:
Override role() and give the hosting nodes that role:

JavaKotlin 
@Override
public Optional<String> role() {
    return Optional.of("backend");
}

override fun role(): Optional<String> = Optional.of("backend")

spring:
  actor:
    cluster:
      roles: [backend]

Nodes without the role still send messages to the entities, through a proxy; they just don't host any.

docs.title: State and passivation
docs.text:
An entity's state lives in memory. It is lost when the entity stops: when its shard moves to another node, when its node stops, or when the entity is passivated.

Passivation is Pekko's: an entity that receives no message for a while is stopped to free memory, and started again on its next message. Pekko's default idle timeout is 2 minutes. Change it with the raw key:

spring:
  actor:
    pekko:
      cluster:
        sharding:
          passivation:
            default-idle-strategy:
              idle-entity:
                timeout: 10m

When the state must survive, load it when the entity starts and save it when it changes, as in State in a Database, or use an event-sourced actor.

docs.title: One entity per id, even in a split
docs.text: In a network split, both sides may start the same shard. A downing strategy stops one side; with spring.actor.cluster.sharding.use-lease: true, each shard also takes a lease before it starts its entities, so a shard never runs on two nodes. See Split Brain and Leases.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text: With actor-metrics and Micrometer, each node reports actor.sharding.regions, actor.sharding.shards and actor.sharding.entities, tagged type with the entity type name. The actors Actuator endpoint lists, for each entity type, the regions and the shards and entities on this node. See Monitoring.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Unstable names or shard counts. Renaming the entity type or changing the number of shards sends existing ids to other entities. Keep both fixed.
  • Blocking in an entity. Entities run on the default dispatcher. Use a non-blocking client, or hand the blocking call off and send the result back with pipeToSelf (see State in a Database).
  • Many messages between entities. Every message to another entity may cross the network. Keep what is used together in one entity.
  • Holding state only in memory. It is gone after passivation or a move. Store what must survive.

docs.title: Cluster Singletons
docs.text:
A cluster singleton is an actor that runs on exactly one node of the cluster. Every node can send it messages through a proxy, and when the node that runs it leaves or fails, the singleton starts again on another node.

Use a singleton for work that must happen once for the whole cluster:

  • a coordinator that hands out work or ids,
  • a scheduler that runs a job every few minutes,
  • an aggregator that collects numbers from every node,
  • a cluster-wide limit, such as a rate limiter shared by all nodes.

Don't use one for work that grows with your traffic. A singleton is one actor on one node: every message for it goes through that node, one at a time. For many independent things (users, orders, devices), use sharded actors instead: one entity per id, spread over the nodes.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Singletons need the cluster starter and cluster mode:

GradleMaven 
implementation("io.github.seonwkim:actor-spring-boot-starter-cluster:$version")

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.seonwkim</groupId>
    <artifactId>actor-spring-boot-starter-cluster</artifactId>
    <version>${actor.version}</version>
</dependency>

spring:
  actor:
    name: orders
    provider: cluster
    remote:
      hostname: 127.0.0.1
      port: 2551
    cluster:
      seed-nodes:
        - pekko://orders@127.0.0.1:2551
        - pekko://orders@127.0.0.1:2552
      downing:
        strategy: keep-majority

See Cluster Formation for how nodes find each other, and Split Brain and Leases for the downing strategy.

docs.title: Write the actor
docs.text:
A singleton is a regular actor. Nothing in the class says it is a singleton: you choose that when you spawn it. Its messages cross the network, so they must be serializable (JsonSerializable or CborSerializable), the same as for sharded actors.

This one is adapted from the cluster example:

JavaKotlin 
@Component
public class ClusterMetricsAggregator implements SpringActor<ClusterMetricsAggregator.Command> {

    public interface Command extends JsonSerializable {}

    public static class RecordMetric implements Command {
        public final String nodeAddress;
        public final String metricName;
        public final long value;

        public RecordMetric(String nodeAddress, String metricName, long value) {
            this.nodeAddress = nodeAddress;
            this.metricName = metricName;
            this.value = value;
        }
    }

    public static class GetTotal extends AskCommand<Long> implements Command {
        public final String metricName;

        public GetTotal(String metricName) {
            this.metricName = metricName;
        }
    }

    @Override
    public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
        Map<String, Long> totals = new HashMap<>();
        return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                .onMessage(RecordMetric.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                    totals.merge(msg.metricName, msg.value, Long::sum);
                    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                })
                .onMessage(GetTotal.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                    msg.reply(totals.getOrDefault(msg.metricName, 0L));
                    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                })
                .build();
    }
}

@Component
class ClusterMetricsAggregator : SpringActor<ClusterMetricsAggregator.Command> {

    sealed interface Command : JsonSerializable

    class RecordMetric(val nodeAddress: String, val metricName: String, val value: Long) : Command

    class GetTotal(val metricName: String) : AskCommand<Long>(), Command

    override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> {
        val totals = mutableMapOf<String, Long>()
        return actorBehavior<Command>(actorContext)
            .onMessage(RecordMetric::class.java) { _, msg ->
                totals.merge(msg.metricName, msg.value, Long::plus)
                SpringActorBehavior.same()
            }
            .onMessage(GetTotal::class.java) { _, msg ->
                msg.reply(totals.getOrDefault(msg.metricName, 0L))
                SpringActorBehavior.same()
            }
            .build()
    }
}

docs.title: Spawn it
docs.text:
Call asClusterSingleton() on the spawn builder:

JavaKotlin 
SpringActorHandle<ClusterMetricsAggregator.Command> aggregator = actorSystem
        .actor(ClusterMetricsAggregator.class)
        .withId("metrics-aggregator")
        .asClusterSingleton()
        .spawn()
        .toCompletableFuture()
        .get();

// In a suspend fun or a coroutine
val aggregator: SpringActorHandle<ClusterMetricsAggregator.Command> = actorSystem
    .actor<ClusterMetricsAggregator, _>()
    .withId("metrics-aggregator")
    .asClusterSingleton()
    .awaitSpawn()

asClusterSingleton(boolean) does the same with a flag, for code that decides at run time.

What you get back is a handle to a proxy on this node, not to the actor itself. The proxy finds the node that runs the singleton and forwards every message there. tell and ask work as on any handle.

Every node spawns the singleton with the same class and id. The class name and the id form the singleton's name (<class name>:<id>), and nodes that use the same name share one singleton. Spawning it again, on the same node or another one, is safe: it returns a proxy to the same singleton and does not start a second one.

The usual place is a bean that spawns it once at startup and keeps the handle:

JavaKotlin 
@Service
public class ClusterSingletonService {

    private final SpringActorSystem actorSystem;
    private SpringActorHandle<ClusterMetricsAggregator.Command> aggregator;

    public ClusterSingletonService(SpringActorSystem actorSystem) {
        this.actorSystem = actorSystem;
    }

    @PostConstruct
    public void init() throws Exception {
        aggregator = actorSystem
                .actor(ClusterMetricsAggregator.class)
                .withId("metrics-aggregator")
                .asClusterSingleton()
                .spawn()
                .toCompletableFuture()
                .get();
    }

    public void record(String name, long value) {
        aggregator.tell(new ClusterMetricsAggregator.RecordMetric(actorSystem.nodeAddress(), name, value));
    }

    public CompletionStage<Long> total(String name) {
        return aggregator
                .ask(new ClusterMetricsAggregator.GetTotal(name))
                .withTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3))
                .execute();
    }
}

@Service
class ClusterSingletonService(private val actorSystem: SpringActorSystem) {

    private lateinit var aggregator: SpringActorHandle<ClusterMetricsAggregator.Command>

    @PostConstruct
    fun init() {
        aggregator = actorSystem
            .actor<ClusterMetricsAggregator, _>()
            .withId("metrics-aggregator")
            .asClusterSingleton()
            .spawn()
            .toCompletableFuture()
            .get()
    }

    fun record(name: String, value: Long) {
        aggregator.tell(ClusterMetricsAggregator.RecordMetric(actorSystem.nodeAddress(), name, value))
    }

    suspend fun total(name: String): Long =
        aggregator.awaitAsk(ClusterMetricsAggregator.GetTotal(name), timeout = 3.seconds)
}

The proxy stays valid for the life of the node, also when the singleton moves. Keep it and reuse it.

The other spawn settings apply to the singleton: withSupervisionStrategy, the dispatcher (withBlockingDispatcher(), withDispatcherFromConfig(...)), the mailbox and tags.

find and exists see only singletons this node spawned

actorSystem.find(...) and exists(...) find a singleton on the nodes that called spawn() with asClusterSingleton() for it. On another node they report no actor: call spawn() with asClusterSingleton() there too (it is idempotent), or getOrSpawn(). A child actor can't be a singleton: only actors spawned from SpringActorSystem can.

In local mode (spring.actor.provider not cluster), the stage returned by spawn() fails with IllegalStateException: "Cluster singleton requested but cluster mode is not enabled. Set spring.actor.provider=cluster and depend on io.github.seonwkim:actor-spring-boot-starter-cluster."

docs.title: Stopping
docs.text: stop() on a singleton's handle throws UnsupportedOperationException, and the singleton and the handle keep working. The handle is this node's proxy: stopping it would not stop the singleton, only cut this node off from it, and every later spawn() on the node would get the same stopped proxy back. A singleton runs as long as the cluster does.

docs.title: Where it runs
docs.text:
The singleton runs on the oldest member of the cluster whose status is Up: the node that joined first. The other nodes run only a proxy.

When What happens A node joins Nothing. The oldest node keeps the singleton. The host shuts down gracefully (SIGTERM, context.close()) It leaves the cluster, the singleton stops there and starts on the next oldest node. The host crashes or stops answering The singleton starts on another node only after the host is downed and removed. That needs a downing strategy; without one, the singleton waits until you remove the node by hand. No node is Up yet Messages wait in the proxy until a host is up.

While the singleton moves, the proxies keep the messages sent to it and deliver them once the new instance runs. Pekko's proxy keeps up to 1000 messages per node and drops what doesn't fit; set spring.actor.pekko.cluster.singleton-proxy.buffer-size to change it. An ask whose reply doesn't come back in time fails with its timeout, or returns its onTimeout value.

docs.title: State is lost when it moves
docs.text:
The new instance is a new actor: it starts from create(...) with empty state. In the example above, the totals start again from zero. If the singleton must keep its state, store it:

  • load it in withState(...) from a table and save it after each change, as in State in a Database, or
  • make the singleton an event-sourced actor, which rebuilds its state from its stored events wherever it starts.

docs.title: Limit it to some nodes
docs.text:
To run singletons only on some nodes, give those nodes a role with spring.actor.cluster.roles and set spring.actor.cluster.singleton.role on every node:

# Nodes that may run singletons
spring:
  actor:
    cluster:
      roles: [backend]
      singleton:
        role: backend

# Other nodes: no role, same singleton.role
spring:
  actor:
    cluster:
      singleton:
        role: backend

The singleton then runs on the oldest Up node with that role. Every node still gets a proxy, and the nodes without the role still spawn it, as in Spawn it. Set the same singleton.role on every node, so all proxies look for the same host. The role applies to every singleton of the application, including the ones the starter starts for projections.

Key Default Meaning spring.actor.cluster.singleton.role none Singletons run only on nodes with this role. Sets Pekko's pekko.cluster.singleton.role.

A sharded actor picks its role in code (role() on the actor, see Sharded Actors). A singleton's role is one setting for the node instead, because Pekko places all singletons of a node by the same role and the actor.cluster.singleton.host gauge reports one host for all of them.

docs.title: Leases: never two at once
docs.text:
A singleton runs on one node only as long as the nodes agree on who is in the cluster. In a network split, each side may see itself as the oldest and start its own singleton. The downing strategy stops one side, but it takes some time.

When two copies would do harm (two schedulers sending the same email, two coordinators handing out the same id), turn on the singleton lease:

spring:
  actor:
    cluster:
      singleton:
        use-lease: true
      lease:
        store: jdbc        # or redis, or custom (your LeaseStore bean)

The singleton then starts only after it takes its lease from the store, and stops when it loses it. A node that can't get the lease keeps retrying, and the singleton does not run on that node meanwhile. Each singleton has its own lease; its name starts with <spring.actor.name>-singleton- and ends with the singleton's name, such as orders-singleton-...:metrics-aggregator. The owner is the node address.

Key Default Meaning spring.actor.cluster.singleton.use-lease false A singleton runs only while it holds its lease. spring.actor.cluster.lease.store none Where leases live: jdbc, redis or custom. Required with use-lease. spring.actor.cluster.lease.ttl 120s How long a lease stays held after its last renewal. spring.actor.cluster.lease.renew-interval 12s How often the holder renews it. spring.actor.cluster.lease.expiry-margin 10s The holder stops this long before the ttl runs out.

The ttl also bounds how long a singleton can stay down after a crash: another node can take the lease only once the crashed node's lease has expired. Pekko's spring.actor.pekko.cluster.singleton.lease-retry-interval sets how often a node retries a refused lease.

With store: redis, a lease can be lost in a Redis failover, and two nodes can hold it for a moment. Use jdbc when a singleton must never run twice. See Leases for the stores, the tables and your own LeaseStore.

docs.title: See where it runs
docs.text:
With actor-metrics and Micrometer, every node reports the gauge actor.cluster.singleton.host: 1 on the node that runs the singletons, 0 on the others. Summed over the nodes it should be 1. The Prometheus rules in monitoring/ alert with ActorClusterSingletonMissing when the sum stays below 1 for 5 minutes.

The gauge means "this node is the oldest Up member with the singleton role" (any member when singleton.role is not set). It does not look at the lease: with use-lease, the host it names may still be waiting for its lease.

The actors Actuator endpoint (/actuator/actors, when exposed) shows the same flag in this node's view of the cluster.

docs.title: Singletons the starter starts
docs.text: Each projection runs as a cluster singleton in cluster mode, so one node handles its events. Its singleton is named projection-<name>.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• One node does all the work. Keep the work a singleton does small, or have it hand work out to sharded entities or routers.
  • Blocking calls. A singleton that calls a database or an HTTP service should run on the blocking dispatcher (withBlockingDispatcher()), like any blocking actor.
  • No downing strategy. Without one, a crashed host keeps the singleton until someone removes the node. The starter logs a warning at startup when no downing strategy is set.
  • Different ids on different nodes. Nodes that spawn with another id start another singleton.
  • State in memory. It is gone when the singleton moves. Store what must survive.

docs.text:

docs.title: Split Brain and Leases
docs.text: When nodes stop hearing from each other (a network split, a long GC pause, a crashed machine), each side sees the other as unreachable. Without a decision, both sides keep running: a cluster singleton and a sharded entity can then run twice, once on each side. A downing strategy (Pekko's split brain resolver) decides which side stays and which side stops. A lease adds a lock in a store both sides can reach, so only one side can hold it.

docs.title: Downing strategy
docs.text:
Set spring.actor.cluster.downing.strategy:

strategy Which side stays keep-majority The side with more nodes; on a tie, the side with the lowest address. lease-majority The side that takes the lease in spring.actor.cluster.lease.store. The bigger side tries first. static-quorum A side with at least downing.quorum-size nodes. Set it above half the cluster's size. keep-oldest The side with the oldest node. down-all No side: all nodes stop. none No downing. Unreachable nodes stay members until removed by hand.

The default is keep-majority with join: discovery, and none otherwise. A cluster with no downing logs a warning at startup. A node that is downed leaves the cluster and its actor system stops; with the default spring.actor.shutdown.exit-process: true, the process exits too, and your platform (Kubernetes, systemd) starts it again as a fresh node.

spring:
  actor:
    provider: cluster
    cluster:
      downing:
        strategy: keep-majority

keep-majority needs no store, but on an even split (2 and 2) only the lowest address decides. When the store is reachable from both sides, lease-majority decides by who takes the lease instead.

docs.title: Leases
docs.text:
A lease is a lock with an owner and an expiry, kept in a store. The holder renews it; when it stops renewing, another node can take it after the lease's ttl. Three things can use one:

Setting Lease Effect downing.strategy: lease-majority one per cluster Only the side that takes it stays up. singleton.use-lease: true one per cluster singleton A singleton starts only after it takes its lease, so it never runs on two nodes. See Cluster Singletons. sharding.use-lease: true one per shard A shard starts its entities only after it takes its lease.

Each needs spring.actor.cluster.lease.store:

store Where leases live Module jdbc The actor_lease table on the application's DataSource actor-jdbc redis Keys with a TTL on the application's RedisConnectionFactory actor-redis custom Your LeaseStore bean none

Whoever can write the lease store can take a lease, so the store is part of the cluster's trust boundary. See Securing the discovery store for the Redis ACL and the database grants.

spring:
  actor:
    provider: cluster
    jdbc:
      initialize-schema: always   # creates actor_peer and actor_lease
    cluster:
      downing:
        strategy: lease-majority
      lease:
        store: jdbc
      singleton:
        use-lease: true
      sharding:
        use-lease: true

Timings:

Key Default Meaning lease.ttl 120s How long a lease stays held after its last renewal before another node may take it. lease.renew-interval 12s How often the holder renews it. Keep it well under the ttl. lease.expiry-margin 10s The holder treats the lease as lost this long before the ttl runs out, so it stops before another node can take over. Must be less than ttl.

Times come from the store's clock (the database's CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, Redis TIME). The holder also counts the ttl on its own clock from the last successful renewal: if the store is unreachable until then (minus the margin), it gives the lease up. A singleton or shard whose lease is lost stops.

Lease names: <name>-pekko-sbr for the downing lease, <name>-singleton-<path> for a singleton and <name>-shard-<type>-<shard id> for a shard, where <name> is spring.actor.name. The owner is <name>@<host>:<port> of the holding node.

docs.title: JDBC
docs.text:
actor_lease is created together with actor_peer when spring.actor.jdbc.initialize-schema is always (or embedded with an embedded database). With never, create it from the schema file for your database in the actor-jdbc jar: io/github/seonwkim/actor/jdbc/schema-{h2,postgresql,mysql,mariadb}.sql.

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS actor_lease (
    lease_name VARCHAR(500) NOT NULL,
    owner VARCHAR(500) NOT NULL,
    expires_at TIMESTAMP(3) NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (lease_name)
);

Taking a lease is one conditional UPDATE (free, expired or already ours), then an INSERT if no row exists. The primary key makes only one of two concurrent inserts succeed.

docs.title: Redis
docs.text: A lease is a key actor:lease:<name> set with SET NX PX; renew and release check the owner first. Redis replicates to replicas asynchronously: if the primary fails right after a node took a lease, the new primary may not have the key, and a second node can take it. Use the JDBC store, or a Redis without failover, when a singleton must never run twice.

docs.title: Your own store
docs.text:
Implement io.github.seonwkim.actor.spi.LeaseStore (in actor-api, no Pekko types), declare it as a bean and set lease.store: custom. A LeaseStore bean of your own also replaces the jdbc and redis stores.

The interface:

public interface LeaseStore {
    boolean tryAcquire(String lease, String owner, Duration ttl); // free, expired or already ours
    boolean renew(String lease, String owner, Duration ttl);      // only while we hold it
    void release(String lease, String owner);                     // only if we hold it
    Optional<String> holder(String lease);                        // the current, unexpired owner
}

An implementation, as a bean:

JavaKotlin 
@Component
public class MyLeaseStore implements LeaseStore {

    private final MyLeaseTable table; // your own storage code

    public MyLeaseStore(MyLeaseTable table) {
        this.table = table;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean tryAcquire(String lease, String owner, Duration ttl) {
        return table.insertOrTakeOver(lease, owner, ttl); // one atomic statement
    }

    @Override
    public boolean renew(String lease, String owner, Duration ttl) {
        return table.extendIfOwner(lease, owner, ttl);
    }

    @Override
    public void release(String lease, String owner) {
        table.deleteIfOwner(lease, owner);
    }

    @Override
    public Optional<String> holder(String lease) {
        return table.unexpiredOwner(lease);
    }
}

@Component
class MyLeaseStore(private val table: MyLeaseTable) : LeaseStore { // MyLeaseTable: your own storage code

    override fun tryAcquire(lease: String, owner: String, ttl: Duration): Boolean =
        table.insertOrTakeOver(lease, owner, ttl) // one atomic statement

    override fun renew(lease: String, owner: String, ttl: Duration): Boolean =
        table.extendIfOwner(lease, owner, ttl)

    override fun release(lease: String, owner: String) =
        table.deleteIfOwner(lease, owner)

    override fun holder(lease: String): Optional<String> =
        table.unexpiredOwner(lease)
}

Duration is java.time.Duration in both.

Each method must be atomic in the store. Methods may block: the starter calls them on the blocking dispatcher, and owns the renewal timers. Run LeaseStoreContract from actor-test against your store to check it (see Testing).
