docs.title: Actors
docs.text:
An actor is an object that owns some state and handles messages one at a time. Code outside the actor never touches that state: it sends a message, and the actor changes its state while it handles the message. Because only one message runs at a time, the actor needs no locks.

Use an actor when something has state that many requests change at once (a counter, a chat room, an order, a session, an AI agent's conversation), when work should run in the background without blocking the caller, or when you want a failure to restart one small part of the system instead of the request.

This page covers defining actors, Spring dependency injection, actor ids, spawning and finding actors, stopping them, and child actors. Sending messages is in Messaging, failures in Supervision, and the tools inside an actor (state, timers, watching) in Behaviors.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text: Add actor-spring-boot-starter to your Spring Boot application, as shown in Getting Started. That starts one actor system for the Spring context and gives you a SpringActorSystem bean to inject. Nothing else is needed for the features on this page.

docs.title: Defining an actor
docs.text:
An actor is a Spring bean that implements SpringActor<C>, where C is the type of the messages it accepts (its commands). It has one method, create, which returns the actor's behavior: which handler runs for which message.

JavaKotlin 
@Component
public class GreeterActor implements SpringActor<GreeterActor.Command> {

    // Every message this actor accepts implements Command.
    public interface Command {}

    // A message that expects no answer.
    public record LogVisit(String name) implements Command {}

    // A message that expects a String answer: it extends AskCommand<String>.
    public static class Greet extends AskCommand<String> implements Command {
        public final String name;

        public Greet(String name) {
            this.name = name;
        }
    }

    @Override
    public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
        return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                .onMessage(LogVisit.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                    ctx.getLog().info("{} visited", msg.name());
                    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                })
                .onMessage(Greet.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                    msg.reply("Hello, " + msg.name + "!");
                    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                })
                .build();
    }
}

@Component
class GreeterActor : SpringActor<GreeterActor.Command> {

    // Every message this actor accepts implements Command.
    sealed interface Command

    // A message that expects no answer.
    data class LogVisit(val name: String) : Command

    // A message that expects a String answer: it extends AskCommand<String>.
    class Greet(val name: String) : AskCommand<String>(), Command

    override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
        behavior<Command>(actorContext) {
            onMessage<LogVisit> { msg ->
                log.info("{} visited", msg.name)
                same()
            }
            onMessage<Greet> { msg ->
                msg.reply("Hello, ${msg.name}!")
                same()
            }
        }
}

What each part does:

  • @Component makes the class a Spring bean. The starter finds every bean that implements SpringActor (or SpringActorWithContext) and registers it as an actor type. A @Bean method works too.
  • Command is the actor's message type. Each message is a class that implements it. Make messages immutable: records or classes with final fields (data class / val in Kotlin).
  • AskCommand<R> marks a message that expects an answer of type R. The handler answers with msg.reply(value). See Messaging.
  • create runs once each time an actor of this class is spawned. It gets the actor's context (actorContext.actorId() is the id it was spawned with) and returns the behavior.
  • onMessage(Type, handler) registers a handler. The handler gets the behavior context (ctx: logger, self reference, timers, children) and the message, and returns the next behavior. same() means "keep handling messages this way". See Behaviors for the other return values and for keeping state in the actor.

In Kotlin, behavior<Command>(actorContext) { ... } comes from the actor-kotlin module and builds the same behavior with SpringActorBehavior.builder: onMessage<Greet> { msg -> ... } is .onMessage(Greet.class, (ctx, msg) -> ...), and the handler runs with the behavior context as this, so log is ctx.getLog(). See the Kotlin guide.

docs.title: Spring dependency injection
docs.text:
Actors are ordinary Spring beans, so they get their dependencies through the constructor (or any other injection style):

JavaKotlin 
@Component
public class OrderActor implements SpringActor<OrderActor.Command> {

    private final OrderRepository orderRepository;

    public OrderActor(OrderRepository orderRepository) {
        this.orderRepository = orderRepository;
    }

    public interface Command {}

    public record MarkPaid(long orderId) implements Command {}

    @Override
    public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
        return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                .onMessage(MarkPaid.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                    orderRepository.markPaid(msg.orderId());
                    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                })
                .build();
    }
}

@Component
class OrderActor(private val orderRepository: OrderRepository) : SpringActor<OrderActor.Command> {

    sealed interface Command

    data class MarkPaid(val orderId: Long) : Command

    override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
        behavior<Command>(actorContext) {
            onMessage<MarkPaid> { msg ->
                orderRepository.markPaid(msg.orderId)
                same()
            }
        }
}

Spring creates one OrderActor bean, and every actor spawned from that class calls create on that same bean. Keep injected services in final fields, and per-actor state in the behavior, as the next section shows.

docs.title: What not to do in an actor bean
docs.text:
Don't

  • Don't keep state in bean fields. A field of the bean is shared by every actor of the class and changed from many threads at once, which breaks the "one message at a time, no locks" guarantee. Keep per-actor state in the behavior: the state object of withState.
  • Don't block the default dispatcher. A JPA repository or a blocking HTTP client holds the thread while it waits, and the default dispatcher's few threads run out. Spawn such actors with withBlockingDispatcher() (see Dispatchers), or call a non-blocking client and turn its CompletionStage into a message with pipeToSelf.
  • Don't put proxy annotations on an actor bean. @Transactional, @Async or @Cacheable make Spring wrap the bean in a proxy, but the handlers run in the behavior that create returns, not through the proxy, so the advice never applies to them, and a transaction can't span messages anyway. Put @Transactional on a separate service the handler calls.
JavaKotlin 
@Service
public class PaymentService {

    @Transactional   // on the service, not on the actor
    public void markPaid(long orderId) {
        // update the order and the ledger in one transaction
    }
}

@Component
public class OrderActor implements SpringActor<OrderActor.Command> {

    private final PaymentService payments;   // wiring: injected and final
    // private int paidCount;                // don't: shared by every OrderActor

    public OrderActor(PaymentService payments) {
        this.payments = payments;
    }

    public interface Command {}

    public record MarkPaid(long orderId) implements Command {}

    @Override
    public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
        return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                .withState(ctx -> new Paid())   // one per actor
                .onMessage(MarkPaid.class, (paid, msg) -> {
                    payments.markPaid(msg.orderId());   // blocks: see the spawn below
                    paid.count++;
                    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                })
                .build();
    }

    private static class Paid {
        int count;   // only this actor's thread touches it
    }
}

// The handler waits on the database, so the actor runs on the blocking dispatcher.
actorSystem.actor(OrderActor.class).withId("order-42").withBlockingDispatcher().getOrSpawn();

@Service
class PaymentService {

    @Transactional   // on the service, not on the actor
    fun markPaid(orderId: Long) {
        // update the order and the ledger in one transaction
    }
}

@Component
class OrderActor(private val payments: PaymentService) : SpringActor<OrderActor.Command> {
    // private var paidCount = 0   // don't: shared by every OrderActor

    sealed interface Command

    data class MarkPaid(val orderId: Long) : Command

    override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
        behavior<Command, Paid>(actorContext, state = { Paid() }) {   // one per actor
            onMessage<MarkPaid> { msg ->
                payments.markPaid(msg.orderId)   // blocks: see the spawn below
                count++
                same()
            }
        }

    private class Paid {
        var count = 0   // only this actor's thread touches it
    }
}

// The handler waits on the database, so the actor runs on the blocking dispatcher.
actorSystem.actor<OrderActor, OrderActor.Command>().withId("order-42").withBlockingDispatcher().getOrSpawn()

The starter checks the first and the last rule when it starts. For each actor bean (SpringActor, SpringShardedActor) it logs a warning for every instance field that is neither static nor final, superclasses included, and for a bean that is a Spring AOP proxy. Fields Spring injects are wiring, not state, and don't count: those annotated with @Autowired, @Value, @Inject or @Resource, those set through a setter with one of these annotations, and properties set on the bean definition. A final field that holds a mutable object (a HashMap, an AtomicInteger) is shared just the same, but the check can't tell it apart from a service, so it doesn't report it.

spring.actor.validation.actor-beans Effect warn (default) Logs one warning per problem, naming the bean, its class and the field fail Stops startup with an error that lists the problems off Doesn't check

docs.title: Actor ids
docs.text:
Every actor has an id: the string you pass to withId(...) or getOrSpawn(..., id). The starter names the actor <fully.qualified.ClassName>:<id>, so:

  • An id is unique per actor class. OrderActor "42" and InvoiceActor "42" are two different actors.
  • An id is unique within its parent. Top-level actors (spawned from SpringActorSystem) share one parent on each node; a child's id only has to be unique among its parent's children.
  • A plain actor lives on the node that spawned it. In cluster mode, get and exists on another node don't see it. For one actor per id across the whole cluster, use sharded actors; for one actor per cluster, use cluster singletons.

Use ids that come from your domain, such as an order id or a user id, so any request can find its actor again.

docs.title: Spawning and finding actors
docs.text:
Inject SpringActorSystem wherever you need an actor. Every call returns a CompletionStage (the Kotlin module adds suspend versions).

Method What it does Default timeout When it does not work out getOrSpawn(Class, id) Returns the running actor, or spawns it with default settings 3 s Fails if the spawn fails find(Class, id) Returns the running actor 3 s Completes with an empty Optional when there is none; fails on timeout exists(Class, id) Says whether the actor runs 3 s Completes with false when there is none; fails on timeout actor(Class) Starts a spawn builder for custom settings (see below) 3 s

Each method has an overload with a Duration timeout as the last argument.

docs.title: getOrSpawn: the usual way
docs.text:
getOrSpawn is the simplest way to use an actor. Call it on every request with the id from the request; the first call spawns the actor, later calls return it.

JavaKotlin 
@Service
public class GreeterService {
    private final SpringActorSystem actorSystem;

    public GreeterService(SpringActorSystem actorSystem) {
        this.actorSystem = actorSystem;
    }

    public CompletionStage<String> greet(String name) {
        return actorSystem.getOrSpawn(GreeterActor.class, "greeter")
                .thenCompose(greeter -> greeter
                        .ask(new GreeterActor.Greet(name))
                        .withTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3))
                        .execute());
    }
}

@Service
class GreeterService(private val actorSystem: SpringActorSystem) {

    // A suspend function: call it from a coroutine or a suspend controller method.
    suspend fun greet(name: String): String =
        actorSystem.awaitGetOrSpawn<GreeterActor, _>("greeter")
            .awaitAsk(GreeterActor.Greet(name), timeout = 3.seconds)
}

In a WebFlux application, wrap the stage with Mono.fromCompletionStage(...) (Java) or use a suspend controller method (Kotlin).

getOrSpawn checks for the running actor and spawns it in one step, so callers that ask for the same new id at the same moment all get the same actor.

docs.title: The spawn builder: custom settings
docs.text:
actorSystem.actor(Class) returns a builder. Set the id and any options, then end with spawn(), getOrSpawn() or spawnAndWait():

JavaKotlin 
CompletionStage<SpringActorHandle<OrderActor.Command>> order = actorSystem
        .actor(OrderActor.class)
        .withId("order-42")
        .withBlockingDispatcher()                       // it calls a JPA repository
        .withMailbox(MailboxConfig.bounded(1_000))
        .withSupervisionStrategy(SupervisionStrategy.restart().withLimit(3, Duration.ofMinutes(1)))
        .withTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
        .getOrSpawn();

// In a suspend function
val order: SpringActorHandle<OrderActor.Command> = actorSystem
    .actor<OrderActor, _>()
    .withId("order-42")
    .withBlockingDispatcher()                       // it calls a JPA repository
    .withMailbox(MailboxConfig.bounded(1_000))
    .withSupervisionStrategy(SupervisionStrategy.restart().withLimit(3, 1.minutes))
    .withTimeout(5.seconds)
    .awaitGetOrSpawn()
Builder method What it sets Default withId(String) The actor id. Required unless you pass a context. none withContext(SpringActorContext) A custom context (see Custom actor context). Its actorId() is the id. a context holding the id withTimeout(Duration) How long to wait for the spawn 3 s withSupervisionStrategy(...) What happens when a handler throws. See Supervision. stop withDefaultDispatcher(), withBlockingDispatcher(), withDispatcherFromConfig(name), withDispatcherSameAsParent() The thread pool. See Dispatchers. default dispatcher withMailbox(MailboxConfig) The mailbox: MailboxConfig.bounded(n) or MailboxConfig.fromConfig(name). See Mailboxes. unbounded withTags(TagsConfig) Tags in the pekkoTags log field. See Logging. none withMdc(MdcConfig) Fixed MDC values on every log line of the actor. See Logging. none asClusterSingleton() One instance in the cluster. Cluster mode only. See Singletons. off Ending Returns Notes spawn() CompletionStage<SpringActorHandle<C>> Fails if an actor with this class and id already runs getOrSpawn() CompletionStage<SpringActorHandle<C>> Returns the running actor if there is one; the options apply only when it spawns spawnAndWait() SpringActorHandle<C> Blocks the calling thread until the actor runs

actorSystem.getOrSpawn(Class, id) is actor(Class).withId(id).getOrSpawn() with every option at its default.

Don't block where threads are shared

spawnAndWait() (and .toCompletableFuture().join() on any stage) blocks the calling thread. That is fine in a test or at startup, but not inside an actor's handler or a WebFlux pipeline: compose the stage instead, or use the suspend functions in Kotlin.

docs.title: find and exists
docs.text:
find returns a handle to a running actor and exists says whether one runs. Neither spawns anything. Use them when an absent actor means something to your code, for example "this order was never opened":

JavaKotlin 
actorSystem.find(OrderActor.class, "order-42").thenAccept(order -> order.ifPresentOrElse(
        o -> o.tell(new OrderActor.MarkPaid(42)),
        () -> log.info("order-42 is not running")));

// In a suspend function
val order = actorSystem.awaitGet<OrderActor, _>("order-42")
if (order == null) {
    log.info("order-42 is not running")
} else {
    order.tell(OrderActor.MarkPaid(42))
}

Both look at the top-level actors of this node and at the cluster singletons this node spawned. When the actor system doesn't answer within the timeout (3 s by default), the stage fails with a TimeoutException; it never reports a running actor as missing.

get(Class, id), which completes with null when no actor runs, is deprecated: use find.

docs.title: Keeping a handle
docs.text:
A SpringActorHandle stays valid for as long as the actor runs, and sending through it costs nothing extra. If a service talks to the same actor on every request, look it up once and keep the stage:

JavaKotlin 
@Service
public class CounterService {
    private final SpringActorSystem actorSystem;
    private final AtomicReference<CompletionStage<SpringActorHandle<CounterActor.Command>>> counter =
            new AtomicReference<>();

    public CounterService(SpringActorSystem actorSystem) {
        this.actorSystem = actorSystem;
    }

    private CompletionStage<SpringActorHandle<CounterActor.Command>> counter() {
        return counter.updateAndGet(existing ->
                existing != null ? existing : actorSystem.getOrSpawn(CounterActor.class, "counter"));
    }

    public CompletionStage<Long> increment() {
        return counter().thenCompose(c -> c.ask(new CounterActor.Increment()).execute());
    }
}

@Service
class CounterService(private val actorSystem: SpringActorSystem) {

    // Spawned on first use; later calls reuse the same handle.
    private val counter = AtomicReference<CompletionStage<SpringActorHandle<CounterActor.Command>>>()

    private fun counter(): CompletionStage<SpringActorHandle<CounterActor.Command>> =
        counter.updateAndGet { existing ->
            existing ?: actorSystem.getOrSpawn(CounterActor::class.java, "counter")
        }

    suspend fun increment(): Long = counter().await().awaitAsk(CounterActor.Increment())
}

A kept handle points at one actor. If that actor stops, messages sent through the handle are lost (they go to dead letters). Keep handles only to actors that live as long as the service, or look the actor up again after it stops.

docs.title: Spawning at startup
docs.text:
A bean may spawn its actors in its constructor or in a @PostConstruct method, as the logging example's OrderService does. Spring may not have created the actor's bean yet at that point (beans are created in an order you don't control); the spawn then asks Spring for the actor bean first, so it gets created on the spot. Blocking with spawnAndWait() is fine there, since startup runs on Spring's own thread.

JavaKotlin 
@Service
public class OrderService {
    private final SpringActorHandle<OrderActor.Command> orders;

    public OrderService(SpringActorSystem actorSystem) {
        this.orders = actorSystem.actor(OrderActor.class).withId("orders").spawnAndWait();
    }
}

@Service
class OrderService(actorSystem: SpringActorSystem) {
    private val orders: SpringActorHandle<OrderActor.Command> =
        actorSystem.actor(OrderActor::class.java).withId("orders").spawnAndWait()
}

The actor class must be a bean of the same application context (for example annotated with @Component). If it isn't, the spawn fails with "No factory registered for class ...".

docs.title: Custom actor context
docs.text:
SpringActor<C> receives a plain SpringActorContext, which holds the actor id. To give an actor more than its id when it starts, define your own context class and implement SpringActorWithContext<C, CTX> instead:

JavaKotlin 
@Component
public class ReportActor implements SpringActorWithContext<ReportActor.Command, ReportActor.ReportContext> {

    public static class ReportContext extends SpringActorContext {
        private final String reportId;
        final String ownerEmail;

        public ReportContext(String reportId, String ownerEmail) {
            this.reportId = reportId;
            this.ownerEmail = ownerEmail;
        }

        @Override
        public String actorId() {
            return reportId;
        }
    }

    public interface Command {}

    public record Build() implements Command {}

    @Override
    public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(ReportContext actorContext) {
        return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                .onMessage(Build.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                    ctx.getLog().info("Building {} for {}", actorContext.actorId(), actorContext.ownerEmail);
                    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                })
                .build();
    }
}

// Spawning it
actorSystem.actor(ReportActor.class)
        .withContext(new ReportActor.ReportContext("report-7", "kim@example.com"))
        .getOrSpawn();

@Component
class ReportActor : SpringActorWithContext<ReportActor.Command, ReportActor.ReportContext> {

    class ReportContext(private val reportId: String, val ownerEmail: String) : SpringActorContext() {
        override fun actorId(): String = reportId
    }

    sealed interface Command

    class Build : Command

    override fun create(actorContext: ReportContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
        behavior<Command>(actorContext) {
            onMessage<Build> {
                log.info("Building {} for {}", actorContext.actorId(), actorContext.ownerEmail)
                same()
            }
        }
}

// Spawning it, in a suspend function
actorSystem.actor<ReportActor, _>()
    .withContext(ReportActor.ReportContext("report-7", "kim@example.com"))
    .awaitGetOrSpawn()

Always spawn such an actor through the builder with withContext(...). A spawn by id alone (actorSystem.getOrSpawn(ReportActor.class, id), or withId(...) without withContext) can't build a ReportContext, so its stage fails with an IllegalArgumentException that names the context type and says to use withContext(...). find and exists work as usual: they only need the id.

docs.title: Stopping actors
docs.text:
An actor runs until it is stopped. There are three ways to stop one:

From How Notes Outside the actor handle.stop() The stop request goes into the mailbox, so messages sent before it are handled first. Inside the actor return SpringActorBehavior.stopped() from a handler Stops after the current message. A parent ctx.stop(childRef) in the parent's handler Only for the parent's own children.

When an actor stops, its PostStop signal handler runs (see Behaviors), its children stop, and messages still in its mailbox are dropped. Stopping is final: to use the id again, spawn a new actor. Stopping takes a moment, so a spawn with the same id right after stop() can still find the name taken; getOrSpawn after the old actor is gone, or watch it and spawn on ActorTerminated.

An idle actor is not stopped for you. If you create one actor per user or per order, stop it when its work is done (for example with a timer that fires after some idle time), or use sharded actors, which can passivate idle entities.

docs.title: Child actors
docs.text:
An actor can spawn its own actors, called children. Use children to split work under one owner: a ParentSupervisor with a worker per task, a chat room with an actor per connection. Children are tied to their parent:

  • A child stops when its parent stops.
  • The parent decides how each child is supervised (see Supervision).
  • A child's id only has to be unique among its parent's children.

docs.title: Enable child operations on the parent
docs.text:
Spawning, finding and checking children works through messages that the parent handles for you. They are turned on when the parent's command type extends FrameworkCommand:

JavaKotlin 
public interface Command extends FrameworkCommand {}

sealed interface Command : FrameworkCommand

Without it, the parent ignores these requests, and every child operation fails with a timeout.

docs.title: Spawning children from inside the parent
docs.text:
Inside a handler, ctx.getSelf() is a handle to the parent. Call child(ChildClass) on it to get a child builder. The spawn is a message to the parent itself, and the parent handles it after the current message. So never wait for it inside the handler (spawnAndWait() or join()): the parent would wait for a message it can't handle until it finishes waiting, and the spawn times out. Use pipeToSelf to get the result back as a message instead:

JavaKotlin 
@Component
public class DispatcherActor implements SpringActor<DispatcherActor.Command> {

    public interface Command extends FrameworkCommand {}

    public record Assign(String workerId, String task) implements Command {}

    // The result of a child spawn, delivered back to this actor as a message.
    record WorkerReady(Assign assign, SpringActorHandle<WorkerActor.Command> worker, Throwable error)
            implements Command {}

    @Override
    public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
        return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                .onMessage(Assign.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                    ctx.pipeToSelf(
                            ctx.getSelf()
                                    .child(WorkerActor.class)
                                    .withId(msg.workerId())
                                    .withSupervisionStrategy(SupervisionStrategy.restart())
                                    .getOrSpawn(),
                            (worker, error) -> new WorkerReady(msg, worker, error));
                    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                })
                .onMessage(WorkerReady.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                    if (msg.error() != null) {
                        ctx.getLog().error("Could not start worker {}", msg.assign().workerId(), msg.error());
                    } else {
                        msg.worker().tell(new WorkerActor.DoTask(msg.assign().task()));
                    }
                    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                })
                .build();
    }
}

@Component
class DispatcherActor : SpringActor<DispatcherActor.Command> {

    sealed interface Command : FrameworkCommand

    data class Assign(val workerId: String, val task: String) : Command

    // The result of a child spawn, delivered back to this actor as a message.
    data class WorkerReady(
        val assign: Assign,
        val worker: SpringActorHandle<WorkerActor.Command>?,
        val error: Throwable?,
    ) : Command

    override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
        behavior<Command>(actorContext) {
            onMessage<Assign> { msg ->
                pipeToSelf(
                    self.child<WorkerActor, _>()
                        .withId(msg.workerId)
                        .withSupervisionStrategy(SupervisionStrategy.restart())
                        .getOrSpawn(),
                ) { worker, error -> WorkerReady(msg, worker, error) }
                same()
            }
            onMessage<WorkerReady> { msg ->
                val worker = msg.worker
                if (msg.error != null || worker == null) {
                    log.error("Could not start worker {}", msg.assign.workerId, msg.error)
                } else {
                    worker.tell(WorkerActor.DoTask(msg.assign.task))
                }
                same()
            }
        }
}

WorkerActor is an ordinary actor (@Component, SpringActor<WorkerActor.Command>). Children get Spring dependency injection like any other actor.

You can also start children when the parent starts, in the withState factory: call spawn() there and don't wait for the result.

docs.title: Child operations
docs.text:
The child builder (handle.child(ChildClass)) has the same shape as the spawn builder:

Method Notes withId(id) or withContext(ctx) Required withSupervisionStrategy(strategy) How the parent handles the child's failures. Default: stop. withTimeout(duration) Default 3 s withDispatcher(DispatcherConfig) DispatcherConfig.blocking(), .sameAsParent(), .fromConfig(name), .defaultDispatcher() withMailbox(MailboxConfig), withTags(TagsConfig), withMdc(MdcConfig) As for top-level actors spawn() Spawns the child. If a child with that class and id already runs, returns it and logs a deprecation warning: use getOrSpawn() for that. In 2.0 it fails, like a top-level spawn(). getOrSpawn() Returns the running child, or spawns it (in one step, so concurrent calls get the same child) spawnAndWait() Blocks until the child runs. Never call it inside the parent. get() Deprecated: use handle.child(ChildClass, id).get(), which returns an Optional exists() Whether the child runs

For lookups only, handle.child(ChildClass, id) returns a child reference whose get() completes with an Optional:

JavaKotlin 
CompletionStage<Optional<SpringActorHandle<WorkerActor.Command>>> worker =
        dispatcher.child(WorkerActor.class, "worker-1").get();
CompletionStage<Boolean> running =
        dispatcher.child(WorkerActor.class, "worker-1").withTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(1)).exists();

// In a suspend function
val worker: SpringActorHandle<WorkerActor.Command>? =
    dispatcher.child<WorkerActor, _>("worker-1").awaitGet()   // null when it doesn't run
val running: Boolean =
    dispatcher.child<WorkerActor, _>("worker-1").withTimeout(1.seconds).awaitExists()

These calls work from outside the parent too: any code with the parent's handle (here dispatcher) can spawn, find or check its children.

Differences from top-level actors:

  • One rule for a taken id: spawn() is for a new actor and getOrSpawn() reuses a running one. A top-level spawn() fails when the id is taken. A child spawn() still returns the running child, with a deprecation warning, until 2.0.
  • A child can't be a cluster singleton.
  • Dispatchers are set with withDispatcher(DispatcherConfig...) instead of the with...Dispatcher() shortcuts.

Inside the parent's handlers, ctx.getChildren() lists the running children and ctx.stop(child) stops one (see Behaviors).

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• State in bean fields. All actors of a class share the bean. Keep per-actor state in withState. See What not to do in an actor bean.
  • Blocking inside an actor. Waiting on a future, spawnAndWait(), Thread.sleep or blocking I/O on the default dispatcher holds a shared thread. Use pipeToSelf, or the blocking dispatcher for blocking I/O.
  • Child operations time out. The parent's command type doesn't extend FrameworkCommand, or the parent is waiting inside a handler.
  • Second spawn() with the same id fails. Use getOrSpawn(), or check exists first.
  • Actors that are never stopped. One actor per request or per user, never stopped, grows memory without bound.

docs.title: Behaviors
docs.text:
An actor's behavior says how it handles each message. You build it in create with SpringActorBehavior.builder(...) (or behavior<C>(...) { } in Kotlin, see the Kotlin guide). This page covers what you can do inside a behavior: keep state, choose the next behavior, react to lifecycle signals, schedule messages with timers, watch other actors, and turn futures into messages.

For defining and spawning actors see Actors; for sending messages see Messaging.

docs.title: The builder
docs.text:
Builder method What it does withState(ctx -> state) Creates the actor's state object when the actor starts (and again on each restart). Handlers then receive the state instead of the context. onMessage(Type.class, (state, msg) -> next) Handles messages of Type. Handlers are tried in the order they were added; the first whose type matches runs. onSignal(Signal.class, (state, signal) -> next) Handles a lifecycle signal: PreRestart, PostStop or ActorTerminated. withSupervisionStrategy(strategy) What happens when a handler throws. See Supervision. withMdc(msg -> map) Log context computed per message. See Logging. build() Returns the behavior.

A message with no matching handler is unhandled: it is dropped (and published as unhandled), and the actor keeps going.

docs.title: State with withState
docs.text:
Without withState, every handler receives the behavior context (ctx). With it, the handlers receive your own state object, which you usually give a reference to the context. Put the actor's fields and its handler methods in that object:

JavaKotlin 
@Component
public class CounterActor implements SpringActor<CounterActor.Command> {

    public interface Command {}

    public record Add(long amount) implements Command {}

    public static class Get extends AskCommand<Long> implements Command {}

    @Override
    public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
        return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                .withState(ctx -> new Counter(ctx, actorContext.actorId()))
                .onMessage(Add.class, Counter::onAdd)
                .onMessage(Get.class, Counter::onGet)
                .build();
    }

    private static class Counter {
        private final SpringBehaviorContext<Command> ctx;
        private final String id;
        private long value;   // only this actor's thread touches it

        Counter(SpringBehaviorContext<Command> ctx, String id) {
            this.ctx = ctx;
            this.id = id;
            ctx.getLog().info("Counter {} started", id);
        }

        SpringActorBehavior<Command> onAdd(Add msg) {
            value += msg.amount();
            return SpringActorBehavior.same();
        }

        SpringActorBehavior<Command> onGet(Get msg) {
            msg.reply(value);
            return SpringActorBehavior.same();
        }
    }
}

@Component
class CounterActor : SpringActor<CounterActor.Command> {

    sealed interface Command

    data class Add(val amount: Long) : Command

    class Get : AskCommand<Long>(), Command

    override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
        behavior<Command, Counter>(actorContext, state = { ctx -> Counter(ctx, actorContext.actorId()) }) {
            // The handlers run with the Counter as `this`.
            onMessage<Add> { msg -> onAdd(msg) }
            onMessage<Get> { msg -> onGet(msg) }
        }

    private class Counter(private val ctx: SpringBehaviorContext<Command>, private val id: String) {
        private var value = 0L   // only this actor's thread touches it

        init {
            ctx.log.info("Counter {} started", id)
        }

        fun onAdd(msg: Add): SpringActorBehavior<Command> {
            value += msg.amount
            return SpringActorBehavior.same()
        }

        fun onGet(msg: Get): SpringActorBehavior<Command> {
            msg.reply(value)
            return SpringActorBehavior.same()
        }
    }
}

The state object belongs to one actor and is only touched while that actor handles a message, so plain fields need no volatile or locks. Don't hand the object (or its mutable collections) to other threads.

The withState factory runs inside the actor when it starts, before the first message. It is the place to load initial data, start timers, register with the receptionist or spawn children. On a restart it runs again and builds a fresh object.

docs.title: What a handler returns
docs.text:
Each handler returns the behavior for the next message:

Return Meaning SpringActorBehavior.same() Keep handling messages the same way. The usual return. SpringActorBehavior.stopped() Stop the actor after this message. Its PostStop handler runs. SpringActorBehavior.unhandled() This handler didn't handle the message after all. The message is published as unhandled; the behavior stays. A new behavior from SpringActorBehavior.builder(...).build() Handle the next messages with this behavior instead.

Returning a new behavior lets an actor change how it reacts, for example a door that ignores Open while locked. Each built behavior has its own handlers and its own state:

JavaKotlin 
@Component
public class DoorActor implements SpringActor<DoorActor.Command> {

    public interface Command {}
    public record Lock() implements Command {}
    public record Unlock() implements Command {}
    public static class IsLocked extends AskCommand<Boolean> implements Command {}

    @Override
    public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
        return unlocked(actorContext);
    }

    private static SpringActorBehavior<Command> unlocked(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
        return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                .onMessage(Lock.class, (ctx, msg) -> locked(actorContext))
                .onMessage(IsLocked.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                    msg.reply(false);
                    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                })
                .build();
    }

    private static SpringActorBehavior<Command> locked(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
        return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                .onMessage(Unlock.class, (ctx, msg) -> unlocked(actorContext))
                .onMessage(IsLocked.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                    msg.reply(true);
                    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                })
                .build();
    }
}

@Component
class DoorActor : SpringActor<DoorActor.Command> {

    sealed interface Command
    class Lock : Command
    class Unlock : Command
    class IsLocked : AskCommand<Boolean>(), Command

    override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
        unlocked(actorContext)

    private fun unlocked(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
        behavior<Command>(actorContext) {
            onMessage<Lock> { locked(actorContext) }
            onMessage<IsLocked> { msg ->
                msg.reply(false)
                same()
            }
        }

    private fun locked(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
        behavior<Command>(actorContext) {
            onMessage<Unlock> { unlocked(actorContext) }
            onMessage<IsLocked> { msg ->
                msg.reply(true)
                same()
            }
        }
}

In the locked behavior, Lock has no handler, so a second Lock is unhandled and dropped. For many actors a status field in one state object is simpler; switch behaviors when the states really accept different messages.

docs.title: Lifecycle signals
docs.text:
Signals are events about the actor's life, not messages from others. Handle them with onSignal:

Signal When it arrives Typical use PreRestart Just before a supervised restart Release resources the old state holds; log what is lost PostStop After the actor stopped (for any reason) Close resources, deregister, log final state ActorTerminated An actor this one watches has stopped; signal.ref() is that actor Replace a worker, clean up a session

An example with PreRestart and PostStop is in Supervision. A signal handler returns the next behavior like a message handler; return same().

docs.title: Timers
docs.text:
A timer sends a message to the actor itself, once or repeatedly. Use timers for timeouts, retries, polling and periodic work. Each timer has a key (any object); starting a timer with a key that is already active replaces it.

Method on the context What it does startSingleTimer(key, message, delay) Sends message once after delay startTimerAtFixedRate(key, message, interval) Sends message every interval until cancelled cancelTimer(key) Cancels the timer; a message it already sent is not delivered JavaKotlin 
@Component
public class SessionActor implements SpringActor<SessionActor.Command> {

    public interface Command {}
    public record Touch() implements Command {}
    private enum IdleTimeout implements Command { INSTANCE }
    private enum Flush implements Command { INSTANCE }

    private static final Duration IDLE = Duration.ofMinutes(30);

    @Override
    public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
        return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                .withState(ctx -> {
                    ctx.startTimerAtFixedRate("flush", Flush.INSTANCE, Duration.ofSeconds(10));
                    ctx.startSingleTimer("idle", IdleTimeout.INSTANCE, IDLE);
                    return ctx;
                })
                .onMessage(Touch.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                    ctx.startSingleTimer("idle", IdleTimeout.INSTANCE, IDLE);   // restart the idle clock
                    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                })
                .onMessage(Flush.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                    ctx.getLog().debug("Flushing");
                    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                })
                .onMessage(IdleTimeout.class, (ctx, msg) -> SpringActorBehavior.stopped())
                .build();
    }
}

@Component
class SessionActor : SpringActor<SessionActor.Command> {

    sealed interface Command
    class Touch : Command
    private data object IdleTimeout : Command
    private data object Flush : Command

    override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
        behavior<Command, _>(actorContext, state = { ctx ->
            ctx.startTimerAtFixedRate("flush", Flush, 10.seconds)
            ctx.startSingleTimer("idle", IdleTimeout, IDLE)
            ctx
        }) {
            onMessage<Touch> {
                startSingleTimer("idle", IdleTimeout, IDLE)   // restart the idle clock
                same()
            }
            onMessage<Flush> {
                log.debug("Flushing")
                same()
            }
            onMessage<IdleTimeout> { stopped() }
        }

    private companion object {
        val IDLE = 30.minutes
    }
}

Timers belong to the actor: they stop when it stops and are cancelled when it restarts. Timer messages go through the mailbox like any other message, so they run one at a time with the rest.

docs.title: Watching other actors
docs.text:
ctx.watch(ref) asks to be told when another actor stops. When it does, this actor receives the ActorTerminated signal with the stopped actor's ref:

JavaKotlin 
.onMessage(Track.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
    ctx.watch(msg.worker());
    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
})
.onSignal(ActorTerminated.class, (ctx, signal) -> {
    ctx.getLog().info("{} stopped", signal.ref().path());
    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
})

onMessage<Track> { msg ->
    watch(msg.worker)
    same()
}
onSignal<ActorTerminated> { signal ->
    log.info("{} stopped", signal.ref.path())
    same()
}

Always handle ActorTerminated when you watch

An actor that watches another and has no onSignal(ActorTerminated.class, ...) handler fails when the watched actor stops, and its supervision strategy applies (stop, by default).

The watched actor can be anywhere: a child, an unrelated actor, or (in cluster mode) an actor on another node; it then also counts as stopped when its node leaves the cluster. The chat example's UserActor watches the actor that represents the WebSocket client so it can clean up when the client goes away.

docs.title: Futures: pipeToSelf
docs.text:
Handlers must not block, and callbacks on a CompletionStage run on another thread, where they must not touch the actor's state. ctx.pipeToSelf(stage, (value, error) -> message) solves both: when the stage completes, the function builds a message, and the actor handles it like any other.

JavaKotlin 
.onMessage(Load.class, (state, msg) -> {
    state.ctx().pipeToSelf(
            profileClient.fetch(msg.userId()),        // CompletionStage<Profile>
            (profile, error) -> new Loaded(profile, error));
    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
})
.onMessage(Loaded.class, (state, msg) -> state.onLoaded(msg))   // update state here

onMessage<Load> { msg ->
    ctx.pipeToSelf(profileClient.fetch(msg.userId)) { profile, error ->   // CompletionStage<Profile>
        Loaded(profile, error)
    }
    same()
}
onMessage<Loaded> { msg -> onLoaded(msg) }   // update state here

Exactly one of value and error is non-null. More examples, including asking another actor, are in Messaging.

docs.title: The behavior context
docs.text:
The context (SpringBehaviorContext<C>) is what an actor can do from its handlers. You get it in the withState factory, and as the first handler argument when there is no withState (in the Kotlin behavior { } DSL, as the handler's this).

Method What it does getSelf() A handle to this actor: pass it as a reply address, or use it for child operations getLog() The actor's logger; its lines carry the actor's path and MDC (see Logging) actorId() The id the actor was spawned with, so handlers don't have to capture it in create path(), nodeAddress() The actor's path and the address of the node it runs on getChild(ChildClass.class, id), getChildren() The running child with that class and id (an Optional), and all running children. getChild(name), which took the internal name <ClassName>:<id>, is deprecated stop(child) Stops one of this actor's children startSingleTimer, startTimerAtFixedRate, cancelTimer Timers watch(ref) Watching pipeToSelf(stage, fn) Futures messageAdapter(Type.class, fn) A ref that accepts another actor's reply type and delivers it as one of this actor's commands. See Messaging. registerWithReceptionist(name) Registers this actor under a service name. See Receptionist. unwrap(Class) The underlying Pekko ActorContext, for features the starter doesn't wrap

Use the context only on the actor's own thread: inside handlers and the withState factory, never in a future callback.

docs.title: Stashing and other Pekko features
docs.text:
The starter has no stash (holding messages back until the actor is ready). The usual replacement is a queue in the state object, as the AgentBrain of the agent example does: while it is busy it adds new Chat messages to a Deque and takes the next one when the turn ends.

For a Pekko feature the starter doesn't wrap, there are two escape hatches. Code that uses them depends on Pekko directly and gets no compatibility promise from the starter.

  • ctx.unwrap(org.apache.pekko.actor.typed.javadsl.ActorContext.class) returns Pekko's context.
  • SpringActorBehavior.wrap(pekkoBehavior) runs a behavior written against Pekko's API. Such a behavior gets none of the starter's features (child operations, MDC, metrics hooks).

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Blocking in a handler. Use pipeToSelf for futures, and the blocking dispatcher for blocking I/O.
  • Touching state from a callback. thenAccept on a future runs on another thread. Send a message with pipeToSelf instead.
  • Watching without handling ActorTerminated. The watcher fails when the watched actor stops.
  • Heavy work in withState. The actor handles no message until the factory returns. Load large data asynchronously with pipeToSelf.
  • Handler order. The first handler whose type matches wins. Register specific types before their supertypes.

docs.title: Dispatchers and Mailboxes
docs.text:
A dispatcher is the thread pool that runs actors. When an actor has messages, the dispatcher gives it a thread, the actor handles a batch of messages, and the thread moves on to another actor. Thousands of actors share a few threads this way.

A mailbox is the queue an actor's messages wait in until it handles them.

Most actors need neither setting: the default dispatcher and the default (unbounded) mailbox fit non-blocking work. Change them when an actor blocks, when a group of actors must not slow down the others, or when a queue must not grow without bound.

docs.title: Choosing a dispatcher
docs.text:
Work in the handler Dispatcher Non-blocking: in-memory state, tell, ask with pipeToSelf Default (nothing to set) Blocking I/O: JDBC/JPA, file I/O, blocking HTTP clients withBlockingDispatcher() Blocking I/O, many concurrent calls, Java 21 The blocking dispatcher on virtual threads A group of actors that must be isolated from the rest A custom dispatcher Work on a thread pool your application already manages A dispatcher on a Spring Executor bean

Never block on the default dispatcher

The default dispatcher has about as many threads as CPU cores. An actor that blocks there holds one of them, and a few blocking actors can stall every other actor in the application.

docs.title: Selecting a dispatcher
docs.text:
Choose the dispatcher when you spawn the actor:

JavaKotlin 
// Blocking work: Pekko's blocking I/O dispatcher
actorSystem.actor(ReportActor.class)
        .withId("report-1")
        .withBlockingDispatcher()
        .spawn();

// A dispatcher defined in configuration (see below)
actorSystem.actor(ReportActor.class)
        .withId("report-2")
        .withDispatcherFromConfig("reports")
        .spawn();

// In a suspend function

// Blocking work: Pekko's blocking I/O dispatcher
actorSystem.actor<ReportActor, _>()
    .withId("report-1")
    .withBlockingDispatcher()
    .awaitSpawn()

// A dispatcher defined in configuration (see below)
actorSystem.actor<ReportActor, _>()
    .withId("report-2")
    .withDispatcherFromConfig("reports")
    .awaitSpawn()

Both the spawn builder and the child builder take every form (the child builder's shortcut methods and the spawn builder's withDispatcher(DispatcherConfig) since 1.1.0):

Shortcut DispatcherConfig form Runs the actor on withDefaultDispatcher() (the default) withDispatcher(DispatcherConfig.defaultDispatcher()) The default dispatcher withBlockingDispatcher() withDispatcher(DispatcherConfig.blocking()) Pekko's default-blocking-io-dispatcher withDispatcherFromConfig(name) withDispatcher(DispatcherConfig.fromConfig(name)) The dispatcher defined under spring.actor.<name> or spring.actor.dispatchers.<name> withDispatcherSameAsParent() withDispatcher(DispatcherConfig.sameAsParent()) The parent's dispatcher

For a child actor:

JavaKotlin 
ctx.getSelf().child(ExportWorker.class)
        .withId("export-1")
        .withBlockingDispatcher()
        .spawn();

ctx.self.child<ExportWorker, _>()
    .withId("export-1")
    .withBlockingDispatcher()
    .spawn()

An unknown dispatcher name makes the spawn fail; the actor system keeps working.

docs.title: The blocking dispatcher
docs.text:
withBlockingDispatcher() uses Pekko's default-blocking-io-dispatcher, a thread pool meant for blocking calls. Pekko gives it 16 threads by default. Its threads are separate from the default dispatcher's, so blocking actors can only slow each other down. Change its size with raw Pekko keys:

spring:
  actor:
    pekko:
      actor:
        default-blocking-io-dispatcher:
          thread-pool-executor:
            fixed-pool-size: 32

docs.title: Custom dispatchers
docs.text:
Define your own dispatcher under spring.actor.<name> with Pekko's dispatcher keys. Every key under spring.actor that the starter doesn't know is passed to Pekko without the prefix, so spring.actor.my-dispatcher becomes Pekko's my-dispatcher (see Configuration). Then spawn with withDispatcherFromConfig("my-dispatcher").

A fixed thread pool, for blocking work you want to keep apart from the rest:

spring:
  actor:
    db-dispatcher:
      type: Dispatcher
      executor: thread-pool-executor
      thread-pool-executor:
        fixed-pool-size: 16
      throughput: 1

A fork-join pool, for CPU-heavy work you want to keep apart:

spring:
  actor:
    cpu-dispatcher:
      type: Dispatcher
      executor: fork-join-executor
      fork-join-executor:
        parallelism-min: 2
        parallelism-factor: 1.0   # threads = CPU cores x factor, within min and max
        parallelism-max: 8
      throughput: 100

A thread pool that grows and shrinks:

spring:
  actor:
    elastic-dispatcher:
      type: Dispatcher
      executor: thread-pool-executor
      thread-pool-executor:
        core-pool-size-min: 4
        core-pool-size-factor: 2.0
        core-pool-size-max: 16
        max-pool-size-min: 8
        max-pool-size-factor: 2.0
        max-pool-size-max: 32
      throughput: 10

Pekko also has type: PinnedDispatcher, which gives each actor its own thread. It uses one thread per actor, so keep it for a handful of actors. All dispatcher keys are in the Pekko dispatcher documentation.

docs.title: Throughput
docs.text: throughput is the number of messages an actor may handle before its thread moves on to the next actor. A high value (100) means fewer switches and more speed; a low value (1) is fairer, so one busy actor can't keep others waiting. Use 1 for dispatchers whose actors block.

docs.title: Spring Executor beans
docs.text:
A dispatcher can run its actors on an Executor bean of your application, for example a ThreadPoolTaskExecutor you already tune and monitor:

JavaKotlin 
@Bean
ThreadPoolTaskExecutor reportExecutor() {
    ThreadPoolTaskExecutor executor = new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor();
    executor.setThreadNamePrefix("reports-");
    executor.setCorePoolSize(8);
    return executor;
}

@Bean
fun reportExecutor(): ThreadPoolTaskExecutor = ThreadPoolTaskExecutor().apply {
    setThreadNamePrefix("reports-")
    corePoolSize = 8
}

spring:
  actor:
    dispatchers:
      reports:
        executor: reportExecutor   # the bean name
        throughput: 10             # optional

Spawn with withDispatcherFromConfig("reports"). The Spring context owns the executor: the actor system never shuts it down, and it keeps running while the actor system stops.

Key Meaning spring.actor.dispatchers.<name>.executor The name of an Executor bean spring.actor.dispatchers.<name>.virtual true for a dispatcher on virtual threads (see below) spring.actor.dispatchers.<name>.throughput Optional throughput

A dispatcher sets either executor or virtual: true, not both. The name may contain letters, digits, - and _.

docs.title: Virtual threads
docs.text:
On Java 21, blocking actors can run on virtual threads: a blocked virtual thread doesn't hold a platform thread, so many blocking calls can wait at once.

spring:
  actor:
    virtual-threads:
      enabled: true            # auto (default) | true | false
    dispatchers:
      virtual-thread-dispatcher:
        virtual: true
  • spring.actor.virtual-threads.enabled runs the blocking dispatcher (withBlockingDispatcher()) on virtual threads. The default, auto, follows Spring Boot's spring.threads.virtual.enabled, so an application that turns on virtual threads for Spring gets them for blocking actors too. false keeps platform threads even when Spring's flag is on.
  • spring.actor.dispatchers.<name>.virtual: true defines a named dispatcher on virtual threads, whatever the switch says. Spawn with withDispatcherFromConfig("<name>").
  • The default dispatcher always stays on its platform fork-join pool: actors that never block gain nothing from virtual threads.
  • A raw spring.actor.pekko.actor.default-blocking-io-dispatcher.executor still wins over the switch, with a warning in the log.

Pinning

A virtual thread that blocks inside a synchronized block, or in some native calls, pins its carrier (platform) thread until it unblocks, and too many pinned carriers stall every virtual thread. Use java.util.concurrent locks (ReentrantLock) around blocking calls, and find pinning with -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=short.

Virtual threads help blocking I/O, not CPU-heavy work. The JVM's own settings (jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism, jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.maxPoolSize) rarely need changes. The virtual-threads example compares platform and virtual threads on the same workload.

docs.title: Mailboxes
docs.text:
By default each actor has an unbounded mailbox: it accepts every message, and a slow actor's queue grows until memory runs out. Set another mailbox when you spawn the actor:

JavaKotlin 
// At most 1,000 waiting messages; further messages go to dead letters
actorSystem.actor(IngestActor.class)
        .withId("ingest")
        .withMailbox(MailboxConfig.bounded(1_000))
        .spawn();

// A mailbox defined in configuration
actorSystem.actor(IngestActor.class)
        .withId("ingest-priority")
        .withMailbox(MailboxConfig.fromConfig("priority-mailbox"))
        .spawn();

// In a suspend function

// At most 1,000 waiting messages; further messages go to dead letters
actorSystem.actor<IngestActor, _>()
    .withId("ingest")
    .withMailbox(MailboxConfig.bounded(1_000))
    .awaitSpawn()

// A mailbox defined in configuration
actorSystem.actor<IngestActor, _>()
    .withId("ingest-priority")
    .withMailbox(MailboxConfig.fromConfig("priority-mailbox"))
    .awaitSpawn()
MailboxConfig Mailbox defaultMailbox() Unbounded (the default) bounded(capacity) Holds at most capacity messages; messages beyond that are dropped to dead letters. capacity must be positive. fromConfig(name) The mailbox defined under spring.actor.<name>

A mailbox from configuration names a Pekko mailbox class, for example a priority mailbox that handles some messages before others:

spring:
  actor:
    priority-mailbox:
      mailbox-type: com.example.PriorityMailbox

Pekko's priority mailboxes (UnboundedPriorityMailbox, UnboundedStablePriorityMailbox, BoundedPriorityMailbox, BoundedStablePriorityMailbox) need a subclass that supplies the ordering; see the Pekko mailbox documentation.

A bounded mailbox drops messages silently from the sender's point of view: tell still returns, and an ask times out. Use it to protect memory, and make senders slow down (with ask, or with streams) when you need back-pressure.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Blocking on the default dispatcher. The most common cause of an application that stops responding under load.
  • One huge blocking pool for everything. Give separate dispatchers to workloads that must not wait for each other (for example, the database and a slow partner API).
  • Unbounded mailboxes in front of slow actors. Watch mailbox sizes (see Monitoring) and bound the ones that can grow.
  • virtual and executor on one dispatcher. The application fails to start; choose one.

docs.title: Logging with MDC and Tags
docs.text:
Logs from actors are harder to follow than logs from request threads: one actor handles messages for many requests, and one request can pass through several actors. The starter gives you three ways to put context on every log line an actor writes:

  • Static MDC: key-value pairs fixed when the actor is spawned (a user id, a service name).
  • Dynamic MDC: key-value pairs computed from each message (an order id, a request id).
  • Tags: labels on an actor (worker, critical), written to the pekkoTags field.

MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context) is SLF4J's map of values that the log pattern can print with %X{key}.

Inside actors, log through the actor's logger, ctx.getLog() (ctx.log in Kotlin): its lines carry the fields below and the actor's MDC.

docs.title: Fields Pekko adds
docs.text:
Every line written through ctx.getLog() already carries these MDC fields:

Field Value Example pekkoSource The actor's path pekko://my-app/user/... pekkoAddress The actor system's address pekko://my-app@10.0.0.5:25520 pekkoTags The actor's tags, comma-separated worker,high-priority sourceActorSystem The actor system's name my-app

docs.title: Static MDC
docs.text:
Set values that stay the same for the actor's whole life when you spawn it:

JavaKotlin 
actorSystem.actor(SessionActor.class)
        .withId("session-" + sessionId)
        .withMdc(MdcConfig.of(Map.of(
                "sessionId", sessionId,
                "userId", userId)))
        .spawn();

// In a suspend function
actorSystem.actor<SessionActor, _>()
    .withId("session-$sessionId")
    .withMdc(MdcConfig.of(mapOf("sessionId" to sessionId, "userId" to userId)))
    .awaitSpawn()

Every line the actor logs then carries sessionId and userId. MdcConfig.of needs at least one entry; MdcConfig.empty() means none.

docs.title: Dynamic MDC
docs.text:
Compute values from each message with withMdc on the behavior builder. The function receives every message and returns the map for the time that message is handled:

JavaKotlin 
@Component
public class OrderProcessorActor implements SpringActor<OrderProcessorActor.Command> {

    public interface Command {}

    public record ProcessOrder(String orderId, String userId, String requestId) implements Command {}

    @Override
    public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
        return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                .withMdc(msg -> {
                    if (msg instanceof ProcessOrder order) {
                        Map<String, String> mdc = new HashMap<>();
                        mdc.put("orderId", order.orderId());
                        mdc.put("userId", order.userId());
                        if (order.requestId() != null) {   // MDC values must not be null
                            mdc.put("requestId", order.requestId());
                        }
                        return mdc;
                    }
                    return Map.of();
                })
                .onMessage(ProcessOrder.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                    ctx.getLog().info("Processing order");   // carries orderId, userId, requestId
                    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                })
                .build();
    }
}

@Component
class OrderProcessorActor : SpringActor<OrderProcessorActor.Command> {

    sealed interface Command

    data class ProcessOrder(val orderId: String, val userId: String, val requestId: String?) : Command

    override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
        actorBehavior<Command>(actorContext)
            .withMdc { msg ->
                when (msg) {
                    is ProcessOrder -> buildMap {
                        put("orderId", msg.orderId)
                        put("userId", msg.userId)
                        msg.requestId?.let { put("requestId", it) }   // MDC values must not be null
                    }
                }
            }
            .onMessage(ProcessOrder::class.java) { ctx, _ ->
                ctx.log.info("Processing order")   // carries orderId, userId, requestId
                SpringActorBehavior.same()
            }
            .build()
}

Return an empty map for messages without context. Static and dynamic MDC combine: a line carries both the spawn-time values and the values of the current message.

docs.title: Carrying a request id into an actor
docs.text:
The MDC of the thread that sends a message does not travel with the message: the actor runs on another thread. To see a request id in the actor's logs, read it on the sending side, put it in the message, and add it back with withMdc. The logging example does this: a WebFilter puts requestId in the MDC of the request, the service reads it and passes it in ProcessOrder, and the actor's withMdc (above) puts it on the actor's lines.

JavaKotlin 
public Mono<OrderProcessed> processOrder(String userId) {
    String requestId = MDC.get("requestId");      // on the request thread
    String orderId = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
    return Mono.fromCompletionStage(actorSystem.getOrSpawn(OrderProcessorActor.class, "order-processor")
            .thenCompose(actor -> actor
                    .ask(new OrderProcessorActor.ProcessOrder(orderId, userId, requestId))
                    .execute()));
}

suspend fun processOrder(userId: String): OrderProcessed {
    val requestId = MDC.get("requestId")          // read before the first suspension point
    val orderId = UUID.randomUUID().toString()
    return actorSystem.awaitGetOrSpawn<OrderProcessorActor, _>("order-processor")
        .awaitAsk(OrderProcessorActor.ProcessOrder(orderId, userId, requestId))
}

(Here ProcessOrder is an AskCommand<OrderProcessed>, as in the example.) With Micrometer Tracing on, the trace itself travels with messages, and lines carry traceId and spanId; see Monitoring.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
Tags label an actor by role, priority or workload. They are written to the pekkoTags field of every line, so you can filter on them:

JavaKotlin 
actorSystem.actor(PaymentProcessor.class)
        .withId("payment-processor")
        .withTags(TagsConfig.of("payment-service", "critical"))
        .spawn();

// In a suspend function
actorSystem.actor<PaymentProcessor, _>()
    .withId("payment-processor")
    .withTags(TagsConfig.of("payment-service", "critical"))
    .awaitSpawn()

TagsConfig.of(...) takes one or more strings or a Set<String>; TagsConfig.empty() means none. Duplicate tags count once.

docs.title: Children
docs.text:
The child builder has the same withMdc and withTags. A child does not inherit its parent's MDC or tags; give it its own:

JavaKotlin 
ctx.getSelf().child(WorkerActor.class)
        .withId("worker-1")
        .withTags(TagsConfig.of("worker"))
        .withMdc(MdcConfig.of(Map.of("parentId", actorContext.actorId())))
        .spawn();

ctx.self.child<WorkerActor, _>()
    .withId("worker-1")
    .withTags(TagsConfig.of("worker"))
    .withMdc(MdcConfig.of(mapOf("parentId" to actorContext.actorId())))
    .spawn()

docs.title: Printing MDC with Logback
docs.text:
MDC values appear only if the log pattern prints them. A console pattern:

<configuration>
    <appender name="CONSOLE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
        <encoder>
            <pattern>%d{ISO8601} %-5level [%X{pekkoSource}] [%X{pekkoTags}] [reqId=%X{requestId}] [userId=%X{userId}] %logger{36} - %msg%n</pattern>
        </encoder>
    </appender>

    <root level="INFO">
        <appender-ref ref="CONSOLE"/>
    </root>
</configuration>

For log aggregation (Elasticsearch, Loki), write JSON with the Logstash encoder and list the MDC keys to include:

<appender name="JSON" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
    <encoder class="net.logstash.logback.encoder.LogstashEncoder">
        <includeMdcKeyName>pekkoSource</includeMdcKeyName>
        <includeMdcKeyName>pekkoTags</includeMdcKeyName>
        <includeMdcKeyName>requestId</includeMdcKeyName>
        <includeMdcKeyName>userId</includeMdcKeyName>
        <includeMdcKeyName>orderId</includeMdcKeyName>
        <includeMdcKeyName>traceId</includeMdcKeyName>
        <includeMdcKeyName>spanId</includeMdcKeyName>
    </encoder>
</appender>

It needs net.logstash.logback:logstash-logback-encoder on the classpath. In production, put file and JSON appenders behind Logback's AsyncAppender so that writing a log line never makes an actor wait on disk. The logging example's logback.xml has console, rolling file and JSON appenders, each async.

docs.title: Good practice
docs.text:
• Use the same MDC key names everywhere (userId, requestId, orderId), so one query finds a request across services and actors.
  • Keep the number of keys small; every key is copied for every message.
  • Never put secrets or personal data (passwords, card numbers, tokens) in MDC or tags.
  • Use tags for what an actor is (role, service, priority) and MDC for what it is working on.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause MDC keys are empty in the output The pattern has no %X{key} for them, or the line was logged outside the actor's handler (for example in a future callback) requestId missing in actor logs Thread MDC doesn't follow messages; pass the id in the message and add it with withMdc pekkoTags empty The actor was spawned without withTags(...), or the pattern lacks %X{pekkoTags}
