docs.title: Messaging
docs.text:
Actors talk only through messages. There are two ways to send one:

  • tell: send and move on. Nothing comes back. Use it for commands and events.
  • ask: send and get a CompletionStage that completes with the actor's reply. Use it when the caller needs an answer, for example to build an HTTP response.

This page covers both, how replies work, what happens on timeouts and errors, how actors reply to each other without ask, and how to design messages. Defining and spawning actors is in Actors.

docs.title: Message rules
docs.text:
• One message at a time. An actor handles its messages one after another, in the order they arrive in its mailbox. Messages from one sender to one actor arrive in the order they were sent.
  • At most once. A message is delivered once or not at all. Messages to an actor that has stopped are dropped (they go to "dead letters"). If a message must not be lost, send it with reliable delivery, or store it first (see Event sourcing).
  • Immutable messages. The sender and the actor may run on different threads. Use records, final fields or Kotlin vals, and immutable collections (List.copyOf).
  • Serializable in a cluster. A message that can cross nodes must implement JsonSerializable or CborSerializable (package io.github.seonwkim.actor.serialization). In local mode messages are passed as objects and need neither. See Cluster formation.

docs.title: Tell
docs.text:
tell puts the message in the actor's mailbox and returns at once:

JavaKotlin 
actorSystem.getOrSpawn(GreeterActor.class, "greeter")
        .thenAccept(greeter -> greeter.tell(new GreeterActor.LogVisit("Kim")));

// In a suspend function
actorSystem.awaitGetOrSpawn<GreeterActor, _>("greeter")
    .tell(GreeterActor.LogVisit("Kim"))

tell never fails and never waits. The caller doesn't learn whether the message was handled. If it needs to know, use ask.

docs.title: Ask: request and reply
docs.text:
A message that expects an answer extends AskCommand<R>, where R is the answer's type. The handler answers with msg.reply(value):

JavaKotlin 
public static class GetBalance extends AskCommand<Long> implements Command {
    public final String accountId;

    public GetBalance(String accountId) {
        this.accountId = accountId;
    }
}

// In create():
.onMessage(GetBalance.class, (state, msg) -> {
    msg.reply(state.balance());
    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
})

class GetBalance(val accountId: String) : AskCommand<Long>(), Command

// In the behavior { } block, whose state object has balance():
onMessage<GetBalance> { msg ->
    msg.reply(balance())
    same()
}

The caller sends it with ask, sets a timeout, and calls execute():

JavaKotlin 
CompletionStage<Long> balance = account
        .ask(new AccountActor.GetBalance("acc-1"))
        .withTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
        .execute();

// In a suspend function: suspends until the reply arrives
val balance: Long = account.awaitAsk(AccountActor.GetBalance("acc-1"), timeout = 2.seconds)

In a WebFlux controller, return Mono.fromCompletionStage(balance) (Java) or make the handler a suspend fun (Kotlin).

How ask works: the starter creates a short-lived reply address and sends a shallow copy of the command that carries it (getReplyTo() on the copy the actor receives). The command you passed is not changed. reply(value) sends the value to that address, and the CompletionStage completes.

docs.title: Timeouts
docs.text:
Every ask has a timeout. When no reply arrives in time, the stage fails with java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException.

Where the handle came from Default ask timeout spawn, getOrSpawn, find, exists, a child builder, ctx.getSelf() 3 s

Set your own with withTimeout(Duration). Pick a timeout that fits the caller (an HTTP request's budget), not the actor.

To return a fallback value instead of failing, add onTimeout:

JavaKotlin 
CompletionStage<Long> balance = account
        .ask(new AccountActor.GetBalance("acc-1"))
        .withTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
        .onTimeout(() -> -1L)
        .execute();

// In a suspend function
val balance: Long = account
    .ask(AccountActor.GetBalance("acc-1"))
    .withTimeout(2.seconds)
    .onTimeout { -1L }
    .await()

onTimeout only handles timeouts. Any other failure still fails the stage.

When you block on the stage (.toCompletableFuture().get()), the TimeoutException arrives wrapped in an ExecutionException; inside thenCompose/exceptionally chains it can arrive wrapped in a CompletionException. Check getCause(). In Kotlin, awaitAsk and await() throw the TimeoutException itself.

docs.title: Errors in the handler
docs.text:
If the handler throws, no reply is sent, and the actor is handled by its supervision strategy (stopped, by default). By default the asker only sees a timeout. Add failFastOnError() to fail the ask at once with the handler's exception instead:

JavaKotlin 
CompletionStage<Long> balance = account
        .ask(new AccountActor.GetBalance("acc-1"))
        .withTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
        .failFastOnError()
        .execute();   // fails with the handler's exception as soon as it throws

// In a suspend function: throws the handler's exception as soon as it throws
val balance: Long = account.awaitAsk(AccountActor.GetBalance("acc-1"), timeout = 2.seconds, failFast = true)

It works for SpringActorBehavior handlers and for the command handlers of event-sourced actors, on a local actor or a sharded entity. When the actor runs on another node, the exception's class is not sent: the ask fails with an exception whose message names the original class and message. The supervision strategy still applies.

failFastOnError() reports bugs and unexpected failures quickly. For an error the caller is expected to handle, make it part of the reply:

JavaKotlin 
public sealed interface WithdrawResult {
    record Done(long balance) implements WithdrawResult {}
    record Rejected(String reason) implements WithdrawResult {}
}

public static class Withdraw extends AskCommand<WithdrawResult> implements Command {
    public final long amount;

    public Withdraw(long amount) {
        this.amount = amount;
    }
}

// In create():
.onMessage(Withdraw.class, (state, msg) -> {
    if (msg.amount > state.balance()) {
        msg.reply(new WithdrawResult.Rejected("insufficient funds"));
    } else {
        msg.reply(new WithdrawResult.Done(state.withdraw(msg.amount)));
    }
    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
})

sealed interface WithdrawResult {
    data class Done(val balance: Long) : WithdrawResult
    data class Rejected(val reason: String) : WithdrawResult
}

class Withdraw(val amount: Long) : AskCommand<WithdrawResult>(), Command

// In the behavior { } block:
onMessage<Withdraw> { msg ->
    if (msg.amount > balance()) {
        msg.reply(WithdrawResult.Rejected("insufficient funds"))
    } else {
        msg.reply(WithdrawResult.Done(withdraw(msg.amount)))
    }
    same()
}

docs.title: Replying later
docs.text:
reply is an ordinary send, so the actor doesn't have to answer inside the handler. It can keep the command and answer when it knows the answer, for example when a human approves something or another actor answers. The ApprovalActor of the agent example keeps pending requests in a map and replies when a decision arrives (simplified):

JavaKotlin 
SpringActorBehavior<Command> onRequest(RequestApproval request) {
    pending.put(request.id(), request);          // keep the command
    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
}

SpringActorBehavior<Command> onDecide(Decide decide) {
    RequestApproval request = pending.remove(decide.requestId());
    if (request != null) {
        request.reply(new ApprovalDecision(decide.approved()));   // answer the original asker
    }
    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
}

fun onRequest(request: RequestApproval): SpringActorBehavior<Command> {
    pending[request.id] = request                 // keep the command
    return SpringActorBehavior.same()
}

fun onDecide(decide: Decide): SpringActorBehavior<Command> {
    pending.remove(decide.requestId)
        ?.reply(ApprovalDecision(decide.approved)) // answer the original asker
    return SpringActorBehavior.same()
}

The asker's timeout still applies: a reply after the timeout is dropped.

docs.title: Ask rules
docs.text:
• A command object can be asked again. ask sends a copy and leaves your object unchanged, so one instance can be asked twice or from several threads at once. (Before 1.1.0, ask stored the reply address in the object itself.)
  • reply needs an ask. Calling reply on a command that was sent with tell throws IllegalStateException. If a command can arrive both ways, check msg.hasReplyTo() first.
  • Reply once. Only the first reply reaches the asker.

docs.title: Asking from inside an actor
docs.text:
Inside a handler, never wait for a reply (join(), get()): the actor would hold its thread and handle nothing else until the reply comes. Send the ask and turn the result into a message to yourself with ctx.pipeToSelf. The AgentBrain of the agent example asks the approval actor this way (simplified):

JavaKotlin 
// A message this actor sends itself when the ask completes.
record ApprovalResolved(boolean approved, String note) implements Command {}

private SpringActorBehavior<Command> askForApproval(PendingApproval request) {
    ctx.pipeToSelf(
            approvals.ask(new ApprovalActor.RequestApproval(request))
                    .withTimeout(Duration.ofMinutes(5))
                    .execute(),
            (decision, error) -> error != null
                    ? new ApprovalResolved(false, "no answer: " + error.getMessage())
                    : new ApprovalResolved(decision.approved(), "answered"));
    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
}

// A message this actor sends itself when the ask completes.
data class ApprovalResolved(val approved: Boolean, val note: String) : Command

private fun askForApproval(request: PendingApproval): SpringActorBehavior<Command> {
    ctx.pipeToSelf(
        approvals.ask(ApprovalActor.RequestApproval(request))
            .withTimeout(5.minutes)
            .execute(),
    ) { decision, error ->
        if (error != null || decision == null) ApprovalResolved(false, "no answer: ${error?.message}")
        else ApprovalResolved(decision.approved, "answered")
    }
    return SpringActorBehavior.same()
}

The function you pass to pipeToSelf gets the value (or null) and the error (or null). It runs when the stage completes, so it must not touch the actor's state; it only builds the message. The actor changes its state when it handles that message. The same pattern works for any CompletionStage: an HTTP client call, a repository call on another thread, an LLM call.

docs.title: Replying to an actor without ask
docs.text:
Ask creates a temporary reply address. Between actors, you can pass a real address instead: put a SpringActorRef in the message, and the receiver tells its answer to that ref. ctx.getSelf() is the current actor's ref.

When the receiver answers with a type that is not one of your commands, use a message adapter: ctx.messageAdapter(Type.class, fn) returns a SpringActorRef<Type> that turns each value it receives into one of your commands. The agent example asks a rate limiter for permits this way:

JavaKotlin 
// The rate limiter answers with a RateLimiterActor.Permit.
// PermitGranted is one of this actor's commands: record PermitGranted(Permit permit) implements Command {}
private final SpringActorRef<RateLimiterActor.Permit> permits;

AgentBrain(SpringBehaviorContext<Command> ctx) {
    this.permits = ctx.messageAdapter(RateLimiterActor.Permit.class, PermitGranted::new);
}

private void requestPermit() {
    rateLimiter.tell(RateLimiterActor.Acquire.replyingTo(permits));
}

// The rate limiter answers with a RateLimiterActor.Permit.
// PermitGranted is one of this actor's commands: data class PermitGranted(val permit: Permit) : Command
private val permits: SpringActorRef<RateLimiterActor.Permit> =
    ctx.messageAdapter(RateLimiterActor.Permit::class.java) { PermitGranted(it) }

private fun requestPermit() {
    rateLimiter.tell(RateLimiterActor.Acquire.replyingTo(permits))
}

Create adapters once, when the actor starts (in the withState factory), not per message.

Refs in messages work across nodes: a SpringActorRef field in a JsonSerializable message is serialized by the starter.

docs.title: Calling actors from Spring code
docs.text:
Typical shapes, from a service or controller:

JavaKotlin 
// Fire and forget
public void visit(String name) {
    actorSystem.getOrSpawn(GreeterActor.class, "greeter")
            .thenAccept(greeter -> greeter.tell(new GreeterActor.LogVisit(name)));
}

// Request and reply, as a Mono for WebFlux
public Mono<String> greet(String name) {
    return Mono.fromCompletionStage(actorSystem.getOrSpawn(GreeterActor.class, "greeter")
            .thenCompose(greeter -> greeter.ask(new GreeterActor.Greet(name))
                    .withTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3))
                    .execute()));
}

// Fire and forget
suspend fun visit(name: String) {
    actorSystem.awaitGetOrSpawn<GreeterActor, _>("greeter").tell(GreeterActor.LogVisit(name))
}

// Request and reply: a suspend function, usable from a suspend WebFlux handler
suspend fun greet(name: String): String =
    actorSystem.awaitGetOrSpawn<GreeterActor, _>("greeter")
        .awaitAsk(GreeterActor.Greet(name), timeout = 3.seconds)

For a stream of values instead of one reply, see Reactor streams. For one message to many actors, see Pub/sub topics and Routers.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Ask timeouts that hide errors. A handler that throws sends no reply. Put expected errors in the reply type, and use failFastOnError() to see unexpected ones without waiting for the timeout.
  • Blocking on ask inside an actor. Use pipeToSelf.
  • Mutable messages. A message changed after sending can be seen half-changed by the actor.
  • Forgetting serialization in cluster mode. A message without JsonSerializable or CborSerializable fails when it crosses nodes.

docs.text:

  • Testing: testing asks and replies

docs.title: Pub/Sub Topics
docs.text:
A topic delivers each published message to every actor subscribed to it. The publisher doesn't know who the subscribers are or how many there are. In cluster mode, a message published on one node reaches the subscribers on every node.

Use a topic for one-to-many messages: chat rooms, live notifications, "this data changed" events that several actors care about. Don't use it for:

  • one-to-one messages: send to the actor directly (Messaging);
  • request and reply: use ask;
  • messages that must not be lost: topics deliver at most once;
  • spreading work so that only one worker handles each message: use a router.

Topics come with the core starter. The SpringTopicManager bean is created for you.

docs.title: Names and message types
docs.text:
A topic is identified by a TopicName: a message type plus a name. Publishers and subscribers that use the same type and name share the topic, on every node. Two topics with the same name but different types are different topics.

The type matters because subscribers receive the messages as commands. A topic's type must be the subscribers' command type (or a supertype of it): an actor of SpringActor<UserActor.Command> can subscribe to a topic of UserActor.Command, and every message published there must be a UserActor.Command.

JavaKotlin 
// In UserActor: the events users receive are some of its commands
public interface Command extends JsonSerializable {}
public record ChatPosted(String roomId, String userId, String text) implements Command {}

// The topic for one room
TopicName<UserActor.Command> room = TopicName.of(UserActor.Command.class, "chat-room-" + roomId);

// In UserActor: the events users receive are some of its commands
sealed interface Command : JsonSerializable
data class ChatPosted(val roomId: String, val userId: String, val text: String) : Command

// The topic for one room
val room: TopicName<UserActor.Command> = TopicName.of(UserActor.Command::class.java, "chat-room-$roomId")

In cluster mode, messages cross nodes, so the message type must implement JsonSerializable or CborSerializable. In local mode they don't have to.

docs.title: Getting a topic
docs.text:
Inject SpringTopicManager and call topic(name), then one of:

Method What it does getOrCreate() Returns the topic, creating it on this node if it doesn't exist yet. Safe to call any number of times. create() Creates the topic; throws TopicAlreadyExistsException if it already exists on this node getOrCreateAsync(), createAsync() The same without blocking: a CompletionStage that completes with the topic or fails with the same exception withTimeout(duration) How long they may wait (default 5 s). On timeout they fail with TopicCreationTimeoutException.

getOrCreate() and create() block the calling thread until the topic is ready (usually much less than a millisecond). That is fine in a service, but not on an actor's thread: there, use the async form and receive the topic as a message with pipeToSelf, as the chat example's room actor does. Call them once and keep the SpringTopicRef, for example in a service field or in an actor's state:

JavaKotlin 
@Service
public class AnnouncementService {
    private final SpringTopicRef<UserActor.Command> announcements;

    public AnnouncementService(SpringTopicManager topics) {
        this.announcements = topics
                .topic(TopicName.of(UserActor.Command.class, "announcements"))
                .getOrCreate();
    }

    public void announce(String text) {
        announcements.publish(new UserActor.ChatPosted("all", "system", text));
    }
}

@Service
class AnnouncementService(topics: SpringTopicManager) {

    private val announcements: SpringTopicRef<UserActor.Command> = topics
        .topic(TopicName.of(UserActor.Command::class.java, "announcements"))
        .getOrCreate()

    fun announce(text: String) {
        announcements.publish(UserActor.ChatPosted("all", "system", text))
    }
}

docs.title: Publishing and subscribing
docs.text:
Method on SpringTopicRef<T> What it does publish(message) Sends the message to every current subscriber. Returns at once. With no subscribers, the message is dropped. subscribe(ref) Delivers the topic's messages to ref until it unsubscribes or stops. Subscribing twice is the same as once. unsubscribe(ref) Stops delivery to ref. Unsubscribing an actor that isn't subscribed does nothing. name() The topic's TopicName unwrap(Class) Pekko's topic actor, for features the starter doesn't wrap

subscribe and unsubscribe take any SpringActorRef: a handle from getOrSpawn, ctx.getSelf(), or a ref received in a message. A subscriber that stops is removed from the topic for you.

Subscribing takes effect shortly after the call, not instantly. A message published right after subscribe can miss the new subscriber. In cluster mode, it also takes a moment for other nodes to learn about a new subscriber.

docs.title: Example: chat rooms
docs.text:
The chat example has one actor per room and one per connected user. The room actor owns the room's topic: it subscribes users when they join and publishes what they say. Simplified from its ChatRoomActor:

JavaKotlin 
@Component
public class ChatRoomActor implements SpringActor<ChatRoomActor.Command> {

    private final SpringTopicManager topics;

    public ChatRoomActor(SpringTopicManager topics) {
        this.topics = topics;
    }

    public interface Command extends JsonSerializable {}

    public record JoinRoom(String userId, SpringActorRef<UserActor.Command> user) implements Command {}
    public record LeaveRoom(String userId, SpringActorRef<UserActor.Command> user) implements Command {}
    public record SendMessage(String userId, String text) implements Command {}

    @Override
    public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
        String roomId = actorContext.actorId();
        SpringTopicRef<UserActor.Command> roomTopic = topics
                .topic(TopicName.of(UserActor.Command.class, "chat-room-" + roomId))
                .getOrCreate();

        return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                .onMessage(JoinRoom.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                    roomTopic.subscribe(msg.user());
                    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                })
                .onMessage(LeaveRoom.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                    roomTopic.unsubscribe(msg.user());
                    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                })
                .onMessage(SendMessage.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                    roomTopic.publish(new UserActor.ChatPosted(roomId, msg.userId(), msg.text()));
                    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                })
                .build();
    }
}

@Component
class ChatRoomActor(private val topics: SpringTopicManager) : SpringActor<ChatRoomActor.Command> {

    sealed interface Command : JsonSerializable

    data class JoinRoom(val userId: String, val user: SpringActorRef<UserActor.Command>) : Command
    data class LeaveRoom(val userId: String, val user: SpringActorRef<UserActor.Command>) : Command
    data class SendMessage(val userId: String, val text: String) : Command

    override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> {
        val roomId = actorContext.actorId()
        val roomTopic: SpringTopicRef<UserActor.Command> = topics
            .topic(TopicName.of(UserActor.Command::class.java, "chat-room-$roomId"))
            .getOrCreate()

        return actorBehavior<Command>(actorContext)
            .onMessage(JoinRoom::class.java) { _, msg ->
                roomTopic.subscribe(msg.user)
                SpringActorBehavior.same()
            }
            .onMessage(LeaveRoom::class.java) { _, msg ->
                roomTopic.unsubscribe(msg.user)
                SpringActorBehavior.same()
            }
            .onMessage(SendMessage::class.java) { _, msg ->
                roomTopic.publish(UserActor.ChatPosted(roomId, msg.userId, msg.text))
                SpringActorBehavior.same()
            }
            .build()
    }
}

This simplified version blocks the actor's thread in create() until the topic exists. The example's real room actor is a sharded actor, so each room lives on one node of the cluster while its users can be on any node, and it gets the topic with getOrCreateAsync() and pipeToSelf instead of blocking.

docs.title: Delivery guarantees
docs.text:
• At most once. A message reaches each subscriber once or not at all. Messages to a subscriber that is stopping, on a node that is unreachable, or that subscribed a moment too late are lost.
  • Order. Messages from one publisher arrive at each subscriber in the order they were published.
  • No history. A new subscriber gets only messages published after it joined. To show recent history, keep it in an actor or a database and send it when someone joins.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Topic type and subscriber type differ. subscribe takes a SpringActorRef<T> of the topic's type, so the compiler stops a mismatch. Make published events part of the subscribers' command type.
  • Creating topics on every call. getOrCreate() blocks the caller briefly. Keep the ref.
  • Blocking an actor's thread. Inside an actor, use getOrCreateAsync() with pipeToSelf.
  • Using create() where getOrCreate() is meant. create() throws if the topic already exists.
  • Expecting delivery. For messages that must arrive, send them directly and confirm with ask, or store them first.

docs.title: Receptionist (Service Discovery)
docs.text:
The receptionist finds actors by a service name instead of by class and id. Actors register under a name; other code looks the name up once, or subscribes and is told whenever the set of registered actors changes. In cluster mode, the registrations are shared across nodes, so a lookup on one node finds actors on every node. It wraps Pekko's typed Receptionist.

Use it when the caller doesn't know (or shouldn't know) the ids of the actors it needs:

  • finding all instances of a worker, wherever they run;
  • reacting when instances of a service start and stop;
  • reaching actors on other cluster nodes without sharding them.

When you know the id, use getOrSpawn or get (Actors) or a sharded actor instead. To send one message to many actors, a topic is simpler.

The SpringReceptionist bean comes with the core starter. It is created with @ConditionalOnMissingBean, so you can replace it with your own bean.

docs.title: Service names
docs.text:
A ServiceName combines a message type and an id. Names with the same type and id are equal on every node. The type is the command type of the registered actors, so lookups return handles you can tell and ask directly.

JavaKotlin 
public static final ServiceName<WorkerActor.Command> WORKERS =
        ServiceName.of(WorkerActor.Command.class, "workers");

val WORKERS: ServiceName<WorkerActor.Command> = ServiceName.of(WorkerActor.Command::class.java, "workers")

The id must not be blank. In cluster mode the messages must implement JsonSerializable or CborSerializable, as for any message that crosses nodes.

docs.title: Registering
docs.text:
An actor can register itself when it starts, in its withState factory:

JavaKotlin 
@Component
public class WorkerActor implements SpringActor<WorkerActor.Command> {

    public interface Command extends JsonSerializable {}

    public record DoJob(String jobId) implements Command {}

    @Override
    public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
        return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                .withState(ctx -> {
                    ctx.registerWithReceptionist(WORKERS);
                    return ctx;
                })
                .onMessage(DoJob.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                    ctx.getLog().info("Running job {}", msg.jobId());
                    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                })
                .build();
    }
}

@Component
class WorkerActor : SpringActor<WorkerActor.Command> {

    sealed interface Command : JsonSerializable

    data class DoJob(val jobId: String) : Command

    override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
        actorBehavior<Command>(actorContext)
            .withState { ctx ->
                ctx.registerWithReceptionist(WORKERS)
                ctx
            }
            .onMessage(DoJob::class.java) { ctx, msg ->
                ctx.log.info("Running job {}", msg.jobId)
                SpringActorBehavior.same()
            }
            .build()
}

Or any code can register an actor it has a ref to, with receptionist.register(name, ref):

JavaKotlin 
SpringActorHandle<WorkerActor.Command> worker = actorSystem.actor(WorkerActor.class)
        .withId("worker-1")
        .spawnAndWait();
receptionist.register(WORKERS, worker);

// In a suspend function
val worker = actorSystem.actor<WorkerActor, _>().withId("worker-1").awaitSpawn()
receptionist.register(WORKERS, worker)

A stopped actor is removed from its services automatically. To remove a running one, call receptionist.deregister(name, ref).

docs.title: Finding
docs.text:
find(name) returns the actors registered under the name right now. The set may be empty.

JavaKotlin 
@Service
public class JobDispatcher {
    private final SpringReceptionist receptionist;

    public JobDispatcher(SpringReceptionist receptionist) {
        this.receptionist = receptionist;
    }

    public CompletionStage<Integer> dispatch(String jobId) {
        return receptionist.find(WORKERS).thenApply(workers -> {
            workers.forEach(w -> w.tell(new WorkerActor.DoJob(jobId)));
            return workers.size();
        });
    }
}

@Service
class JobDispatcher(private val receptionist: SpringReceptionist) {

    suspend fun dispatch(jobId: String): Int {
        val workers = receptionist.find(WORKERS).await()
        workers.forEach { it.tell(WorkerActor.DoJob(jobId)) }
        return workers.size
    }
}

find(name) waits up to 3 seconds for the receptionist's answer; find(name, timeout) sets another limit. The result is a Set<SpringActorHandle<T>>; each handle supports tell and ask.

docs.title: Subscribing to changes
docs.text:
subscribe(name, listener) calls the listener with the current set right away, then with the full new set every time an actor registers, deregisters or stops:

JavaKotlin 
SpringReceptionistSubscription<WorkerActor.Command> subscription =
        receptionist.subscribe(WORKERS, workers -> log.info("{} workers available", workers.size()));

// later, for example in a @PreDestroy method
subscription.cancel();

val subscription: SpringReceptionistSubscription<WorkerActor.Command> =
    receptionist.subscribe(WORKERS) { workers -> log.info("{} workers available", workers.size) }

// later, for example in a @PreDestroy method
subscription.cancel()
  • The listener runs on an actor thread. Keep it short and never block in it. A common pattern is to copy the set into a field (an AtomicReference) that request code reads.
  • If the listener throws, the error is logged and the subscription stays.
  • Each subscription is backed by a small helper actor. cancel() stops it and is safe to call twice; after cancel() returns, the listener isn't called again. isCancelled() tells whether it was cancelled, and whenTerminated() completes once the helper actor has stopped.

docs.title: Cluster mode
docs.text:
In a cluster, registrations are replicated to all nodes. find on node 2 can return an actor that runs on node 1, and tell on the returned handle goes over the network.

Eventually consistent

Replication takes time. Right after an actor registers on one node, a lookup on another node can still return an empty or older set. Don't treat an empty result as final: retry with a bounded wait, or use subscribe and act when the actor appears.

Registrations of a node that leaves the cluster are removed once the node is removed from membership.

docs.title: API summary
docs.text: Method Description ServiceName.of(type, id) Creates a service name register(name, ref) Registers an actor under a name deregister(name, ref) Removes an actor from a name find(name), find(name, timeout) One-time lookup; default timeout 3 s subscribe(name, listener) Calls the listener now and on every change; returns a cancellable subscription SpringBehaviorContext.registerWithReceptionist(name) Registers the current actor from inside it

docs.title: Reliable Delivery
docs.text:
tell is at most once: a message that is lost, or that reaches an actor whose handler fails, is gone. Reliable delivery makes a send at least once, handled once per key: the sender retries the message until the receiving actor acknowledges it, and the receiver remembers the idempotency keys it handled, so a retry doesn't run the handler again. It works for local actors and sharded entities.

Use it for commands that must not be dropped while the application runs: an order to an order actor, a payment step to a sharded entity.

Don't use it when:

  • a lost message is fine (a UI refresh, a cache warm-up): plain tell is cheaper;
  • the caller needs an answer: use ask;
  • the message must survive a restart of the sending node, or the receiver's deduplication must survive a restart of the receiving actor: see Limits. Store the work first, for example with event sourcing.

docs.title: Receiving: wrap the behavior
docs.text:
The receiving actor wraps the behavior its create returns with ReliableDelivery.consumer(...). Its handlers and its supervision stay as they are.

JavaKotlin 
@Component
public class OrderActor implements SpringActor<OrderActor.Command> {

    public interface Command {}

    public record PlaceOrder(String orderId) implements Command {}

    private final OrderRepository orders;

    public OrderActor(OrderRepository orders) {
        this.orders = orders;
    }

    @Override
    public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
        return ReliableDelivery.consumer(SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                .withSupervisionStrategy(SupervisionStrategy.restart())
                .onMessage(PlaceOrder.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                    orders.save(msg.orderId()); // throws: no ack, the sender retries
                    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                })
                .build());
    }
}

@Component
class OrderActor(private val orders: OrderRepository) : SpringActor<OrderActor.Command> {

    sealed interface Command

    data class PlaceOrder(val orderId: String) : Command

    override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
        ReliableDelivery.consumer(
            actorBehavior<Command>(actorContext)
                .withSupervisionStrategy(SupervisionStrategy.restart())
                .onMessage(PlaceOrder::class.java) { _, msg ->
                    orders.save(msg.orderId) // throws: no ack, the sender retries
                    SpringActorBehavior.same()
                }
                .build(),
        )
}
  • Ack: a reliable message is acknowledged when one of the actor's handlers returned. If the handler threw, or no handler matched the message, there is no ack and the sender retries.
  • Deduplication: the actor remembers the key of every message it handled, with a fingerprint of its payload (its hashCode). A message whose key it remembers is acknowledged again without calling the handler.
  • Payload conflict: the same key with a different payload is not a duplicate. The handler doesn't run, and the send fails at once with PAYLOAD_CONFLICT (see Outcomes). Give reliable messages value equality (records, data classes): a class that keeps Object's hashCode has no fingerprint, so its payloads aren't compared.
  • How long: keys are remembered for spring.actor.delivery.idempotency-ttl (default 10 minutes). One actor can override it: ReliableDelivery.consumer(behavior, Duration.ofHours(1)).
  • How many: at most spring.actor.delivery.max-remembered-keys keys per actor (default 10,000). Past that, the oldest keys are forgotten first, so a burst can't grow the memory without limit.
  • Plain messages: tell and ask to the same actor keep working, without deduplication.

The behavior must come from SpringActorBehavior.builder(...). Sharded entities wrap their behavior the same way, in their create(SpringShardedActorContext).

docs.title: Stale generation: not the owner yet, or anymore
docs.text:
During a deployment a message can reach an actor that doesn't own its state: a new instance still loading it, or an old one that a newer generation replaced. The handler says so by throwing StaleGenerationException. The message is not acknowledged and its key is not remembered, the actor is not restarted, and the sender retries the same key and payload, which reaches the active owner once it is ready.

JavaKotlin 
.onMessage(PlaceOrder.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
    if (!ownership.isActive(msg.orderId())) {
        throw new StaleGenerationException("order " + msg.orderId() + " is not active here");
    }
    orders.save(msg.orderId());
    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
})

.onMessage(PlaceOrder::class.java) { _, msg ->
    if (!ownership.isActive(msg.orderId)) {
        throw StaleGenerationException("order ${msg.orderId} is not active here")
    }
    orders.save(msg.orderId)
    SpringActorBehavior.same()
}

ownership stands for your own check, such as a lease or an epoch in your database. For blue-green deployments, DeploymentGeneration.check(epoch) is that check: it throws StaleGenerationException for work stamped by a generation that is no longer active (The active generation). For a plain tell, the exception is an ordinary failure for the actor's supervision.

docs.title: Sending to an actor
docs.text:
Inject the SpringReliableDelivery bean and build a sender for an actor handle. send returns a CompletionStage that completes when the actor acknowledged the message.

JavaKotlin 
@Service
public class OrderService {
    private final ReliableSender<OrderActor.Command> orders;

    public OrderService(SpringActorSystem actorSystem, SpringReliableDelivery reliableDelivery) {
        SpringActorHandle<OrderActor.Command> orderActor =
                actorSystem.actor(OrderActor.class).withId("orders").spawnAndWait();
        this.orders = reliableDelivery.to(orderActor).build();
    }

    public CompletionStage<Void> placeOrder(String orderId) {
        // The order id is the key: placing the same order twice runs the handler once.
        return orders.send(new OrderActor.PlaceOrder(orderId), orderId);
    }
}

@Service
class OrderService(actorSystem: SpringActorSystem, reliableDelivery: SpringReliableDelivery) {

    private val orders: ReliableSender<OrderActor.Command> = reliableDelivery
        .to(actorSystem.actor(OrderActor::class.java).withId("orders").spawnAndWait())
        .build()

    // Suspends until the actor acknowledged the order (kotlinx.coroutines.future.await).
    // The order id is the key: placing the same order twice runs the handler once.
    suspend fun placeOrder(orderId: String) {
        orders.send(OrderActor.PlaceOrder(orderId), orderId).await()
    }
}

Idempotency keys:

  • send(message): the starter makes a new key for this send. Its retries run the handler once, but sending the same message again is a new message.
  • send(message, key): you pass a business id, such as an order id or a payment id. Any send with that key runs the handler once while the receiver remembers it: re-sends from another sender, from another node, or after the sender's node restarted.

A sender holds no resources: build one per receiver and keep it, or build one per call.

docs.title: Retries
docs.text:
A send is retried with exponential backoff and full jitter until it is acknowledged. Every attempt carries the same idempotency key and the same payload. The backoff doubles from initialBackoff up to maxBackoff, and the pause before the next attempt is random, from zero to the backoff, so senders that failed together don't retry together.

RetryPolicy Property Default maxAttempts spring.actor.delivery.retry.max-attempts 5 attempts in total, including the first timeout spring.actor.delivery.retry.timeout 30s from the first attempt; no attempt starts after it attemptTimeout spring.actor.delivery.retry.attempt-timeout 3s how long one attempt waits for the ack initialBackoff / maxBackoff spring.actor.delivery.retry.initial-backoff / .max-backoff 200ms / 5s the backoff doubles up to the maximum

The properties set the policy of every sender. One sender can set its own:

JavaKotlin 
ReliableSender<OrderActor.Command> orders = reliableDelivery.to(orderActor)
        .withRetry(RetryPolicy.defaults()
                .withMaxAttempts(10)
                .withTimeout(Duration.ofMinutes(1))
                .withBackoff(Duration.ofMillis(100), Duration.ofSeconds(10)))
        .build();

val orders: ReliableSender<OrderActor.Command> = reliableDelivery.to(orderActor)
    .withRetry(
        RetryPolicy.defaults()
            .withMaxAttempts(10)
            .withTimeout(Duration.ofMinutes(1))
            .withBackoff(Duration.ofMillis(100), Duration.ofSeconds(10)),
    )
    .build()

docs.title: Outcomes
docs.text:
A send that fails completes its stage with ReliableDeliveryException. Its reason() says why, and reason().isRetryable() whether sending again can succeed:

Reason Retryable When Suggested HTTP response STALE_GENERATION yes the handler threw StaleGenerationException on every attempt 409 Conflict with Retry-After TIMEOUT yes the last attempt waited its attemptTimeout without an ack 504 Gateway Timeout UNAVAILABLE yes the last attempt failed at once, for example because the actor is stopped 503 Service Unavailable PAYLOAD_CONFLICT no the receiver handled the key with a different payload; not retried 409 Conflict or 422 Unprocessable Entity

A retryable failure means the retry policy ran out. The message may still have been handled (only the acks may have been lost), so a client can send it again with the same key and payload: within the receiver's TTL it runs once. A payload conflict fails the same way every time: the client must not retry it, and should use a new key for a new payload.

An application that sends from an HTTP handler can map the reasons once:

JavaKotlin 
@RestControllerAdvice
public class ReliableDeliveryErrors {

    @ExceptionHandler(ReliableDeliveryException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<String> deliveryFailed(ReliableDeliveryException e) {
        return switch (e.reason()) {
            case STALE_GENERATION -> ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CONFLICT)
                    .header(HttpHeaders.RETRY_AFTER, "1")
                    .body("Not ready yet, retry with the same key");
            case TIMEOUT -> ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.GATEWAY_TIMEOUT).body("Timed out, retry");
            case UNAVAILABLE -> ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE).body("Unavailable, retry");
            case PAYLOAD_CONFLICT -> ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CONFLICT)
                    .body("Key " + e.idempotencyKey() + " was used for a different request");
        };
    }
}

@RestControllerAdvice
class ReliableDeliveryErrors {

    @ExceptionHandler(ReliableDeliveryException::class)
    fun deliveryFailed(e: ReliableDeliveryException): ResponseEntity<String> =
        when (e.reason()) {
            ReliableDeliveryException.Reason.STALE_GENERATION -> ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CONFLICT)
                .header(HttpHeaders.RETRY_AFTER, "1")
                .body("Not ready yet, retry with the same key")
            ReliableDeliveryException.Reason.TIMEOUT ->
                ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.GATEWAY_TIMEOUT).body("Timed out, retry")
            ReliableDeliveryException.Reason.UNAVAILABLE ->
                ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE).body("Unavailable, retry")
            ReliableDeliveryException.Reason.PAYLOAD_CONFLICT -> ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CONFLICT)
                .body("Key ${e.idempotencyKey()} was used for a different request")
        }
}

The exception reaches the handler when the controller returns the send's stage or waits for it, as await() does in Kotlin.

docs.title: Sending to sharded entities
docs.text:
In cluster mode, toSharded(...) builds one sender for all entities of a sharded actor class. send takes the entity id.

JavaKotlin 
ShardedReliableSender<OrderEntity.Command> payments =
        reliableDelivery.toSharded(OrderEntity.class).build();

payments.send("order-42", new OrderEntity.Pay(1_000), "payment-77")
        .thenRun(() -> log.info("order-42 acknowledged payment-77"));

val payments: ShardedReliableSender<OrderEntity.Command> =
    reliableDelivery.toSharded(OrderEntity::class.java).build()

// In a suspend function
payments.send("order-42", OrderEntity.Pay(1_000), "payment-77").await()

A retry reaches the entity wherever it runs; if the entity stopped or moved, the retry starts it again. Messages must implement JsonSerializable or CborSerializable, as for any message that crosses nodes.

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text:
• Per message: one ask and one ack, and one more of each per retry. No extra actors stay alive.
  • On the receiver: a key and an expiry for each handled message, up to the TTL and the key limit (10,000 keys of about 100 bytes each is about 1 MB per actor).
  • While a receiver is down: each pending send retries until it gives up; with the defaults, at most 5 asks over about 30 seconds.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Dedupe memory is in the actor. So is the payload fingerprint: a conflict is found only while the key is remembered. The memory is lost when the receiving actor restarts by its spawn supervision, stops, or (sharded) is passivated or moves to another node. After that, a retry or a re-send with the same key runs the handler again. Make handlers safe to run twice when that matters. A durable key store is a planned follow-up.
  • Stopped local actors don't come back. Retries to a local actor that stopped fail when the retry policy runs out. A sharded entity starts again on the next retry.
  • No ordering. Retries can overtake later messages: send one at a time (wait for the stage) when the order matters.
  • Not durable on the sender. A send in progress is lost when the sending node stops; the caller sees no result. Re-send with the same key when it restarts.

docs.title: Routers
docs.text:
A router is an actor that owns a pool of identical worker actors and passes each message it receives to one of them (or to all of them). You send to the router as if it were one actor; the work runs on several workers at once.

Use a router when one actor can't keep up and the work doesn't depend on shared state: sending emails, resizing images, calling a slow API. If the work belongs to an entity (an order, a user), use one actor per entity instead (see Actors or Sharded actors); a router with consistent hashing sits in between.

A router lives on one node, and its workers are its children. Routers come with the core starter; no extra dependency or configuration is needed.

docs.title: Creating a router
docs.text:
A router has two parts: the worker actor that does the work, and the router actor that holds the pool. They share one command type.

JavaKotlin 
// The worker: an ordinary actor bean
@Component
public class ResizeWorker implements SpringActor<ImageRouter.Command> {

    private final ImageService imageService;

    public ResizeWorker(ImageService imageService) {
        this.imageService = imageService;
    }

    @Override
    public SpringActorBehavior<ImageRouter.Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
        return SpringActorBehavior.builder(ImageRouter.Command.class, actorContext)
                .onMessage(ImageRouter.Resize.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
                    imageService.resize(msg.imageId(), msg.width());
                    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
                })
                .build();
    }
}

// The router: its behavior is a pool of ResizeWorkers
@Component
public class ImageRouter implements SpringActor<ImageRouter.Command> {

    public interface Command {}

    public record Resize(String imageId, int width) implements Command {}

    @Override
    public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
        return SpringRouterBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                .withRoutingStrategy(RoutingStrategy.roundRobin())
                .withPoolSize(8)
                .withWorkerActors(ResizeWorker.class)
                .withSupervisionStrategy(SupervisionStrategy.restart())
                .build();
    }
}

// The worker: an ordinary actor bean
@Component
class ResizeWorker(private val imageService: ImageService) : SpringActor<ImageRouter.Command> {

    override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<ImageRouter.Command> =
        actorBehavior<ImageRouter.Command>(actorContext)
            .onMessage(ImageRouter.Resize::class.java) { _, msg ->
                imageService.resize(msg.imageId, msg.width)
                SpringActorBehavior.same()
            }
            .build()
}

// The router: its behavior is a pool of ResizeWorkers
@Component
class ImageRouter : SpringActor<ImageRouter.Command> {

    sealed interface Command

    data class Resize(val imageId: String, val width: Int) : Command

    override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
        SpringRouterBehavior.builder(Command::class.java, actorContext)
            .withRoutingStrategy(RoutingStrategy.roundRobin())
            .withPoolSize(8)
            .withWorkerActors(ResizeWorker::class.java)
            .withSupervisionStrategy(SupervisionStrategy.restart())
            .build()
}

Spawn and use the router like any other actor:

JavaKotlin 
@Service
public class ImageResizer {
    private final SpringActorSystem actorSystem;

    public ImageResizer(SpringActorSystem actorSystem) {
        this.actorSystem = actorSystem;
    }

    public void resizeLater(String imageId) {
        actorSystem.getOrSpawn(ImageRouter.class, "image-router")
                .thenAccept(router -> router.tell(new ImageRouter.Resize(imageId, 640)));
    }
}

@Service
class ImageResizer(private val actorSystem: SpringActorSystem) {

    suspend fun resizeLater(imageId: String) {
        actorSystem.awaitGetOrSpawn<ImageRouter, _>("image-router")
            .tell(ImageRouter.Resize(imageId, 640))
    }
}

docs.title: Builder options
docs.text:
Method Required Default Notes withRoutingStrategy(strategy) yes none build() throws IllegalStateException without it withWorkerActors(Class) yes none A SpringActor bean whose command type is the router's withPoolSize(n) no 5 Must be positive withSupervisionStrategy(strategy) no stop Applies to each worker. See Worker failures.

Each worker's create(actorContext) gets its own id, worker-<uuid> (actorContext.actorId()), which it keeps across restarts. Use it to tell workers apart in logs.

docs.title: Routing strategies
docs.text: Strategy Who gets a message Use it for RoutingStrategy.roundRobin() Each worker in turn Tasks that take about the same time RoutingStrategy.random() A random worker Simple spreading with no bookkeeping RoutingStrategy.broadcast() Every worker Telling all workers something, such as "clear your cache" RoutingStrategy.consistentHashing() The worker chosen by the message's key Keeping all messages for one key on one worker

docs.title: Broadcast
docs.text: With broadcast(), every message is handled once per worker: 10 messages to a pool of 5 means 50 handler calls. Use it for rare control messages, not for regular work. A broadcast ask gets the first worker's reply; the other replies are dropped.

docs.title: Consistent hashing
docs.text:
consistentHashing() sends messages with the same key to the same worker, as long as the pool doesn't change. A worker can then keep a cache per key, or handle one customer's messages in order. Give a message its key by implementing ConsistentHashable:

JavaKotlin 
public record ProcessOrder(String customerId, String orderId) implements Command, ConsistentHashable {
    @Override
    public String getConsistentHashKey() {
        return customerId;   // one customer's orders always go to the same worker
    }
}

// In the router's create():
return SpringRouterBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
        .withRoutingStrategy(RoutingStrategy.consistentHashing())
        .withPoolSize(10)
        .withWorkerActors(OrderWorker.class)
        .build();

data class ProcessOrder(val customerId: String, val orderId: String) : Command, ConsistentHashable {
    // one customer's orders always go to the same worker
    override fun getConsistentHashKey(): String = customerId
}

// In the router's create():
SpringRouterBehavior.builder(Command::class.java, actorContext)
    .withRoutingStrategy(RoutingStrategy.consistentHashing())
    .withPoolSize(10)
    .withWorkerActors(OrderWorker::class.java)
    .build()
  • The key must not be null; a null key fails the routing with IllegalStateException.
  • A message that doesn't implement ConsistentHashable is hashed by its toString(). Records and data classes have a stable toString(); most other classes don't, so implement ConsistentHashable.
  • consistentHashing(virtualNodesFactor) sets how many points each worker gets on the hash ring (default 10, minimum 1). More points spread keys more evenly.
  • This is not a replacement for sharding: the mapping changes when a worker is replaced, and it stays on one node. For one actor per key across a cluster, use sharded actors.

docs.title: Ask through a router
docs.text:
A router forwards AskCommands like any message, and the worker that handles it replies to the asker:

JavaKotlin 
public static class Validate extends AskCommand<Boolean> implements Command {
    public final String data;

    public Validate(String data) {
        this.data = data;
    }
}

// In the worker:
.onMessage(Validate.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
    msg.reply(!msg.data.isBlank());
    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
})

// The caller:
CompletionStage<Boolean> valid = router.ask(new ValidationRouter.Validate("payload"))
        .withTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
        .execute();

class Validate(val data: String) : AskCommand<Boolean>(), Command

// In the worker:
.onMessage(Validate::class.java) { _, msg ->
    msg.reply(msg.data.isNotBlank())
    SpringActorBehavior.same()
}

// The caller, in a suspend function:
val valid: Boolean = router.awaitAsk(ValidationRouter.Validate("payload"), timeout = 2.seconds)

docs.title: Worker failures
docs.text: The router's withSupervisionStrategy applies to each worker. Without it, a worker whose handler throws stops and leaves the pool, so the pool shrinks with every failure. For a pool that should keep its size, set SupervisionStrategy.restart() (or restart().withLimit(...)). With restart, the failed message is dropped and the other messages are still handled, as the router tests check. See Supervision for what each strategy does.

docs.title: Workers and Spring beans
docs.text:
Every worker in a pool is created from the same worker bean, so:

  • Injected services are shared by all workers (and by every pool that uses the bean). That is what you want for repositories, clients and connection pools.
  • Per-worker state belongs in the worker's withState object, not in a field of the bean.
  • Workers don't have ids of their own. All workers of a pool get the same generated actorContext.actorId() (worker-<uuid>), so don't use it to tell workers apart.

A worker that blocks (JDBC, blocking HTTP) holds a thread of the router's dispatcher. Spawn the router with withBlockingDispatcher() or a custom dispatcher in that case.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• No routing strategy. build() fails; there is no default strategy.
  • Pool that shrinks. Without a restart strategy, failing workers stop for good.
  • Shared state in the worker bean. All workers of all pools share it.
  • Ordering. Round robin and random spread consecutive messages over different workers, so they can be handled out of order. Use consistent hashing (or one actor per key) when order per key matters.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Actors: spawning the router
  • Supervision: worker strategies
  • Dispatchers: thread pools for blocking workers
  • Sharded actors: one actor per key across a cluster
  • Pekko routers: the pool router the starter uses

docs.title: Supervision
docs.text:
Supervision decides what happens to an actor when one of its handlers throws an exception. Instead of try/catch around every handler, you choose a strategy once: restart the actor with fresh state, keep it running and skip the message, or stop it. A failure then stays inside that one actor, and the rest of the application keeps working.

Use supervision for failures you can't handle where they happen: a bug, a corrupted in-memory state, a dependency that throws. For expected outcomes (a rejected payment, an invalid input), reply with a result instead (see Errors in the handler).

docs.title: Strategies
docs.text:
SupervisionStrategy has three strategies:

Strategy What happens after a failure Use it when SupervisionStrategy.stop() The actor stops. This is the default when no strategy is set. A failed actor should not keep going; a caller or parent will create a new one if needed SupervisionStrategy.restart() The actor starts again with fresh state, under the same id and ref. No limit. The state can be rebuilt (from a database, a snapshot, or from nothing) SupervisionStrategy.restart().withLimit(n, window) Restarts, but stops the actor once it has restarted n times within window Most restarts in production: it stops an actor that fails on every message SupervisionStrategy.resume() The actor keeps its state and goes on with the next message. The failed message is dropped. The failure doesn't damage the state, and losing one message is fine

Default: stop

With no strategy, a failing actor stops. Earlier versions of these docs said the default was restart; it is stop.

The message that failed is never retried, whatever the strategy. If the sender asked, it gets no reply and sees a timeout.

docs.title: Where to set the strategy
docs.text:
There are four places. Set it in one of them per actor.

JavaKotlin 
// 1. When spawning a top-level actor
actorSystem.actor(OrderActor.class)
        .withId("order-42")
        .withSupervisionStrategy(SupervisionStrategy.restart().withLimit(3, Duration.ofMinutes(1)))
        .spawn();

// 2. In the actor's own behavior: applies however the actor is spawned
@Override
public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
    return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
            .withSupervisionStrategy(SupervisionStrategy.restart().withLimit(10, Duration.ofMinutes(1)))
            .withState(ctx -> new OrderState(ctx))
            .onMessage(Pay.class, OrderState::onPay)
            .build();
}

// 3. When a parent spawns a child
ctx.getSelf().child(WorkerActor.class)
        .withId("worker-1")
        .withSupervisionStrategy(SupervisionStrategy.resume())
        .spawn();

// 4. For the workers of a router
SpringRouterBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
        .withRoutingStrategy(RoutingStrategy.roundRobin())
        .withWorkerActors(WorkerActor.class)
        .withSupervisionStrategy(SupervisionStrategy.restart())
        .build();

// 1. When spawning a top-level actor (in a suspend function)
actorSystem.actor<OrderActor, _>()
    .withId("order-42")
    .withSupervisionStrategy(SupervisionStrategy.restart().withLimit(3, 1.minutes))
    .awaitSpawn()

// 2. In the actor's own behavior: applies however the actor is spawned
override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
    behavior<Command, OrderState>(actorContext, state = { ctx -> OrderState(ctx) }) {
        withSupervisionStrategy(SupervisionStrategy.restart().withLimit(10, 1.minutes))
        onMessage<Pay> { msg -> onPay(msg) }
    }

// 3. When a parent spawns a child
ctx.self.child<WorkerActor, _>()
    .withId("worker-1")
    .withSupervisionStrategy(SupervisionStrategy.resume())
    .spawn()

// 4. For the workers of a router
SpringRouterBehavior.builder(Command::class.java, actorContext)
    .withRoutingStrategy(RoutingStrategy.roundRobin())
    .withWorkerActors(WorkerActor::class.java)
    .withSupervisionStrategy(SupervisionStrategy.restart())
    .build()

Which one to pick:

  • Put it in the behavior (2) when the strategy belongs to the actor itself, for example "this actor reloads its state on restart, so restarting is always safe". Every spawn then gets it.
  • Put it at the spawn site (1, 3) when the caller decides, for example a parent that treats some children as disposable.
  • Sharded actors set it in their behavior (2); see Sharded actors.

docs.title: What a restart keeps and what it loses
docs.text:
A restart builds the actor's behavior again from its withState factory. create is not called again.

Kept Lost The actor's id, path and ref: handles held by others keep working The state object: the withState factory runs again and builds a new one Messages already waiting in the mailbox The message that failed The actor's dispatcher, mailbox settings, tags and MDC Timers: they are cancelled. Timers started in the withState factory start again because it runs again. The Spring bean and its injected dependencies Child actors: Pekko stops them when the parent restarts

So anything an actor must not lose on restart has to live outside the state object: in a database, a snapshot, or an event-sourced journal. The AgentBrain of the agent example restarts up to 10 times a minute and reloads its conversation from the last snapshot in its constructor, which the withState factory calls on every start:

JavaKotlin 
return builder.withSupervisionStrategy(SupervisionStrategy.restart().withLimit(10, Duration.ofMinutes(1)))
        .withState(ctx -> new AgentBrain(ctx, agentId, dependencies))   // reloads the snapshot
        .onMessage(AgentActor.Chat.class, AgentBrain::onChat)
        .build();

builder.withSupervisionStrategy(SupervisionStrategy.restart().withLimit(10, 1.minutes))
    .withState { ctx -> AgentBrain(ctx, agentId, dependencies) }   // reloads the snapshot
    .onMessage(AgentActor.Chat::class.java) { brain, chat -> brain.onChat(chat) }
    .build()

docs.title: Reacting to restarts and stops
docs.text:
Two signals tell an actor about its own lifecycle. Register them with onSignal:

  • PreRestart arrives just before a restart. Release what the old state holds (open files, subscriptions) or log what is lost.
  • PostStop arrives after the actor stopped, whether a handler returned stopped(), someone called stop(), or supervision stopped it.
JavaKotlin 
return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
        .withSupervisionStrategy(SupervisionStrategy.restart())
        .withState(ctx -> new WorkerState(ctx))
        .onMessage(DoTask.class, WorkerState::onDoTask)
        .onSignal(PreRestart.class, (state, signal) -> {
            state.ctx().getLog().warn("Restarting; {} completed tasks are lost", state.completed());
            return SpringActorBehavior.same();
        })
        .onSignal(PostStop.class, (state, signal) -> {
            state.ctx().getLog().info("Stopped after {} tasks", state.completed());
            return SpringActorBehavior.same();
        })
        .build();

behavior<Command, WorkerState>(actorContext, state = { ctx -> WorkerState(ctx) }) {
    withSupervisionStrategy(SupervisionStrategy.restart())
    onMessage<DoTask> { msg -> onDoTask(msg) }
    onSignal<PreRestart> {
        ctx.log.warn("Restarting; {} completed tasks are lost", completed)
        same()
    }
    onSignal<PostStop> {
        ctx.log.info("Stopped after {} tasks", completed)
        same()
    }
}

Keep signal handlers short and don't throw from them. More on signals in Behaviors.

docs.title: Supervising children
docs.text:
A parent chooses a strategy for each child when it spawns it (place 3 above). A child's failure does not fail the parent: with stop, the child just stops. To find out, the parent watches the child and handles the ActorTerminated signal, for example to spawn a replacement or to tell a caller:

JavaKotlin 
.onMessage(WorkerReady.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
    ctx.watch(msg.worker());              // ActorTerminated arrives when the worker stops
    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
})
.onSignal(ActorTerminated.class, (ctx, signal) -> {
    ctx.getLog().warn("Worker {} stopped", signal.ref().path());
    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
})

onMessage<WorkerReady> { msg ->
    watch(msg.worker)                      // ActorTerminated arrives when the worker stops
    same()
}
onSignal<ActorTerminated> { signal ->
    log.warn("Worker {} stopped", signal.ref.path())
    same()
}

Common choices by role:

Child role Strategy Stateless worker restart() Worker in production that might fail on every message restart().withLimit(3, Duration.ofMinutes(1)) Validator or one-shot task that should fail fast stop() Logger or metrics forwarder where one lost message is fine resume()

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Relying on the default. With no strategy, the first exception stops the actor, and later messages to it are lost. Set a strategy on every long-lived actor.
  • Unlimited restarts. restart() without a limit restarts an actor that fails on every message forever. Prefer withLimit.
  • State that must survive. A restart throws the state object away. Persist what matters.
  • resume on damaged state. If the exception left the state half-updated, resume keeps the half-updated state.
  • Errors meant for the caller. The asker of a failed message only sees a timeout. Reply with an error result for expected failures.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Actors: spawning actors and children
  • Behaviors: withState, signals and watching
  • Messaging: replies, timeouts and errors
  • Event sourcing: state that survives restarts and node failures

docs.title: Event-Sourced Actors
docs.text:
An event-sourced actor stores what happened (events) instead of its current state. Each command decides which events to store; each event changes the state. When the actor starts again, after a restart, a deploy or a crash, it rebuilds its state from the stored events.

The actor-persistence module runs event-sourced actors on Pekko Persistence. The journal and the snapshots live in tables on your application's DataSource: no second connection pool, no Pekko configuration, and no Pekko types in your code.

Event sourcing or a state store?

If you only need the latest state of an actor, keep it in a table with Spring Data, as in State in a Database. Use event sourcing when the history matters: an audit trail, rebuilding read models with projections, or undoing a bug by replaying events.

docs.title: Add the module
docs.text:
dependencies {
    implementation("io.github.seonwkim:actor-spring-boot-starter:$version")
    implementation("io.github.seonwkim:actor-persistence:$version")
    implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-jdbc") // or data-jpa: any DataSource
    runtimeOnly("org.postgresql:postgresql")
}

docs.title: Write an event-sourced actor
docs.text:
An event-sourced actor is a SpringActor whose create returns a SpringEventSourcedBehavior:

JavaKotlin 
@Component
public class AccountActor implements SpringActor<AccountActor.Command> {

    public interface Command {}

    public static final class Deposit extends AskCommand<Long> implements Command {
        public final long amount;
        public Deposit(long amount) { this.amount = amount; }
    }

    public static final class GetBalance extends AskCommand<Long> implements Command {}

    // Events and the state are stored: they must be serializable.
    public interface Event extends JsonSerializable {}
    public record Deposited(long amount) implements Event {}

    public record Account(long balance) implements JsonSerializable {
        Account add(long amount) { return new Account(balance + amount); }
    }

    @Override
    public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
        return SpringEventSourcedBehavior.builder(
                        Command.class,
                        Event.class,
                        PersistenceId.of("Account", actorContext.actorId()),
                        new Account(0))
                .onCommand(Deposit.class, (ctx, account, cmd) -> ctx.persist(new Deposited(cmd.amount))
                        .thenReply(cmd, Account::balance))
                .onCommand(GetBalance.class, (ctx, account, cmd) -> ctx.none()
                        .thenReply(cmd, Account::balance))
                .onEvent(Deposited.class, (account, event) -> account.add(event.amount()))
                .snapshotEvery(100)
                .build();
    }
}

@Component
class AccountActor : SpringActor<AccountActor.Command> {

    sealed interface Command

    class Deposit(val amount: Long) : AskCommand<Long>(), Command

    class GetBalance : AskCommand<Long>(), Command

    // Events and the state are stored: they must be serializable.
    sealed interface Event : JsonSerializable
    data class Deposited(val amount: Long) : Event

    data class Account(val balance: Long) : JsonSerializable {
        fun add(amount: Long) = Account(balance + amount)
    }

    override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
        SpringEventSourcedBehavior.builder(
            Command::class.java,
            Event::class.java,
            PersistenceId.of("Account", actorContext.actorId()),
            Account(0),
        )
            .onCommand(Deposit::class.java) { ctx, _, cmd ->
                ctx.persist(Deposited(cmd.amount)).thenReply(cmd) { it.balance }
            }
            .onCommand(GetBalance::class.java) { ctx, _, cmd ->
                ctx.none().thenReply(cmd) { it.balance }
            }
            .onEvent(Deposited::class.java) { account, event -> account.add(event.amount) }
            .snapshotEvery(100)
            .build()
}

Spawn it and send it commands like any other actor:

JavaKotlin 
SpringActorHandle<AccountActor.Command> account =
        actorSystem.actor(AccountActor.class).withId("alice").spawnAndWait();
long balance = account.ask(new AccountActor.Deposit(5)).execute().toCompletableFuture().join();

// In a suspend fun or a coroutine
val account = actorSystem.actor<AccountActor, _>().withId("alice").awaitSpawn()
val balance: Long = account.awaitAsk(AccountActor.Deposit(5))

Spawn alice again after a restart and it has the same balance.

docs.title: The parts
docs.text: Part What it does PersistenceId.of(entityType, entityId) The key of the actor's events: Account\|alice. It must be unique in the application and the same on every start. empty state The state before any event. onCommand(type, (ctx, state, command) -> effect) Decides what to do with a command. It returns an Effect; it must not change the state itself. onEvent(type, (state, event) -> newState) Applies a stored event. It runs after the event is stored and again on every recovery, so it must not have side effects. snapshotEvery(n) Stores a snapshot of the state every n events and keeps the latest two. Recovery loads the latest snapshot and replays only the events after it. withTagger(event -> Set.of(...)) Tags stored with each event, for projections.

docs.title: Effects
docs.text:
Start from the context, which knows the event and state types:

Effect Meaning ctx.persist(event), ctx.persist(List.of(e1, e2)) Store the events (a list atomically), then apply them ctx.none() Store nothing ctx.unhandled() The command isn't handled in this state ctx.stop() Store nothing and stop the actor .thenReply(cmd, state -> value) Reply to an AskCommand with the state after the events .thenRun(state -> ...) Any other side effect, after the events are stored .thenStop() Stop after the side effects

Side effects run only after the events are stored, never during recovery. ctx.actorContext() gives the actor's own context (getSelf(), getLog(), timers).

docs.title: Serialization
docs.text: Events and states are written to the database with Jackson. Implement JsonSerializable (or CborSerializable) from io.github.seonwkim.actor.serialization on your events and your state. Once events are stored, their JSON shape is a contract: add fields with defaults rather than renaming or removing them.

docs.title: Tables
docs.text:
The journal (event_journal, event_tag) and the snapshots (snapshot) are the tables of Pekko Persistence JDBC 1.1. spring.actor.persistence.initialize-schema decides when the starter creates them:

Value When embedded (default) Only in an embedded database, such as H2 in tests always On every start (the scripts use CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS) never You create them, for example with Flyway

The scripts are in the actor-persistence jar as io/github/seonwkim/actor/persistence/schema-<db>.sql for h2, postgresql, mysql and mariadb (tested on H2, PostgreSQL 16 and MySQL 8.4). Copy the one for your database into a Flyway or Liquibase migration for production. For Oracle and SQL Server the starter picks the matching dialect but ships no script and has no test: create their tables from the schema/oracle or schema/sqlserver scripts in the pekko-persistence-jdbc jar.

The actor system starts after the database is initialized (the starter's scripts, Flyway or Liquibase), so an actor can recover as soon as it is spawned.

The JDBC calls run on their own threads, as many as your Hikari pool has connections (10 otherwise). The starter never closes your DataSource.

docs.title: Tags for projections
docs.text:
A projection reads the events of one tag in the order they were stored, for example to fill a read model or publish to Kafka:

JavaKotlin 
.withTagger(event -> Set.of("accounts"))

.withTagger { setOf("accounts") }

See Projections.

docs.title: Failures
docs.text: If storing an event fails, the actor stops (Pekko's default) and the command gets no reply; an ask times out. Spawn the actor again to recover it from the stored events. Commands are never stored: a command that was being handled when the application stopped is lost, so let the caller retry.

docs.title: In a cluster
docs.text:
Run at most one actor per persistence id at a time: two actors that store events under the same id conflict on their sequence numbers. On one node, a regular actor with a given id runs once. On several nodes, each node could spawn its own copy of a regular actor, so don't spawn event-sourced actors per id with actorSystem.actor(...) in a cluster.

Make it a sharded entity. Sharding runs each entity id on one node of the cluster at a time, so there is one writer per persistence id. Return a SpringEventSourcedBehavior from a SpringShardedActor, with the entity id in the persistence id:

JavaKotlin 
@Component
public class AccountEntity implements SpringShardedActor<AccountEntity.Command> {

    // Commands cross nodes in a cluster: make them serializable too.
    public interface Command extends JsonSerializable {}

    public static final ShardedEntityType<Command> TYPE = ShardedEntityType.of(Command.class, "Account");

    @Override
    public ShardedEntityType<Command> entityType() {
        return TYPE;
    }

    @Override
    public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringShardedActorContext<Command> ctx) {
        return SpringEventSourcedBehavior.builder(
                        Command.class, Event.class, PersistenceId.of("Account", ctx.getEntityId()), new Account(0))
                .onCommand(Deposit.class, (es, account, cmd) -> es.persist(new Deposited(cmd.amount))
                        .thenReply(cmd, Account::balance))
                .onEvent(Deposited.class, (account, event) -> account.add(event.amount()))
                .build();
    }
}

@Component
class AccountEntity : SpringShardedActor<AccountEntity.Command> {

    // Commands cross nodes in a cluster: make them serializable too.
    interface Command : JsonSerializable

    override fun entityType(): ShardedEntityType<Command> = TYPE

    override fun create(ctx: SpringShardedActorContext<Command>): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
        SpringEventSourcedBehavior.builder(
            Command::class.java, Event::class.java, PersistenceId.of("Account", ctx.entityId), Account(0))
            .onCommand(Deposit::class.java) { es, _, cmd ->
                es.persist(Deposited(cmd.amount)).thenReply(cmd, Account::balance)
            }
            .onEvent(Deposited::class.java) { account, event -> account.add(event.amount) }
            .build()

    companion object {
        val TYPE: ShardedEntityType<Command> = ShardedEntityType.of(Command::class.java, "Account")
    }
}

When the entity's node leaves the cluster, the entity starts on another node and rebuilds its state from the journal. All nodes must use the same database. The starter's build tests this (ShardedEventSourcedActorTest in actor-persistence): three nodes send commands to one entity, the node that runs it leaves, and the entity answers from another node with the state from all the events stored before.

For a single global event-sourced actor, use a cluster singleton.

docs.title: Not supported yet
docs.text:
• R2DBC. The R2DBC plugin for Pekko 1.1 (pekko-persistence-r2dbc 1.0) supports only PostgreSQL and Yugabyte, and its next version needs Pekko 1.2. The journal runs on JDBC for now.
  • Framework commands (FrameworkCommand, spawning children by message) are not handled by event-sourced actors.
