docs.title: Projections
docs.text:
A projection reads the events that event-sourced actors store and writes them somewhere else: a read model in your database through Spring Data, or a Kafka topic through Spring Kafka. It remembers how far it got (its offset) in your database, so after a restart it resumes where it stopped.

The actor-projection module runs projections on Pekko Projections, with no Pekko types in your code.

docs.title: Add the module
docs.text:
dependencies {
    implementation("io.github.seonwkim:actor-spring-boot-starter:$version")
    implementation("io.github.seonwkim:actor-projection:$version") // brings actor-persistence
    implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-jdbc") // or data-jpa
}

docs.title: Tag the events
docs.text:
A projection reads the events of one tag. Tag them in the event-sourced actor:

JavaKotlin 
SpringEventSourcedBehavior.builder(Command.class, Event.class, PersistenceId.of("Account", id), new Account(0))
        // ...
        .withTagger(event -> Set.of("accounts"))
        .build();

SpringEventSourcedBehavior.builder(Command::class.java, Event::class.java, PersistenceId.of("Account", id), Account(0))
    // ...
    .withTagger { setOf("accounts") }
    .build()

Only events stored after you add the tagger carry the tag.

docs.title: Write a projection
docs.text:
A projection is a bean that implements SpringProjection:

JavaKotlin 
@Component
public class BalanceProjection implements SpringProjection<AccountActor.Event> {

    private final BalanceRepository balances; // a Spring Data repository

    public BalanceProjection(BalanceRepository balances) {
        this.balances = balances;
    }

    @Override
    public String name() {
        return "balances";
    }

    @Override
    public String tag() {
        return "accounts";
    }

    @Override
    public void handle(ProjectedEvent<AccountActor.Event> event) {
        if (event.event() instanceof AccountActor.Deposited deposited) {
            Balance balance = balances.findById(event.persistenceId()).orElseGet(() -> new Balance(event.persistenceId()));
            balance.add(deposited.amount());
            balances.save(balance);
        }
    }
}

@Component
class BalanceProjection(
    private val balances: BalanceRepository, // a Spring Data repository
) : SpringProjection<AccountActor.Event> {

    override fun name() = "balances"

    override fun tag() = "accounts"

    override fun handle(event: ProjectedEvent<AccountActor.Event>) {
        val deposited = event.event() as? AccountActor.Deposited ?: return
        val balance = balances.findById(event.persistenceId()).orElseGet { Balance(event.persistenceId()) }
        balance.add(deposited.amount)
        balances.save(balance)
    }
}

Every SpringProjection bean starts when the application starts. handle gets the events of its tag one at a time, in the order they were stored, with the id of the actor that stored each one (persistenceId(), such as Account|alice), its sequence number and its timestamp.

name() identifies the stored offset. Rename a projection and it starts again from the first event, which is also how you rebuild a read model.

docs.title: Exactly once or at least once
docs.text:
delivery() decides when the offset is stored:

delivery() Offset stored Use it for EXACTLY_ONCE (default) In the same transaction as handle Writes to the application's database: repositories, JdbcTemplate AT_LEAST_ONCE After handle, in batches Writes elsewhere, such as Kafka

handle always runs in a Spring transaction on your DataSource, using your PlatformTransactionManager bean when there is exactly one (otherwise a JdbcTransactionManager on the DataSource). With EXACTLY_ONCE, the rows handle writes and the new offset commit together, or roll back together.

When handle throws, the transaction rolls back and the projection restarts after a backoff, from the stored offset, so the event is handled again.

docs.title: Spring Kafka
docs.text:
Publish with AT_LEAST_ONCE, and wait for the send so a failed send fails the event:

JavaKotlin 
@Component
public class AccountEventsToKafka implements SpringProjection<AccountActor.Event> {

    private final KafkaTemplate<String, AccountActor.Event> kafka;

    public AccountEventsToKafka(KafkaTemplate<String, AccountActor.Event> kafka) {
        this.kafka = kafka;
    }

    @Override public String name() { return "account-events-to-kafka"; }
    @Override public String tag() { return "accounts"; }
    @Override public Delivery delivery() { return Delivery.AT_LEAST_ONCE; }

    @Override
    public void handle(ProjectedEvent<AccountActor.Event> event) throws Exception {
        kafka.send("account-events", event.persistenceId(), event.event()).get();
    }
}

@Component
class AccountEventsToKafka(
    private val kafka: KafkaTemplate<String, AccountActor.Event>,
) : SpringProjection<AccountActor.Event> {

    override fun name() = "account-events-to-kafka"

    override fun tag() = "accounts"

    override fun delivery() = Delivery.AT_LEAST_ONCE

    override fun handle(event: ProjectedEvent<AccountActor.Event>) {
        kafka.send("account-events", event.persistenceId(), event.event()).get()
    }
}

After a crash the last events are published again: consumers should ignore an event they have already seen (the persistence id and sequence number identify it).

docs.title: Tables
docs.text: The offsets live in pekko_projection_offset_store and pekko_projection_management. spring.actor.persistence.initialize-schema creates them together with the journal tables (embedded by default, always, or never). The scripts are in the actor-projection jar as io/github/seonwkim/actor/projection/schema-<db>.sql for h2, postgresql, mysql and mariadb (tested on H2, PostgreSQL 16 and MySQL 8.4); copy them into a Flyway or Liquibase migration for production.

docs.title: Cluster
docs.text: In cluster mode each projection runs as a cluster singleton named projection-<name>, so one node handles its events. When that node leaves, the projection starts on another node and resumes from the stored offset.

docs.title: Not supported yet
docs.text:
• Kafka as the source. Projections read events stored by event-sourced actors. Reading a Kafka topic (pekko-projection-kafka) is not wrapped: consume it with Spring Kafka's @KafkaListener.
  • Several instances of one projection. A projection reads its tag with one consumer. To spread a busy tag, split it into several tags (for example accounts-0 to accounts-3 by entity id) and declare one projection per tag.

docs.title: State in a Database
docs.text:
An actor's fields live in memory. They are lost when the actor stops: after a restart of the application, a deploy, a passivated or moved sharded entity, or a singleton that moves to another node. To keep the state, store it in your database with the tools you already use: Spring Data JPA, JdbcTemplate, R2DBC.

The pattern is simple: the actor loads its state when it starts and saves it in the message handler that changes it. Actors are Spring beans, so repositories and services are injected into them like into any other bean. No module of the starter is needed for this.

Use this when you need the latest state only. When the history of changes matters (an audit trail, read models, replays), use event sourcing instead.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Add Spring Data and your database driver next to the starter:

GradleMaven 
implementation("io.github.seonwkim:actor-spring-boot-starter:$version")
implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-data-jpa")
runtimeOnly("org.postgresql:postgresql")

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.postgresql</groupId>
    <artifactId>postgresql</artifactId>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
</dependency>

Configure the DataSource as usual (spring.datasource.*). The samples below use an Order JPA entity and this repository, from the persistence example:

JavaKotlin 
public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, String> {
    Optional<Order> findByOrderId(String orderId);
}

interface OrderRepository : JpaRepository<Order, String> {
    fun findByOrderId(orderId: String): Optional<Order>
}

docs.title: Load on start, save on change
docs.text:
The actor id is the key of the row. withState runs once when the actor starts: load the row there. Each handler that changes the state saves it before it replies.

JavaKotlin 
@Component
public class OrderActor implements SpringActor<OrderActor.Command> {

    private final OrderRepository orderRepository;

    public OrderActor(OrderRepository orderRepository) {
        this.orderRepository = orderRepository;
    }

    public interface Command {}

    public static class CreateOrder extends AskCommand<OrderResponse> implements Command {
        public final String customerId;
        public final double amount;

        public CreateOrder(String customerId, double amount) {
            this.customerId = customerId;
            this.amount = amount;
        }
    }

    public static class GetOrder extends AskCommand<OrderResponse> implements Command {}

    public record OrderResponse(boolean success, Order order, String message) {}

    @Override
    public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
        String orderId = actorContext.actorId();
        return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                .withState(ctx -> new OrderBehavior(
                        ctx, orderId, orderRepository, orderRepository.findByOrderId(orderId).orElse(null)))
                .onMessage(CreateOrder.class, OrderBehavior::onCreate)
                .onMessage(GetOrder.class, OrderBehavior::onGet)
                .build();
    }

    private static class OrderBehavior {
        private final SpringBehaviorContext<Command> ctx;
        private final String orderId;
        private final OrderRepository repository;
        private Order current; // null until the order is created

        OrderBehavior(SpringBehaviorContext<Command> ctx, String orderId, OrderRepository repository, Order current) {
            this.ctx = ctx;
            this.orderId = orderId;
            this.repository = repository;
            this.current = current;
        }

        SpringActorBehavior<Command> onCreate(CreateOrder msg) {
            if (current != null) {
                msg.reply(new OrderResponse(false, current, "Order already exists"));
                return SpringActorBehavior.same();
            }
            current = repository.save(new Order(orderId, msg.customerId, msg.amount));
            ctx.getLog().info("Order created: {}", orderId);
            msg.reply(new OrderResponse(true, current, "Order created"));
            return SpringActorBehavior.same();
        }

        SpringActorBehavior<Command> onGet(GetOrder msg) {
            msg.reply(current == null
                    ? new OrderResponse(false, null, "Order not found")
                    : new OrderResponse(true, current, "OK"));
            return SpringActorBehavior.same();
        }
    }
}

@Component
class OrderActor(private val orderRepository: OrderRepository) : SpringActor<OrderActor.Command> {

    sealed interface Command

    class CreateOrder(val customerId: String, val amount: Double) : AskCommand<OrderResponse>(), Command

    class GetOrder : AskCommand<OrderResponse>(), Command

    data class OrderResponse(val success: Boolean, val order: Order?, val message: String)

    override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> {
        val orderId = actorContext.actorId()
        return actorBehavior<Command>(actorContext)
            .withState { ctx ->
                OrderBehavior(ctx, orderId, orderRepository, orderRepository.findByOrderId(orderId).orElse(null))
            }
            .onMessage(CreateOrder::class.java) { state, msg -> state.onCreate(msg) }
            .onMessage(GetOrder::class.java) { state, msg -> state.onGet(msg) }
            .build()
    }

    class OrderBehavior(
        private val ctx: SpringBehaviorContext<Command>,
        private val orderId: String,
        private val repository: OrderRepository,
        private var current: Order?, // null until the order is created
    ) {
        fun onCreate(msg: CreateOrder): SpringActorBehavior<Command> {
            if (current != null) {
                msg.reply(OrderResponse(false, current, "Order already exists"))
                return SpringActorBehavior.same()
            }
            current = repository.save(Order(orderId, msg.customerId, msg.amount))
            ctx.log.info("Order created: {}", orderId)
            msg.reply(OrderResponse(true, current, "Order created"))
            return SpringActorBehavior.same()
        }

        fun onGet(msg: GetOrder): SpringActorBehavior<Command> {
            msg.reply(
                current?.let { OrderResponse(true, it, "OK") }
                    ?: OrderResponse(false, null, "Order not found"),
            )
            return SpringActorBehavior.same()
        }
    }
}

Because an actor handles one message at a time, the state and the row never see two changes at once. The database is still the source of truth: the next time the actor starts, it reads what was saved.

Save before you reply

Reply only after the save has succeeded. If the save throws, the caller gets no success reply, and the actor's field and the row don't drift apart. Catch the exception and reply with an error when the caller should learn about it instead of waiting for its timeout.

docs.title: Run it on the blocking dispatcher
docs.text:
JPA and JDBC calls block their thread until the database answers. On the default dispatcher, which every actor shares, a few slow queries can hold all its threads and stall unrelated actors. Spawn actors that block on the blocking dispatcher with withBlockingDispatcher():

JavaKotlin 
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/orders")
public class OrderController {

    private final SpringActorSystem actorSystem;

    public OrderController(SpringActorSystem actorSystem) {
        this.actorSystem = actorSystem;
    }

    @PostMapping("/{orderId}")
    public CompletionStage<OrderActor.OrderResponse> createOrder(
            @PathVariable String orderId, @RequestParam String customerId, @RequestParam double amount) {
        return actorSystem
                .actor(OrderActor.class)
                .withId(orderId)
                .withBlockingDispatcher()
                .getOrSpawn() // the running actor, or a new one on the blocking dispatcher
                .thenCompose(order -> order.ask(new OrderActor.CreateOrder(customerId, amount))
                        .withTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
                        .execute());
    }
}

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/orders")
class OrderController(private val actorSystem: SpringActorSystem) {

    // A suspend handler: see the Kotlin guide for what it needs on the classpath
    @PostMapping("/{orderId}")
    suspend fun createOrder(
        @PathVariable orderId: String,
        @RequestParam customerId: String,
        @RequestParam amount: Double,
    ): OrderActor.OrderResponse =
        actorSystem
            .actor<OrderActor, _>()
            .withId(orderId)
            .withBlockingDispatcher()
            .awaitGetOrSpawn() // the running actor, or a new one on the blocking dispatcher
            .awaitAsk(OrderActor.CreateOrder(customerId, amount), timeout = 5.seconds)
}

Use getOrSpawn() on the spawn builder, as above, rather than actorSystem.getOrSpawn(OrderActor.class, id): only the builder carries the dispatcher.

The blocking dispatcher is Pekko's default blocking dispatcher, a fixed pool of threads. To run it on virtual threads instead, set spring.actor.virtual-threads.enabled: true (or keep the default auto and turn on Spring Boot's spring.threads.virtual.enabled). See Dispatchers.

docs.title: Non-blocking calls with R2DBC
docs.text:
Spring Data R2DBC returns a Mono instead of blocking, so the actor can stay on the default dispatcher. Turn the result into a message with pipeToSelf: the actor handles it like any other message, one at a time, so its state stays safe without locks.

JavaKotlin 
@Component
public class ReactiveOrderActor implements SpringActor<ReactiveOrderActor.Command> {

    private final ReactiveOrderRepository repository; // a Spring Data R2DBC repository

    public ReactiveOrderActor(ReactiveOrderRepository repository) {
        this.repository = repository;
    }

    public interface Command {}

    public record SaveOrder(Order order) implements Command {}

    // The result of a save, sent by the actor to itself.
    private record SaveDone(Order saved, Throwable failure) implements Command {}

    @Override
    public SpringActorBehavior<Command> create(SpringActorContext actorContext) {
        return SpringActorBehavior.builder(Command.class, actorContext)
                .withState(ReactiveBehavior::new)
                .onMessage(SaveOrder.class, ReactiveBehavior::onSave)
                .onMessage(SaveDone.class, ReactiveBehavior::onSaveDone)
                .build();
    }

    private class ReactiveBehavior {
        private final SpringBehaviorContext<Command> ctx;
        private Order current;

        ReactiveBehavior(SpringBehaviorContext<Command> ctx) {
            this.ctx = ctx;
        }

        SpringActorBehavior<Command> onSave(SaveOrder msg) {
            // Returns at once; the save runs on R2DBC's threads, not the actor's.
            ctx.pipeToSelf(repository.save(msg.order()).toFuture(), SaveDone::new);
            return SpringActorBehavior.same();
        }

        SpringActorBehavior<Command> onSaveDone(SaveDone done) {
            if (done.failure() != null) {
                ctx.getLog().error("Save failed", done.failure());
            } else {
                current = done.saved(); // state changes only inside a message handler
            }
            return SpringActorBehavior.same();
        }
    }
}

@Component
class ReactiveOrderActor(
    private val repository: ReactiveOrderRepository, // a Spring Data R2DBC repository
) : SpringActor<ReactiveOrderActor.Command> {

    sealed interface Command

    data class SaveOrder(val order: Order) : Command

    // The result of a save, sent by the actor to itself.
    private data class SaveDone(val saved: Order?, val failure: Throwable?) : Command

    override fun create(actorContext: SpringActorContext): SpringActorBehavior<Command> =
        actorBehavior<Command>(actorContext)
            .withState { ctx -> ReactiveBehavior(ctx) }
            .onMessage(SaveOrder::class.java) { state, msg -> state.onSave(msg) }
            .onMessage(SaveDone::class.java) { state, done -> state.onSaveDone(done) }
            .build()

    private inner class ReactiveBehavior(private val ctx: SpringBehaviorContext<Command>) {
        private var current: Order? = null

        fun onSave(msg: SaveOrder): SpringActorBehavior<Command> {
            // Returns at once; the save runs on R2DBC's threads, not the actor's.
            ctx.pipeToSelf(repository.save(msg.order).toFuture()) { saved, failure -> SaveDone(saved, failure) }
            return SpringActorBehavior.same()
        }

        fun onSaveDone(done: SaveDone): SpringActorBehavior<Command> {
            if (done.failure != null) {
                ctx.log.error("Save failed", done.failure)
            } else {
                current = done.saved // state changes only inside a message handler
            }
            return SpringActorBehavior.same()
        }
    }
}

To reply to the caller once the save is done, carry the AskCommand in the result message and call reply in its handler.

Don't touch state in a callback

Never change actor state in subscribe(...), thenAccept(...) or any other callback: it runs on another thread, alongside the actor. Send the result to the actor with pipeToSelf and change state in the handler.

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
When one change writes several tables, put the writes in a @Transactional method of a Spring service and call it from the actor. Spring's transaction works as anywhere else, because the call runs on the actor's thread from start to end.

JavaKotlin 
@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final OrderRepository orders;
    private final OrderItemRepository items;

    public OrderService(OrderRepository orders, OrderItemRepository items) {
        this.orders = orders;
        this.items = items;
    }

    @Transactional
    public Order createWithItems(String orderId, String customerId, double amount, List<OrderItem> newItems) {
        Order order = orders.save(new Order(orderId, customerId, amount));
        for (OrderItem item : newItems) {
            item.setOrder(order);
            items.save(item);
        }
        return order;
    }
}

@Service
class OrderService(
    private val orders: OrderRepository,
    private val items: OrderItemRepository,
) {
    @Transactional
    fun createWithItems(orderId: String, customerId: String, amount: Double, newItems: List<OrderItem>): Order {
        val order = orders.save(Order(orderId, customerId, amount))
        for (item in newItems) {
            item.setOrder(order)
            items.save(item)
        }
        return order
    }
}

Inject OrderService into the actor instead of the repositories, and call it in the handler. Run the actor on the blocking dispatcher, as above. Don't put @Transactional on the actor class: the actor's handlers are not called through a Spring proxy.

docs.title: Snapshots of large state
docs.text:
When building the state from many rows is slow, store a snapshot of it now and then: serialize the state to JSON in a snapshot table every N changes or every few seconds, and on start, load the latest snapshot before falling back to the rows. The persistence example's SnapshotOrderActor does this with its own SnapshotStrategy and HybridSnapshotStrategy classes. These classes belong to the example, not to the starter.

Event-sourced actors have snapshots built in (snapshotEvery(n)).

docs.title: Choosing an approach
docs.text: Approach Use it when What to watch JPA or JDBC on the blocking dispatcher The app already uses JPA, as most Spring apps do Each call holds a thread of the blocking dispatcher. Size the pool, or use virtual threads R2DBC with pipeToSelf Many actors talk to the database at once, or the app is already reactive Every result comes back as a message, so each call needs a result message type Event sourcing with actor-persistence The history of changes matters, not only the latest state Events are a stored contract: their JSON shape must stay readable. See Event-Sourced Actors

docs.title: One writer per row
docs.text:
The pattern is safe because one actor owns one row. Keep it that way:

  • One node. A regular actor with a given id runs once per node, so one node never has two writers.
  • Several nodes. Each node can spawn its own OrderActor with the same id, and then two actors write the same row. Make the actor a sharded entity (one per id in the cluster) or, for a single global actor, a singleton. For extra safety, add a version column (@Version in JPA) so a stale write fails instead of overwriting.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Blocking on the default dispatcher. Always spawn JPA and JDBC actors with withBlockingDispatcher().
  • Changing state in callbacks. Use pipeToSelf.
  • Replying before saving. The caller then sees a success that may not be stored.
  • Lazy JPA associations. The actor keeps the entity after the transaction has ended; load what you need in the query (JOIN FETCH) or map it to your own class.

docs.title: Configuration Reference
docs.text:
This page lists every configuration key the starter and its modules read, with its default and what it does.

The keys are published as Spring Boot configuration metadata (META-INF/spring-configuration-metadata.json in the actor-autoconfigure and actor-metrics jars), so IDEs offer completion and documentation for them in application.yml and application.properties.

There are three kinds of settings:

  • Typed keys (spring.actor.*, management.*): bound to a properties class and checked at startup.
  • Raw Pekko keys (any other key under spring.actor.*): passed to Pekko as they are.
  • Environment variables (ACTOR_METRICS_*): read only by the optional metrics Java agent.

docs.title: Where the keys live
docs.text:
All typed keys are bound by three @ConfigurationProperties classes. The store and persistence modules (actor-jdbc, actor-redis, actor-persistence, actor-projection) have no properties class of their own: their keys are part of ActorProperties, and they take their connection from the application's DataSource or RedisConnectionFactory.

Class Prefix Module ActorProperties spring.actor actor-autoconfigure (in every starter) PekkoManagementProperties spring.actor.pekko.management actor-autoconfigure ActorMetricsProperties spring.actor.metrics actor-metrics

Typed keys are validated when the application starts. A bad value stops it with a message that names the key, for example spring.actor.remote.port must be between 0 and 65535, got 70000.

docs.title: Actor system
docs.text: Key Default Sets Pekko key Description spring.actor.enabled true none Whether the starter starts an actor system. false turns off every actor auto-configuration while the starter stays on the classpath. spring.actor.name system pekko.name Name of the actor system. Letters, digits, - and _, starting with a letter or digit. Nodes of one cluster must use the same name. spring.actor.provider local pekko.actor.provider How actors reach each other: local (one JVM), remote (reachable from other nodes, no cluster membership) or cluster. remote and cluster need actor-spring-boot-starter-cluster.

docs.title: Remoting
docs.text:
Used with provider: remote or provider: cluster.

Key Default Sets Pekko key Description spring.actor.remote.hostname Pekko's default pekko.remote.artery.canonical.hostname Host name or address other nodes use to reach this node. spring.actor.remote.port Pekko's default (25520) pekko.remote.artery.canonical.port Port this node listens on for other nodes, 0 to 65535. 0 picks a free port.

docs.title: Cluster
docs.text: Used with provider: cluster. See Cluster Formation and Split Brain and Leases.

docs.title: Joining
docs.text: Key Default Sets Pekko key Description spring.actor.cluster.join seed-nodes none How this node finds the cluster: seed-nodes (the listed nodes) or discovery (peers found through discovery.method, with Pekko Cluster Bootstrap). spring.actor.cluster.seed-nodes none pekko.cluster.seed-nodes Nodes to join at startup, as pekko://<name>@<host>:<port>. Not with join: discovery. spring.actor.cluster.join-self false none Joins this node to itself: a one-node cluster without seed nodes, also on port 0. For local runs and tests. Not with seed-nodes or join: discovery. With Pekko Management on the classpath, Cluster Bootstrap is not started for this node. spring.actor.cluster.roles none pekko.cluster.roles Roles of this node. Sharded actors and singletons can be limited to a role.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
Used with join: discovery.

Key Default Sets Pekko key Description spring.actor.cluster.discovery.method none pekko.discovery.method Where peers are found: jdbc (needs actor-jdbc), redis (needs actor-redis), custom (your PeerRegistry bean), kubernetes-api, dns or config. Required with join: discovery. A PeerRegistry bean of your own replaces the jdbc and redis stores. spring.actor.cluster.discovery.heartbeat-interval 5s none How often a node renews its own entry (jdbc, redis, custom). Must be positive. spring.actor.cluster.discovery.ttl 30s none How long an entry counts as alive after its last renewal (jdbc, redis, custom). Must be positive.

docs.title: Downing (split brain resolver)
docs.text: Key Default Sets Pekko key Description spring.actor.cluster.downing.strategy keep-majority with join: discovery, else none pekko.cluster.downing-provider-class, pekko.cluster.split-brain-resolver.active-strategy Which side of a network split stays up: keep-majority, lease-majority, static-quorum, keep-oldest, down-all or none. A cluster without downing logs a warning. spring.actor.cluster.downing.quorum-size none pekko.cluster.split-brain-resolver.static-quorum.quorum-size Nodes a side needs to stay up. Required with static-quorum; at least 1. Set it above half the cluster's size.

docs.title: Leases
docs.text: Key Default Sets Pekko key Description spring.actor.cluster.lease.store none none Where leases live: jdbc (needs actor-jdbc), redis (needs actor-redis) or custom (your LeaseStore bean). Required by downing.strategy: lease-majority, singleton.use-lease and sharding.use-lease. spring.actor.cluster.lease.ttl 120s spring-actor.lease.heartbeat-timeout How long a lease stays held after its last renewal before another node may take it. spring.actor.cluster.lease.renew-interval 12s spring-actor.lease.heartbeat-interval How often the holder renews a lease. spring.actor.cluster.lease.expiry-margin 10s spring-actor.lease.expiry-margin The holder treats its lease as lost this long before the ttl ends, so it stops before another node can take the lease. Must be less than ttl. spring.actor.cluster.singleton.role none pekko.cluster.singleton.role Cluster singletons run only on nodes with this role. Set the same value on every node. spring.actor.cluster.singleton.use-lease false pekko.cluster.singleton.use-lease A cluster singleton runs only while it holds a lease, so two nodes never run it at once, even during a split. spring.actor.cluster.sharding.use-lease false pekko.cluster.sharding.use-lease Each shard runs only while it holds a lease.

docs.title: Pekko Management
docs.text: Key Default Description spring.actor.pekko.management.enabled true Whether to start the Pekko Management HTTP server and Cluster Bootstrap in cluster mode, when the Pekko Management libraries are on the classpath. The server's own settings (spring.actor.pekko.management.http.port, ...) are raw Pekko keys.

docs.title: Database tables
docs.text: Key Default Description spring.actor.jdbc.initialize-schema embedded When to create the actor-jdbc tables (actor_peer, actor_lease): embedded (only in an embedded database), always, or never (you create them from the schema-*.sql files in actor-jdbc). spring.actor.persistence.initialize-schema embedded When to create the actor-persistence tables (event_journal, event_tag, snapshot) and the actor-projection offset tables: embedded, always or never. See Event-Sourced Actors and Projections.

docs.title: Dispatchers and threads
docs.text:
See Dispatchers.

Key Default Sets Pekko key Description spring.actor.dispatchers.<name>.executor none <name>.* Declares a dispatcher that runs on the named Spring Executor bean (for example a ThreadPoolTaskExecutor). Actors pick it with withDispatcherFromConfig("<name>"). spring.actor.dispatchers.<name>.virtual false <name>.executor Declares a dispatcher that runs on virtual threads, one per task. Set either executor or virtual: true, not both. spring.actor.dispatchers.<name>.throughput Pekko's default (5) <name>.throughput Messages an actor processes before its thread moves to the next actor. At least 1. spring.actor.virtual-threads.enabled auto pekko.actor.default-blocking-io-dispatcher.executor Runs the blocking dispatcher (withBlockingDispatcher()) on virtual threads: auto, true or false. auto follows spring.threads.virtual.enabled. The default dispatcher always stays on platform threads.

A dispatcher name is letters, digits, - and _, and must not be pekko or the name of a typed key (name, cluster, dispatchers, ...).

docs.title: Startup checks
docs.text:
See What not to do in an actor bean.

Key Default Description spring.actor.validation.actor-beans warn What happens when an actor bean has a mutable instance field (neither static, final nor injected) or is a Spring AOP proxy: warn logs each problem, fail stops startup, off skips the checks.

docs.title: Reliable delivery
docs.text:
See Reliable Delivery. A receiver can override idempotency-ttl in code, and a sender its whole RetryPolicy.

Key Default Sets Pekko key Description spring.actor.delivery.idempotency-ttl 10m spring-actor.delivery.idempotency-ttl How long a receiver remembers the idempotency key of a message it handled; a message with a remembered key is acknowledged again without running the handler. Must be positive. spring.actor.delivery.max-remembered-keys 10000 spring-actor.delivery.max-remembered-keys The most keys one receiver remembers; past it, the oldest are forgotten first. At least 1. spring.actor.delivery.retry.max-attempts 5 none Attempts in total, including the first. spring.actor.delivery.retry.timeout 30s none Time from the first attempt after which a sender gives up; no attempt starts after it. spring.actor.delivery.retry.attempt-timeout 3s none How long one attempt waits for the ack. spring.actor.delivery.retry.initial-backoff 200ms none The backoff before the second attempt; it doubles up to max-backoff, with full jitter. spring.actor.delivery.retry.max-backoff 5s none The longest backoff between attempts.

docs.title: Blue-green generation
docs.text:
See The active generation. Blue-green activation is on when color is set.

Key Default Description spring.actor.generation.color none This deployment's color, for example blue or green. Setting it turns on blue-green activation, DeploymentGeneration and the generation Actuator endpoint; each color runs with its own value. spring.actor.generation.store none Where the active generation is kept: jdbc (the actor_generation table, needs actor-jdbc), redis (needs actor-redis) or custom (your GenerationStore bean). spring.actor.generation.name spring.actor.name Name of the record both colors share in the store. spring.actor.generation.refresh 1s How long a read of the active generation is reused before the store is read again: the longest a node takes to see an activation made elsewhere. 0 reads the store every time. Must not be negative.

docs.title: Shutdown
docs.text:
See Graceful shutdown.

Key Default Description spring.actor.shutdown.timeout 20s How long closing the Spring context waits for the actor system's coordinated shutdown. Must be positive. spring.actor.shutdown.exit-process true When the actor system terminates by itself (for example after this node is downed), the context closes; with this set, the process then exits with status 1 so an orchestrator restarts it.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Needs actor-metrics and a Micrometer MeterRegistry. See Monitoring.

Key Default Description spring.actor.metrics.enabled true Whether to register the actor meters, the actor MetricsRegistry bean and, in cluster mode, the actor.cluster.* and actor.sharding.* meters. spring.actor.metrics.path-tag-limit 0 How many actor paths get their own actor.path tag on the actor.message.* meters; the rest share actor.path=other. 0 adds no actor.path tag, so the series count never grows with the number of actors.

docs.title: Actuator
docs.text:
Need Spring Boot Actuator. See Health checks and The actors endpoint.

Key Default Description management.health.actor.enabled true Whether to add the actorSystem and (in cluster mode) actorCluster health components. management.endpoint.actors.access unrestricted Access to the actors endpoint (cluster mode): unrestricted, read-only or none. none turns it off. Spring Boot adds this key for every endpoint. management.endpoint.actors.cache.time-to-live 0ms How long a response of the actors endpoint may be cached. Spring Boot adds this key for every endpoint.

management.endpoint.actors.enabled also appears in the metadata. Spring Boot generates it for every endpoint and marks it deprecated; use access instead.

docs.title: Spring Boot keys that matter
docs.text:
These are Spring Boot's own keys. The starter reads or depends on them:

Key Why spring.threads.virtual.enabled spring.actor.virtual-threads.enabled: auto follows it. server.shutdown: graceful and spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase The web server drains requests before the actor system stops. See Shutdown order. management.endpoints.web.exposure.include The actors and prometheus endpoints are exposed over HTTP only when listed here. management.endpoint.health.group.readiness.include Add actorCluster to gate traffic on cluster membership.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
spring:
  actor:
    name: orders
    provider: cluster
    remote:
      hostname: 10.0.0.7
      port: 25520
    cluster:
      seed-nodes:
        - pekko://orders@10.0.0.7:25520
        - pekko://orders@10.0.0.8:25520
      roles: api
      downing:
        strategy: keep-majority
    shutdown:
      timeout: 25s

docs.title: Raw Pekko keys (spring.actor.*)
docs.text:
Every other key under spring.actor.* is passed unchanged to the Pekko actor system configuration, with the spring.actor prefix removed. For example, spring.actor.pekko.loglevel becomes pekko.loglevel, and a dispatcher defined at spring.actor.my-dispatcher becomes my-dispatcher. Comma-separated string values are turned into lists, and a single value for a key that Pekko reads as a list is a one-item list: spring.actor.pekko.cluster.seed-nodes=pekko://orders@10.0.0.7:25521 works like seed-nodes[0]. See the Pekko reference configuration for the available keys.

spring:
  actor:
    pekko:
      loglevel: INFO
      coordinated-shutdown:
        phases:
          cluster-leave:
            timeout: 10s

Raw keys win

When a raw key and a typed key set the same Pekko key to different values, the raw key wins and the starter logs a warning that names both, for example spring.actor.pekko.name=raw overrides spring.actor.name=typed. Prefer the typed key.

docs.title: Metrics agent environment variables (ACTOR_METRICS_*)
docs.text:
Not Spring keys

These are environment variables, read by the optional metrics Java agent and by the metrics registry builder with System.getenv (falling back to a JVM system property of the same name). They are not Spring configuration keys: setting them in application.yml or application.properties has no effect, and they do not appear in the Spring configuration metadata.

Variable Default Description ACTOR_METRICS_ENABLED true Read by the agent at JVM startup: false skips all instrumentation. Also read by the metrics registry builder to set the enabled flag of the metrics configuration. ACTOR_METRICS_INSTRUMENT_<MODULE> true Read by the agent: false skips instrumentation for one module. <MODULE> is the module id in upper case with - replaced by _: ACTOR_LIFECYCLE, MESSAGE_PROCESSING, MAILBOX, SYSTEM, SCHEDULER, STASH. ACTOR_METRICS_TAG_<NAME> none Adds a global tag to every agent metric. The tag name is <NAME> in lower case with _ replaced by .; for example ACTOR_METRICS_TAG_APPLICATION=my-app adds the tag application=my-app. ACTOR_METRICS_SAMPLING_RATE 1.0 Sampling rate between 0.0 and 1.0. 
ACTOR_METRICS_TAG_APPLICATION=my-app \
ACTOR_METRICS_INSTRUMENT_MAILBOX=false \
java -javaagent:actor-metrics-{version}-agent.jar -jar app.jar

docs.title: Deployments
docs.text:
This guide covers how to release a new version of a clustered actor application without failing requests: rolling updates, canary releases and blue-green switches, and how to change messages so that two versions can run side by side.

The commands come from the Kubernetes example (example/kubernetes), which runs the chat example as a three-pod cluster on a local kind cluster. The ideas apply to any platform.

docs.title: Choosing a strategy
docs.text:
Strategy What runs Traffic Versions mix in one cluster Script Rolling update One cluster; old and new pods side by side during the rollout Moves pod by pod Yes kubectl set image Canary One cluster; a few new pods join the running cluster Share = canary pods / all pods Yes scripts/canary.sh Blue-green Two separate clusters (blue and green) Switches in one step No scripts/blue-green.sh
  • Use a rolling update for most releases. It needs no extra capacity beyond one pod.
  • Use a canary when you want a few real requests on the new version first, with a quick way back.
  • Use blue-green when the new version cannot talk to the old one (an incompatible message change) or when you want to switch all traffic at once. It needs twice the pods for a while, and in-memory state does not move.

All three rely on the graceful shutdown settings: each old pod leaves the cluster on purpose, so its sharded entities and singletons move instead of waiting for the split brain resolver.

docs.title: Rolling update
docs.text:
A rolling update replaces pods one at a time inside one cluster. The example's Deployment adds a new pod before it removes an old one, so the cluster never drops below its size:

spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 0    # never fewer than 3 ready pods
      maxSurge: 1          # start one new pod before stopping an old one

Each new pod joins the running cluster. Its readiness probe includes actorCluster, so it gets traffic only once it is an Up member (see Health checks). Then Kubernetes stops an old pod: the preStop sleep lets the load balancer drop it, and coordinated shutdown moves its entities to the other nodes.

kubectl set image deployment/spring-actor spring-actor=spring-actor-chat:v2 -n spring-actor
kubectl rollout status deployment/spring-actor -n spring-actor

# Go back to the previous version
kubectl rollout undo deployment/spring-actor -n spring-actor

docs.title: Canary
docs.text:
A canary runs a few pods of the new version in the same cluster as the main pods. canary.sh start copies the live Deployment as spring-actor-canary with the new image and a track: canary label. The Services select app=spring-actor, so they send the canary pods their share of the requests: with three main pods and one canary, about one in four.

cd example/kubernetes
scripts/canary.sh start spring-actor-chat:v3      # one canary pod; `start <image> 2` for two
scripts/canary.sh promote                         # roll the main pods to v3, then remove the canary
# scripts/canary.sh abort                         # or remove the canary and keep the main pods as they are

Because the canary is a member of the same cluster, sharded entities can move to it and it exchanges messages with the old pods. Both versions must read each other's messages and entity state (see Message compatibility).

docs.title: Blue-green
docs.text:
Blue-green starts the new version as a second, separate cluster. blue-green.sh deploy copies the live Deployment as spring-actor-green with the new image, labels its pods app=spring-actor-green, and points its Kubernetes API discovery at that label (--spring.actor.pekko.discovery.kubernetes-api.pod-label-selector=app=spring-actor-green). So green forms its own cluster and never exchanges messages with blue.

Before green starts, deploy also copies each NetworkPolicy that selects app=spring-actor (for example spring-actor-green from spring-actor, and spring-actor-green-store from spring-actor-store in the discovery overlays), with every app=spring-actor selector changed to app=spring-actor-green. Green gets the same restrictions as blue, and remoting (25520) and management (7626) open only between pods of the same color: blue and green cannot reach each other's cluster ports. A canary keeps app=spring-actor, so blue's policies cover it.

docs.title: The release pipeline
docs.text:
A blue-green release runs in four stages. Each one waits for a signal before the next starts:

Stage Command Waits for 1. Warm up blue-green.sh deploy <image> every green pod answers UP on /actuator/health/warmup, then is ready 2. Activate blue-green.sh activate the generation endpoint accepts green; then the HTTP Service's selector picks the green pods 3. Verify blue-green.sh verify the generation record says green, and the Service's ready endpoints are exactly the green pods 4. Retire blue-green.sh retire run it once green has served for a while; it deletes blue 
cd example/kubernetes
scripts/blue-green.sh deploy spring-actor-chat:v4   # start green beside blue and wait until it is warm
scripts/blue-green.sh activate                      # green becomes the active generation; the Service selects it
scripts/blue-green.sh verify                        # wait until only green pods serve
# scripts/blue-green.sh rollback                    # activate blue again (a new epoch) and select it
scripts/blue-green.sh retire                        # delete blue

The first stage gates on warm-up, not on kubectl rollout status or the Deployment's Available condition. Those follow traffic readiness, and in a pipeline where the standby color refuses traffic until it is activated they never come. The warm-up group says only that the pod can be activated:

  • the pod is an Up member of its cluster,
  • the cluster has at least management.health.actor.warmup.min-members Up members (the example sets 2),
  • and the discovery store answers, when the cluster forms through jdbc or redis discovery.

It never depends on which color is active. The three probes stay apart: liveness says whether to restart the pod, readiness whether to send it traffic, and warm-up whether it can be activated (see Health checks).

In-memory state does not move: entities, singletons and topics start empty on green. Keep state that must survive the switch in a database or event journal both clusters read (State in a Database, Event-Sourced Actors). Until retire, rollback sends traffic back to blue, which still has its state.

docs.title: The active generation
docs.text:
Which color is active is a record in the store the cluster already uses (Redis or the database), not only a Service selector. Each record is a generation: a color, an epoch that grows by one with every activation, the deployment operation ID that activated it, and when. The application can read it, and the pipeline changes it only through a compare-and-set:

  • Competing deploys fail loudly. An activation names the epoch it expects to be active. If another deploy activated in between, it is rejected (EPOCH_MISMATCH, HTTP 409) and nothing changes. Of several activations that expect the same epoch, exactly one wins.
  • Retries are idempotent. An activation carries an operation ID. Retrying it with the same color and expected epoch returns the generation it activated the first time (ALREADY_ACTIVATED, HTTP 200), even after the epoch has moved on. The same operation ID with another color or epoch is OPERATION_CONFLICT (409). A pipeline keeps the expected epoch and the operation ID it used, and sends both again when it retries.
  • Old work stays fenced. Blue, then green, then blue again gives epochs 1, 2 and 3. Work that blue stamped in its first turn carries epoch 1 and is refused in its second (epoch 3), because the epoch never goes back.

Turn it on in each color with its color and a store:

spring:
  actor:
    generation:
      color: blue          # green in the other deployment
      store: redis         # jdbc: the actor_generation table; custom: your GenerationStore bean
      # name: orders       # the record both colors share; default: spring.actor.name
      # refresh: 1s        # how long a node reuses a read of the record
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,generation
  endpoint:
    generation:
      access: unrestricted   # activation is a write: read-only by default

The generation endpoint. GET /actuator/generation returns this node's color and the active generation. POST /actuator/generation with color, expectedEpoch (0 before the first activation) and operationId activates a color:

curl -u deployer:$PASSWORD -X POST localhost:8080/actuator/generation \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"color":"green","expectedEpoch":1,"operationId":"release-2026-11-11-1"}'
# {"outcome":"ACTIVATED","generation":{"color":"green","epoch":2,"operationId":"release-2026-11-11-1",...}}

Activation needs an authenticated user: a request without one is answered 401 (UNAUTHENTICATED). Secure the endpoint with Spring Security like any other write endpoint, for example with a role:

JavaKotlin 
@Bean
SecurityFilterChain actuator(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http.securityMatcher(EndpointRequest.to("generation"))
            .authorizeHttpRequests(requests -> requests
                    .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.POST).hasRole("DEPLOYER")
                    .anyRequest().permitAll())
            .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults())
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable()) // called by a pipeline, not a browser session
            .build();
}

@Bean
fun actuator(http: HttpSecurity): SecurityFilterChain =
    http.securityMatcher(EndpointRequest.to("generation"))
        .authorizeHttpRequests {
            it.requestMatchers(HttpMethod.POST).hasRole("DEPLOYER")
                .anyRequest().permitAll()
        }
        .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults())
        .csrf { it.disable() } // called by a pipeline, not a browser session
        .build()

Audit. Every attempt that reaches the endpoint, or DeploymentGeneration.activate in your code, publishes an ActivationEvent (an ApplicationEvent) with the requested color, expected epoch, operation ID, the user's name and the result. The starter also logs it (INFO when accepted, WARN when rejected) and counts it in actor.generation.activations, tagged with outcome. A request that Spring Security turns away never reaches the endpoint, so it shows in Spring Security's events instead.

Fencing in your code. Inject DeploymentGeneration. Stamp work with stamp() where it starts (it fails when this node's color is not active), and check(epoch) it where it runs. A stale epoch throws StaleGenerationException, the retryable outcome of reliable delivery:

JavaKotlin 
long epoch = generation.stamp();                       // where the work starts
sender.send(new ChargeOrder(orderId, epoch), key);

.onMessage(ChargeOrder.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
    generation.check(msg.epoch());                     // StaleGenerationException if it is old
    payments.charge(msg.orderId());
    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
})

val epoch = generation.stamp()                         // where the work starts
sender.send(ChargeOrder(orderId, epoch), key)

.onMessage(ChargeOrder::class.java) { _, msg ->
    generation.check(msg.epoch)                        // StaleGenerationException if it is old
    payments.charge(msg.orderId)
    SpringActorBehavior.same()
}

A node reuses a read of the record for spring.actor.generation.refresh (1 second), so for up to that long after an activation elsewhere it still accepts the old epoch. Where that matters, keep the epoch with the data and compare it in the write itself (UPDATE ... WHERE epoch <= ?).

Stores. jdbc keeps one row per activation in actor_generation (created with the other actor-jdbc tables): the primary key on deployment and epoch is the compare-and-set. redis keeps the record and the operation IDs in two hashes and changes them in one Lua script. Redis replicates asynchronously, so a failover can lose an activation it had just accepted; use jdbc where that is not acceptable. Your own GenerationStore bean replaces both, and must pass GenerationStoreContract from actor-test.

docs.title: Requests at the cutover
docs.text:
In the example the Service selector switches the colors, and readiness does not depend on the color. So deploy waits for warm-up and then for the green pods to be ready. Warm-up alone is not enough there: a pod can be warm before its readiness probe first passes (the example's probe starts after 30 seconds), and a Service that selects only pods that are not ready yet has no endpoints. Measured on kind with test-strategies.sh (four workers asking sharded entities):

deploy waited for Requests Failed Service served only green warm-up only 15,057 20, all within 10 seconds after activate 15 seconds after activate warm-up, then ready (the script today) 23,151 and 22,890 (two runs) 0 and 0 at the first check after activate

Blue keeps running and serving until retire, so a node whose proxy rules still point at blue for a moment after the switch still gets answers.

When readiness itself switches the colors (the standby refuses traffic until it is activated, and one Service selects both), the cutover waits for readiness to propagate: each pod's readiness probe has to pass (periodSeconds times successThreshold for the new color, periodSeconds times failureThreshold for the old one), then the endpoint controller and every node's kube-proxy update. Shorter probe intervals shorten that window but don't close it: requests routed during it reach a pod that is about to leave or none at all. This mode was not measured here. Close the window with draining instead:

  • switch with the Service selector (or another routing change) while both colors are ready, and keep the old pods running until verify shows the Service no longer selects them (retire comes last);
  • the preStop sleep (10 seconds in the example) keeps a terminating pod serving while the endpoint removal propagates;
  • server.shutdown: graceful finishes the requests the pod has already accepted.

scripts/test-strategies.sh prints, for the blue-green step, how long the Service took to serve only green and how many requests failed from activation on.

docs.title: Testing the strategies under load
docs.text:
scripts/test-strategies.sh runs all three strategies on the kind cluster from setup-local.sh while scripts/load.sh sends requests, and fails if any request failed:

cd example/kubernetes
./setup-local.sh
scripts/test-strategies.sh
# rolling        total=... ok=... failed=0 ok
# canary         total=... ok=... failed=0 ok
# blue-green     total=... ok=... failed=0 ok

It runs, in order: a rolling update to v2 (120 seconds of load), a canary of v3 that is then promoted (180 seconds), and a blue-green release of v4 through the four stages above (90 seconds, then retire). Each step's load runs four workers that ask sharded entities (/hello?message=hi&entityId=e<0-49>).

What it checks and what it does not:

  • load.sh counts a request as ok only when the actor replied. The chat app answers 200 with Request timed out ... when an ask fails, so the HTTP status alone would hide lost messages.
  • The new versions are retags of the same image, so it checks the rollout mechanics (joining, leaving, entities moving, the Service switching), not a change in the code.

docs.title: Message compatibility across versions
docs.text:
Rolling updates and canaries mix versions in one cluster. Old and new pods exchange messages, and a sharded entity can move from an old pod to a new one. Every message and every piece of entity state that crosses nodes must be readable by both versions:

  • Add fields as optional. The old version must accept a message with the new field, and the new version a message without it.
  • Don't rename or remove fields or message types in the same release.
  • Keep each type on the same serializer (JsonSerializable or CborSerializable).
  • Make an incompatible change in two releases: first one that reads both formats, then one that writes the new format.

For example, a second release adds an optional field to a command:

JavaKotlin 
// v1
public static class SayHello extends AskCommand<String> implements Command {
    public final String message;

    public SayHello(String message) {
        this.message = message;
    }
}

// v2: a new, optional field. Messages from v1 nodes don't have it.
public static class SayHello extends AskCommand<String> implements Command {
    public final String message;
    @Nullable public final String language;

    public SayHello(String message, @Nullable String language) {
        this.message = message;
        this.language = language;
    }
}

// v1
class SayHello(val message: String) : AskCommand<String>(), Command

// v2: a new, optional field. Messages from v1 nodes don't have it.
class SayHello(val message: String, val language: String? = null) : AskCommand<String>(), Command

The starter's build checks this on every change: MixedVersionMessageTest runs two nodes in one JVM, one with a message class and one with the same class plus a field, and sends a message each way between sharded entities. The old node reads the new message and ignores the field it doesn't know; the new node reads the old message with the missing field as null. The test covers JsonSerializable messages with the starter's default Jackson settings. It does not cover a renamed or removed field, a renamed class, or stored events and snapshots. To run the same check on your own messages, see Two versions of a message in one cluster.

On Kubernetes, this was also measured on kind with a canary of the chat app: adding a field to SayHello lost no requests (28,842 of 28,842), while renaming the class lost 104 of 7,105, which timed out because the old nodes could not read the new type.

Blue-green never mixes versions. The two clusters never exchange messages, so the message format can change freely. Stored state is different: events and snapshots in a journal or database must still be readable by the new version (see Event-Sourced Actors).

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text: Strategy How to go back Rolling update kubectl rollout undo deployment/spring-actor -n spring-actor: a rolling update in the other direction, so the same compatibility rules apply Canary scripts/canary.sh abort removes the canary pods; the main pods were never changed Blue-green scripts/blue-green.sh rollback until retire; blue still has its in-memory state

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
This guide covers how to see what your actors do in production: Micrometer meters for actors, mailboxes, dispatchers, the cluster and sharding; the read-only actors Actuator endpoint; traces that cross tell and ask; log lines with actor context; and a ready-made Grafana dashboard with Prometheus alerts.

None of it needs a Java agent. An optional agent adds a few more meters (see The optional Java agent).

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Add actor-metrics, Actuator and a Micrometer registry (Prometheus here):

GradleMaven 
dependencies {
    implementation 'io.github.seonwkim:actor-metrics:1.0.0'
    implementation 'org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-actuator'
    implementation 'io.micrometer:micrometer-registry-prometheus'
}

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.seonwkim</groupId>
    <artifactId>actor-metrics</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
    <artifactId>micrometer-registry-prometheus</artifactId>
</dependency>

Expose the Prometheus endpoint:

management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info,metrics,prometheus

That is all. With a MeterRegistry bean (Actuator registers one), every actor the starter spawns is metered. spring.actor.metrics.enabled=false turns every meter on this page off.

docs.title: Actor meters
docs.text:
The actor system the starter builds records these from hooks it owns: a behavior interceptor, an instrumented default mailbox and the default dispatchers' executors.

Meter Type Tags What actor.message.processed Counter actor.class, dispatcher, system Messages actors processed actor.message.processing.time Timer actor.class, dispatcher, system Time spent processing a message actor.message.failures Counter actor.class, dispatcher, system Messages whose processing threw actor.lifecycle.restarts Counter actor.class, dispatcher, system Restarts by supervision actor.lifecycle.active Gauge actor.class, dispatcher, system Actors running actor.mailbox.size Gauge actor.class, dispatcher, system Messages waiting in mailboxes actor.mailbox.time Timer actor.class, dispatcher, system Time a message waited in the mailbox actor.dispatcher.threads Gauge dispatcher, system Threads in the dispatcher's pool actor.dispatcher.threads.active Gauge dispatcher, system Threads running tasks actor.dispatcher.queued Gauge dispatcher, system Tasks waiting for a thread
  • actor.class is the simple name of the actor's class (for a sharded actor, its SpringShardedActor class), dispatcher the Pekko dispatcher id (pekko.actor.default-dispatcher), system the actor system's name.
  • Meters are per actor class, not per actor, so the series count does not grow with the number of actors: 10,000 entities of one class have the same series as one. A test spawns 10,000 actors and checks it.
  • Path tags are opt-in and capped: spring.actor.metrics.path-tag-limit=50 adds actor.path to the actor.message.* meters for the first 50 actor paths seen, and actor.path=other for every other actor.

What is not covered:

  • Mailbox meters and actor.lifecycle.active count actors on the default mailbox. An actor spawned with a bounded or a configured mailbox keeps that mailbox and has only the actor.message.* and restart meters.
  • Dispatcher meters cover the default and the blocking dispatcher (and dispatchers that inherit their executor) on Pekko's fork-join or thread-pool executor. A dispatcher on a Spring Executor bean is measured by Spring Boot's own executor metrics; one on virtual threads has no pool to measure.
  • A behavior from SpringActorBehavior.wrap (a raw Pekko behavior) is metered outside its own supervision, so its failures and restarts are not seen.

docs.title: Overhead
docs.text:
ActorMetersBenchmark (./gradlew :actor-autoconfigure:actorMetersBenchmark) sends bursts of 1,000,000 tells to one actor in two actor systems side by side, one with the meters off and one with them on, alternating rounds. On an Apple M5 laptop with Java 21 and a SimpleMeterRegistry (the machine was busy with other builds, so treat the numbers as rough):

ns per message (median of 15 rounds) meters off 126 meters on 379 overhead about 250

The cost per message is two timer updates (processing time and time in mailbox), four System.nanoTime() calls and one small object in the mailbox; actor.message.processed reads the processing timer's count and costs nothing. An actor that does real work (microseconds per message) pays a small fraction of that; one that only forwards messages pays about three times the bare cost. Run the benchmark on your hardware before relying on these numbers, and set spring.actor.metrics.enabled=false where the overhead matters more than the meters.

docs.title: Cluster and sharding meters
docs.text:
With spring.actor.provider=cluster, these meters are added too.

Meter Type Tags What actor.cluster.members Gauge none Members this node sees actor.cluster.unreachable Gauge none Of them, how many are unreachable actor.cluster.leader Gauge none 1 while this node is the leader, else 0. Pekko's leader is the Up member with the lowest address, not the oldest actor.cluster.singleton.host Gauge none 1 while this node runs the cluster singletons (it is the oldest member that is up and has spring.actor.cluster.singleton.role, if set), else 0 actor.cluster.events Counter event Cluster events this node received after the application started: MemberUp, MemberRemoved, UnreachableMember and the other cluster event types. Every type has a series from the start, so a dashboard sees 0, not a gap actor.sharding.regions Gauge type Shard regions that host the entity type in the cluster actor.sharding.shards Gauge type The entity type's shards on this node actor.sharding.entities Gauge type The entity type's running entities on this node

The actor.sharding.* gauges ask every shard region in the cluster, so a scrape never waits for the answer: each read shows the answer to the previous read. Sum actor.sharding.entities over the nodes for the cluster total.

Pekko reports no rebalance events, so there is no rebalance counter. A shard that moves shows up as actor.sharding.shards going down on one node and up on another.

Alert on actor.cluster.unreachable > 0 for longer than the split brain resolver's stable-after, and on a members count below the replica count. The alert rules do the first.

docs.title: Prometheus names
docs.text:
Micrometer's Prometheus registry turns the dots into underscores and adds a suffix per type:

Meter type Example Prometheus series Counter actor.message.processed actor_message_processed_total Timer actor.mailbox.time actor_mailbox_time_seconds_count, _seconds_sum, _seconds_max (and _seconds_bucket with histograms on) Gauge actor.cluster.members actor_cluster_members

Tags become labels the same way: actor.class is actor_class.

docs.title: The actors endpoint
docs.text:
With Actuator on the classpath, cluster mode adds a read-only actors endpoint. Like every Actuator endpoint except health, it is not exposed over HTTP until you name it:

management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,actors

GET /actuator/actors returns:

  • node: this node's address.
  • cluster: this node's view of the cluster: its own status (selfStatus), whether it is unreachable or terminated, the member and unreachable counts, whether it is the leader and the singletonHost, and nodes, each member oldest first with its address, status, roles and whether it is reachable.
  • sharding: for each sharded entity type, its type, the regions in the cluster, and the shards and entities on this node.

A read asks every shard region, so it can take up to 3 seconds. management.endpoint.actors.access=none turns the endpoint off.

docs.title: Health
docs.text: The actorSystem and actorCluster health components are described in Running in Production.

docs.title: Tracing
docs.text:
With an ObservationRegistry bean (Spring Boot Actuator creates one) and a tracer such as micrometer-tracing-bridge-otel or micrometer-tracing-bridge-brave, the trace of the current request crosses tell and ask. Without an ObservationRegistry, messages are sent as they are and nothing is added.

  • Sending a message in an observation (an HTTP request, another actor's message) creates an actor.send span (tell Order, ask GetBalance). For ask it ends when the reply or the timeout arrives.
  • The receiving actor handles the message inside an actor.receive span, a child of the send. Its log lines carry traceId and spanId in the MDC, as Spring Boot's tracing sets them.
  • Between nodes, sharded messages and messages to remote actors carry the W3C traceparent fields next to the message, which keeps its own serializer (JsonSerializable, CborSerializable).
  • Spans carry the low-cardinality tags actor.operation and actor.message (the message class); the receive span also has the actor path as a high-cardinality tag.

The trace is the observation current on the sending thread. A tell or ask from a CompletionStage callback (getOrSpawn().thenCompose(actor -> actor.ask(...))) runs on an actor thread with no observation, so it starts no span. Get the handle first, then send from the request's thread, or carry the context into the callback with Micrometer's ContextSnapshot. In Kotlin, awaitGetOrSpawn followed by awaitAsk in a suspend function avoids the callback.

Messages that ask replies are not traced: the caller is already in the trace. Messages sent through a plain SpringActorRef (a replyTo, a ref inside a message) are not traced either; handles from SpringActorSystem, getSelf(), children, the receptionist and sharding are.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text: Actor log lines carry MDC values: the actor path and system, any static or per-message MDC you add, actor tags, and with tracing, traceId and spanId. Logging with MDC and Tags shows how to add them and how to print them with Logback, also as JSON.

docs.title: Dashboard and alerts
docs.text: The repository's monitoring/ directory has a Grafana dashboard and Prometheus alert rules for the meters on this page, under their Prometheus names. A test (MonitoringFilesTest) checks that every metric they query is a meter described on this page.

docs.title: The Actors dashboard
docs.text:
monitoring/grafana/actor-dashboard.json. Set up Grafana loads it; you can also import it by hand and pick your Prometheus data source. The variables instance and system filter by instance and actor system.

Row Panels Messages Messages processed per second, message failures per second, average and longest processing time (per actor class) Mailboxes and actors Messages waiting in mailboxes, average time in mailbox, running actors, restarts Dispatchers Pool threads, tasks waiting for a thread Cluster Members, unreachable, leader, singleton host, members by node, cluster events Sharding Entities by type, shards by node, shard regions

docs.title: Alert rules
docs.text:
monitoring/prometheus/actor-alerts.yaml is a PrometheusRule for the Prometheus Operator. Without the operator, its spec is a plain rules file:

yq '.spec' monitoring/prometheus/actor-alerts.yaml > actor-alerts.rules.yml
Alert Fires when Severity ActorClusterMemberUnreachable a member is unreachable for 5 minutes warning ActorClusterNoLeader no node is the leader for 5 minutes critical ActorClusterViewsDiffer nodes see different member counts for 10 minutes warning ActorClusterSingletonMissing no node runs the singletons for 5 minutes critical ActorMessageFailures an actor class keeps failing messages for 10 minutes warning ActorRestartsFrequent an actor class restarts more than 10 times in 15 minutes warning ActorMailboxBacklog more than 1,000 messages wait for an actor class on one instance for 10 minutes warning ActorMailboxWaitHigh messages wait more than a second on average for 10 minutes warning ActorDispatcherSaturated every thread of a dispatcher is busy and more than 100 tasks wait for 10 minutes warning

The thresholds are starting points; tune them to your load. The rules group by namespace, the label the Prometheus Operator adds; with another setup, change it to the label that tells your applications apart.

docs.title: Download the files for your version
docs.text:
Use the files of the release you depend on: the dashboard on main may query meters a later release added. Each GitHub release attaches them, with the version in their names:

https://github.com/seonWKim/actor-spring-boot-starter/releases/download/v<version>/actor-grafana-dashboard-<version>.json
https://github.com/seonWKim/actor-spring-boot-starter/releases/download/v<version>/actor-prometheus-alerts-<version>.yaml
https://github.com/seonWKim/actor-spring-boot-starter/releases/download/v<version>/actor-monitoring-<version>.zip

The dashboard carries the version as a v<version> tag and at the end of its description. The zip holds the monitoring/ directory for that version: the dashboard, the alert rules, the provisioning files and docker-compose.yml.

docs.title: Provisioning
docs.text:
To load the dashboard into your own Grafana without clicks, copy the two provisioning files into Grafana's provisioning directory (/etc/grafana/provisioning by default) and the dashboard into the directory the dashboard provider reads:

File Goes to Change monitoring/grafana/provisioning/datasources/prometheus.yaml provisioning/datasources/ url: your Prometheus. Skip the file if Grafana already has a default Prometheus data source monitoring/grafana/provisioning/dashboards/actor.yaml provisioning/dashboards/ options.path if you keep dashboards elsewhere monitoring/grafana/actor-dashboard.json /var/lib/grafana/dashboards/actor/ (the provider's options.path)

The dashboard's Data source variable starts on Grafana's default Prometheus data source.

docs.title: Run it locally
docs.text:
With your application running on port 8080 and exposing /actuator/prometheus:

cd monitoring                     # or the unzipped actor-monitoring-<version>/
docker compose up -d
  • Grafana: http://localhost:3000 (admin / admin), dashboard Actors in the Actors folder.
  • Prometheus: http://localhost:9090, the alert rules under Alerts, the scrape target under Status > Targets.

Prometheus scrapes host.docker.internal:8080/actuator/prometheus. Set ACTOR_TARGET for another address:

ACTOR_TARGET=host.docker.internal:9000 docker compose up -d
docker compose down -v            # stop and remove the containers and the generated files

The setup service writes the scrape target and turns actor-alerts.yaml into a plain rules file (its spec) before Prometheus starts. The cluster alerts group by namespace, which a local stack doesn't have, so they treat everything Prometheus scrapes as one group.

docs.title: Installing on Kubernetes
docs.text:
With the Prometheus Operator in the cluster (for example kube-prometheus-stack), the Kubernetes example installs both in one command:

cd example/kubernetes
./scripts/monitoring.sh          # apply; `render` prints the manifests, `delete` removes them

It applies a ServiceMonitor that scrapes /actuator/prometheus, the actor-alerts PrometheusRule, and the dashboard as a ConfigMap labelled grafana_dashboard: "1", which Grafana's dashboard sidecar loads. Your Prometheus must select them: kube-prometheus-stack selects rules and monitors by its release label unless you set prometheus.prometheusSpec.ruleSelectorNilUsesHelmValues=false and serviceMonitorSelectorNilUsesHelmValues=false, and its sidecar searches other namespaces only with grafana.sidecar.dashboards.searchNamespace=ALL.

docs.title: The optional Java agent
docs.text:
The ByteBuddy agent in actor-metrics instruments Pekko internals for a few meters no public hook exposes (stash size, dead letters, unhandled messages, scheduled tasks, per-message-type tags). It breaks more easily with Pekko upgrades, so use it only when you need those.

./gradlew :actor-metrics:agentJar

java -javaagent:actor-metrics-{version}-agent.jar -jar your-app.jar

With the agent attached, it records the message, mailbox and lifecycle meters below under the same names, and the hooks register only actor.message.failures and the actor.dispatcher.* meters: no meter is registered twice.

docs.title: Agent meters
docs.text:
Meter Type Tags What actor.lifecycle.created Counter actor.class Actors created actor.lifecycle.terminated Counter actor.class Actors terminated actor.lifecycle.restarts Counter actor.class Supervision restarts actor.lifecycle.resumes Counter actor.class Supervision resumes actor.lifecycle.active Gauge none Currently active actors actor.mailbox.size Gauge actor.class Mailbox queue size actor.mailbox.size.max Gauge actor.class Peak mailbox size actor.mailbox.time Timer actor.class, message.type Time in mailbox actor.mailbox.overflow Counter none Bounded mailbox drops actor.message.processed Counter actor.class, message.type Messages processed actor.message.processing.time Timer actor.class, message.type Processing duration actor.stash.size Gauge actor.class Stashed messages system.dead-letters Counter none Undeliverable messages system.unhandled-messages Counter none Unhandled messages scheduler.tasks.scheduled Counter none Tasks via scheduleOnce

Typed actors use actor.class=TypedActor; use message.type to tell behaviors apart. The agent records no failure meter of its own: failures are actor.message.failures, which the hooks record with or without the agent.

docs.title: Agent settings
docs.text:
The agent reads environment variables, not Spring keys: ACTOR_METRICS_ENABLED, ACTOR_METRICS_INSTRUMENT_<MODULE>, ACTOR_METRICS_TAG_<NAME> and ACTOR_METRICS_SAMPLING_RATE. The Configuration Reference describes each. Module ids: actor-lifecycle, mailbox, message-processing, system, scheduler, stash.

To set tags or sampling in code, declare your own MetricsRegistry bean:

JavaKotlin 
import io.github.seonwkim.actor.metrics.core.MetricsConfiguration.SamplingConfig;
import io.github.seonwkim.actor.metrics.core.MetricsRegistry;
import io.github.seonwkim.actor.metrics.micrometer.MicrometerMetricsRegistryBuilder;

@Configuration
public class ActorMetricsConfig {

    @Bean
    public MetricsRegistry actorMetricsRegistry(MeterRegistry meterRegistry) {
        return MicrometerMetricsRegistryBuilder.fromEnvironment(meterRegistry)
                .tag("custom-tag", "value")
                .sampling(SamplingConfig.rateBased(0.1))
                .build();
    }
}

import io.github.seonwkim.actor.metrics.core.MetricsConfiguration.SamplingConfig
import io.github.seonwkim.actor.metrics.core.MetricsRegistry
import io.github.seonwkim.actor.metrics.micrometer.MicrometerMetricsRegistryBuilder

@Configuration
class ActorMetricsConfig {

    @Bean
    fun actorMetricsRegistry(meterRegistry: MeterRegistry): MetricsRegistry =
        MicrometerMetricsRegistryBuilder.fromEnvironment(meterRegistry)
            .tag("custom-tag", "value")
            .sampling(SamplingConfig.rateBased(0.1))
            .build()
}

docs.title: How the agent starts
docs.text:
The agent must rewrite bytecode before Pekko classes load, but Micrometer only exists after Spring starts. So it starts in two steps:

  1. JVM startup: MetricsAgent.premain() finds the modules through ServiceLoader and uses ByteBuddy to instrument Pekko classes. No meters are recorded yet.
  2. Spring context: the auto-configuration creates a MetricsRegistry with a Micrometer backend and hands it to the agent. Meters start recording. The registry is created before the actor system bean.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Problem What to check /actuator/prometheus is 404 prometheus is in management.endpoints.web.exposure.include and micrometer-registry-prometheus is on the classpath. No actor_* series actor-metrics is on the classpath and spring.actor.metrics.enabled is not false. Counters appear after the first message. No actor_cluster_* series spring.actor.provider is cluster. No agent meters The log has [MetricsAgent] Metrics agent installed successfully, and -javaagent is on the command line. Agent jar missing Run ./gradlew :actor-metrics:agentJar.
