docs.title: Running in Production
docs.text:
This guide covers what matters when you run an actor application in production, for example on Kubernetes: how it shuts down without losing work, how health checks report the actor system and the cluster, a checklist to go through before the first release, and GraalVM native images.

For metrics, tracing and alerts, see Monitoring. For rolling, canary and blue-green releases, see Deployments.

docs.title: Graceful shutdown
docs.text: When the Spring application context closes (on SIGTERM, or when you call context.close()), the starter shuts the actor system down through Pekko coordinated shutdown. In cluster mode the node leaves the cluster on purpose: other nodes see it go Leaving → Exiting → Removed, sharded entities and cluster singletons move to the remaining nodes, and the node is never reported as unreachable or downed by the split brain resolver.

docs.title: Shutdown order
docs.text:
The starter registers a Spring SmartLifecycle bean, ActorSystemShutdownLifecycle, at phase ActorSystemShutdownLifecycle.PHASE (Integer.MAX_VALUE - 4096). Spring stops lifecycle beans from the highest phase to the lowest before it destroys any bean, so on shutdown:

  1. With server.shutdown=graceful, the web server stops accepting requests and drains in-flight ones (Spring Boot's web server lifecycles run at higher phases).
  2. The actor system runs coordinated shutdown and the starter waits for it to terminate, at most the configured timeout.
  3. Spring destroys the remaining beans, including the services, repositories and connection pools your actors use. Actors are already stopped, so they never call a destroyed bean.

The wait is bounded: if an actor blocks shutdown (for example a handler stuck on blocking I/O), closing the context returns after the timeout with a warning in the log, and the process can exit instead of hanging.

The shutdown runs once. If the actor system has already terminated, for example because the node was downed and Pekko shut itself down, closing the context does nothing more and does not fail.

docs.title: Shutdown timeout
docs.text:
spring:
  actor:
    shutdown:
      timeout: 20s   # default

spring.actor.shutdown.timeout is how long closing the context waits for the actor system to terminate. It takes any Spring Boot duration (15s, 500ms, PT20S). The default is 20s.

Keep Pekko's own coordinated shutdown phase timeouts (pekko.coordinated-shutdown.phases.<phase>.timeout) shorter than this setting, so the phases that matter for a graceful leave (cluster-leave, cluster-sharding-shutdown-region, cluster-exiting) finish inside the wait.

docs.title: When the actor system stops by itself
docs.text: If the actor system terminates while the application runs (for example after the split brain resolver downed this node), the Spring context closes and the process exits with status 1, so Kubernetes or systemd restarts it. Set spring.actor.shutdown.exit-process=false to only close the context. Your code can wait for this with SpringActorSystem.whenTerminated().

docs.title: Kubernetes: terminationGracePeriodSeconds and the preStop hook
docs.text:
When Kubernetes stops a pod it runs the preStop hook, then sends SIGTERM, and sends SIGKILL once terminationGracePeriodSeconds has passed since the start, whatever is still running. A pod killed with SIGKILL cannot leave the cluster and is seen as unreachable by the other nodes. So the grace period must cover all three steps:

terminationGracePeriodSeconds >= preStop sleep
                                 + web server drain (spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase)
                                 + spring.actor.shutdown.timeout
                                 + a few seconds margin

A preStop sleep gives the readiness probe time to fail and the load balancer time to stop sending traffic before the application begins to shut down:

spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45
  containers:
    - name: app
      lifecycle:
        preStop:
          exec:
            command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 10"]

With matching application settings:

server:
  shutdown: graceful
spring:
  lifecycle:
    timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 10s   # web server drain
  actor:
    shutdown:
      timeout: 20s                    # actor system coordinated shutdown
    pekko:
      coordinated-shutdown:
        phases:
          cluster-leave:
            timeout: 10s
          cluster-sharding-shutdown-region:
            timeout: 10s

Here the worst case is 10s (preStop) + 10s (web drain) + 20s (actor system) = 40s, inside the 45s grace period. If you must keep terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30 with a 10s preStop sleep, lower spring.actor.shutdown.timeout (for example to 15s) and the web drain timeout so the sum stays under 30s.

docs.title: Health checks
docs.text:
With Spring Boot Actuator on the classpath, /actuator/health gets these components:

Component When Status actorSystem always UP while the actor system runs, DOWN once it has terminated. Details: the system's name. actorCluster spring.actor.provider=cluster UP when this node is an Up member; OUT_OF_SERVICE while it has not joined yet, is joining, weakly up, leaving or shutting down; DOWN when it was downed or removed, or other members report it unreachable actorWarmup spring.actor.provider=cluster UP when this node is an Up member, the cluster has at least management.health.actor.warmup.min-members (default 1) Up members, and the discovery store answers (with jdbc or redis discovery); OUT_OF_SERVICE otherwise

actorCluster details hold this node's status (selfStatus, NOT_JOINED before it joins), whether it is unreachable (selfUnreachable), the member count (members) and the unreachable count (unreachable), never addresses. An unreachable peer shows only in the count: one partitioned peer does not make every node unhealthy. actorWarmup details hold selfUp, upMembers, minMembers and discovery (REACHABLE, UNREACHABLE or NOT_USED). management.health.actor.enabled=false turns all of them off.

Neither is in the Kubernetes probe groups by default. Add actorCluster to readiness, so a pod gets traffic only once it is a cluster member and stops getting it as soon as it leaves:

management:
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes:
        enabled: true
      group:
        readiness:
          include: readinessState,actorCluster

Keep it out of liveness: a node that is still joining is not broken, and restarting it would only delay the join. Cluster Bootstrap reaches pods through Pekko Management, not through the readiness-gated Service, so a cluster still forms while no pod is ready yet.

docs.title: Actuator on its own port
docs.text:
Actuator's endpoints (/actuator/health, /actuator/metrics, /actuator/prometheus, /actuator/info) tell anyone who can call them about the application. Serve them on a separate port, so the network can open the application port to clients and the Actuator port only to monitoring and the kubelet:

server:
  port: 8080          # application traffic
management:
  server:
    port: 8081        # Actuator: probes and Prometheus

Point the probes, the ServiceMonitor or PodMonitor and any prometheus.io/port annotation at 8081, and let a NetworkPolicy admit 8081 only from the monitoring namespace. The kubelet's probes come from the node, which most network plugins let through whatever the policy says; if yours doesn't, add an ipBlock for the node addresses on 8081. The Kubernetes example does all of this.

docs.title: Warm-up
docs.text:
In cluster mode the starter adds a third health group beside Spring Boot's liveness and readiness: warmup (/actuator/health/warmup), with the actorWarmup component. It answers "can this node be activated?", which a delivery pipeline asks before it switches traffic to a new deployment (Blue-green):

Group Question Who asks Depends on traffic liveness Restart this pod? kubelet no readiness Send this pod traffic? the Service yes warmup Is this pod ready to be activated? the delivery pipeline no

Set min-members to the number of members a new deployment must have before it takes traffic:

management:
  health:
    actor:
      warmup:
        min-members: 2

Like actorCluster, keep actorWarmup out of liveness. A group named warmup in management.endpoint.health.group replaces the starter's. The group shows components and details as the main health endpoint does (management.endpoint.health.show-details).

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
Go through this list before the first release of a clustered application.

Cluster formation and downing

  • [ ] Every node uses the same spring.actor.name.
  • [ ] Nodes find each other through seed-nodes or join: discovery, not join-self (Cluster Formation).
  • [ ] A downing strategy is set. With join: discovery the default is keep-majority; with seed nodes the default is none and the starter logs a warning (Split Brain and Leases).
  • [ ] If a singleton or a shard must never run on two nodes at once, it uses a lease (singleton.use-lease, sharding.use-lease).
  • [ ] The network lets pods reach each other on the remoting port (25520 by default) and the Pekko Management port. The Kubernetes example lists the rules to ask for.
  • [ ] With jdbc or redis discovery or leases, only the nodes can write the store: a dedicated Redis ACL user or database user, TLS and auth (Securing the discovery store).

Messages

  • [ ] Every message that crosses nodes (sharded commands, replies, topic messages) implements JsonSerializable or CborSerializable. The Kubernetes example also sets spring.actor.pekko.actor.allow-java-serialization: off.
  • [ ] Message changes stay readable by the previous version during a rolling or canary release (Message compatibility).

Shutdown

  • [ ] server.shutdown: graceful is set.
  • [ ] terminationGracePeriodSeconds covers the preStop sleep, the web drain and spring.actor.shutdown.timeout (above).
  • [ ] spring.actor.shutdown.exit-process stays true, so a downed node restarts.

Health and monitoring

  • [ ] The readiness group includes actorCluster; liveness does not.
  • [ ] Actuator runs on its own port (management.server.port), open only to monitoring and the kubelet (above).
  • [ ] actor-metrics is on the classpath and Prometheus scrapes /actuator/prometheus.
  • [ ] The dashboard and alert rules from monitoring/ are installed (Monitoring).
  • [ ] spring.actor.metrics.path-tag-limit stays 0, or is small, so the series count does not grow with the number of actors.

Data

  • [ ] With actor-jdbc or actor-persistence, initialize-schema is never and the tables come from your Flyway or Liquibase migrations (Configuration Reference).
  • [ ] State that must survive a restart or a blue-green switch lives in a database or event journal, not only in actor memory.

Blocking work

  • [ ] Actors that call blocking I/O (JDBC, blocking HTTP clients) run on withBlockingDispatcher() or a dispatcher of their own (Dispatchers).

docs.title: Native images (GraalVM)
docs.text:
Experimental

No native image of an actor application has been built and run in this project yet. The Native image workflow (.github/workflows/native-image.yml) builds the simple example every week. Until it passes, treat native images as experimental.

Spring AOT reads META-INF/spring/aot.factories during a native build. The starter's modules use it to register these runtime hints:

  • Pekko's configuration files: every reference.conf, plus the version.conf and pekko-http-version.conf they include, and your application.conf if you have one.
  • The starter's classes that Pekko creates by name from configuration: the executor of a bean-backed dispatcher, the cluster discovery and lease adapters, the serializer for traced messages, and the persistence database provider. Also the Pekko Jackson serializers the starter configures.
  • AskCommand's reply address, which Jackson writes into every ask that crosses nodes.
  • The schema files of actor-jdbc, actor-persistence and actor-projection.

docs.title: Your message classes
docs.text:
Jackson reads and writes your messages by reflection whenever Pekko serializes them. That covers messages that cross nodes (sharded commands, replies, topic messages) and the events and state of event-sourced actors. Pekko writes each message's class name into the serialized form and loads the class by that name when it reads the message, so register every concrete message class, not only the JsonSerializable interface. @RegisterReflectionForBinding on a configuration class registers each class with its constructors, fields and property types:

JavaKotlin 
@Configuration
@RegisterReflectionForBinding({HelloActor.SayHello.class, OrderPlaced.class})
public class NativeHintsConfiguration {}

@Configuration
@RegisterReflectionForBinding(HelloActor.SayHello::class, OrderPlaced::class)
class NativeHintsConfiguration

Messages between actors in one JVM aren't serialized (Pekko's serialize-messages is off by default), so they need no hints. To register classes you can't list in an annotation, write a RuntimeHintsRegistrar and import it with @ImportRuntimeHints.

docs.title: Pekko's own classes
docs.text:
Pekko 1.1 ships no native image metadata. It creates its extensions, mailboxes, serializers, loggers and actor ref providers by reflection, from the class names in its reference.conf, and the starter's hints don't cover them. One way to collect them is the GraalVM tracing agent. Run the application and its tests on the JVM with -agentlib:native-image-agent=config-output-dir=src/main/resources/META-INF/native-image/<group>/<artifact>, use the features you need (cluster, sharding, persistence), and check in the generated files.

The actor-metrics Java agent (-javaagent:actor-metrics-<version>-agent.jar) can't attach to a native image.

docs.title: Reactor Streams
docs.text:
actor-streams connects actors to Project Reactor. It gives you three things, all as Mono and Flux:

You want Method Backpressure The reply of one ask ask(askBuilder) n/a To send a stream of elements to an actor askEach(elements, parallelism, ask) at most parallelism asks in flight The messages an actor sends messages(type)...flux(onSubscribe) a bounded buffer, or an acknowledgement per message

No Pekko type appears in this API. Pekko Streams runs underneath and stays an implementation detail.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Add the module next to the starter:

GradleMaven 
implementation("io.github.seonwkim:actor-spring-boot-starter:$version")
implementation("io.github.seonwkim:actor-streams:$version")

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.seonwkim</groupId>
    <artifactId>actor-streams</artifactId>
    <version>${actor.version}</version>
</dependency>

With actor-streams on the classpath, the application has an ActorStreams bean. Inject it where you need it:

JavaKotlin 
@Service
public class OrderService {
    private final ActorStreams streams;
    private final SpringActorSystem actorSystem;

    public OrderService(ActorStreams streams, SpringActorSystem actorSystem) {
        this.streams = streams;
        this.actorSystem = actorSystem;
    }
}

@Service
class OrderService(
    private val streams: ActorStreams,
    private val actorSystem: SpringActorSystem,
)

docs.title: Mono of an ask
docs.text:
Pass the ask builder you already use. The command is sent when the Mono is subscribed, not when it is created, and again on each new subscription. The builder's timeout and onTimeout fallback apply.

JavaKotlin 
Mono<Order> order = streams.ask(orders.ask(new GetOrder(id)).withTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2)));

val order: Mono<Order> = streams.ask(orders.ask(GetOrder(id)).withTimeout(2.seconds))

It works the same for a sharded entity's handle.

docs.title: Feeding an actor from a Flux
docs.text:
askEach asks an actor about each element and emits the replies in the order of the elements:

JavaKotlin 
Flux<Receipt> receipts = streams.askEach(payments, 8, payment -> ledger.ask(new Charge(payment)));

val receipts: Flux<Receipt> = streams.askEach(payments, 8) { payment -> ledger.ask(Charge(payment)) }

At most parallelism asks (here 8) wait for a reply at once. Until one of them is answered, askEach requests nothing more from payments. So a slow actor slows the upstream Flux (a Kafka consumer, a database cursor, an HTTP body) instead of filling its mailbox.

A failed ask, for example a timeout, fails the Flux. Give the builder onTimeout(...) for a fallback reply, or use Reactor's onErrorResume and retry operators.

The actor replies as for any ask:

JavaKotlin 
.onMessage(Charge.class, (ctx, msg) -> {
    msg.reply(ledger.charge(msg.payment()));
    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
})

.onMessage(Charge::class.java) { _, msg ->
    msg.reply(ledger.charge(msg.payment))
    SpringActorBehavior.same()
}

docs.title: A Flux of the messages an actor sends
docs.text:
messages(type) creates, for each subscriber, a reference that actors can send messages to. Whatever they send to it comes out of the Flux. Pass the reference to the actor in flux(onSubscribe):

JavaKotlin 
Flux<Price> prices = streams.messages(Price.class)
        .onClose(ref -> ticker.tell(new Unsubscribe(ref)))
        .flux(ref -> ticker.tell(new Subscribe(ref)));

val prices: Flux<Price> = streams.messages(Price::class.java)
    .onClose { ref -> ticker.tell(Unsubscribe(ref)) }
    .flux { ref -> ticker.tell(Subscribe(ref)) }

The reference is a SpringActorRef<Price>, so the actor stores it and calls tell like on any other reference. In this ticker, the state holds the behavior context (ctx) and a set of subscribers:

JavaKotlin 
.onMessage(Subscribe.class, (state, msg) -> {
    state.subscribers().add(msg.subscriber());
    state.ctx().watch(msg.subscriber());
    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
})
.onMessage(PriceChanged.class, (state, msg) -> {
    state.subscribers().forEach(subscriber -> subscriber.tell(msg.price()));
    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
})
.onSignal(ActorTerminated.class, (state, signal) -> {
    state.subscribers().remove(signal.ref());
    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
})

.onMessage(Subscribe::class.java) { state, msg ->
    state.subscribers.add(msg.subscriber)
    state.ctx.watch(msg.subscriber)
    SpringActorBehavior.same()
}
.onMessage(PriceChanged::class.java) { state, msg ->
    state.subscribers.forEach { subscriber -> subscriber.tell(msg.price) }
    SpringActorBehavior.same()
}
.onSignal(ActorTerminated::class.java) { state, signal ->
    state.subscribers.removeIf { it == signal.ref() }
    SpringActorBehavior.same()
}

docs.title: When the subscriber goes away
docs.text:
When the subscriber cancels (an HTTP client disconnects, a take(10) is satisfied), the reference stops. The actor can learn it in two ways; use either:

  • It watches the reference and receives ActorTerminated, as above.
  • onClose runs with the reference when the Flux ends for that subscriber: completed, failed or cancelled. Tell the actor to forget it there.

Messages sent to a stopped reference go to dead letters.

docs.title: Ending the stream from the actor
docs.text:
completeWhen names the message that ends the Flux. Messages sent before it are still emitted; it is not:

JavaKotlin 
Flux<Event> events = streams.messages(Event.class)
        .completeWhen(event -> event instanceof Done)
        .flux(ref -> job.tell(new Watch(ref)));

val events: Flux<Event> = streams.messages(Event::class.java)
    .completeWhen { event -> event is Done }
    .flux { ref -> job.tell(Watch(ref)) }

docs.title: Buffer and overflow
docs.text:
A subscriber may request fewer messages than the actor sends. The reference keeps up to bufferSize messages (default 256) that the subscriber has not requested yet. When the buffer is full, overflow decides:

Overflow Effect FAIL (default) The Flux fails with an error DROP_OLDEST The oldest buffered message is dropped DROP_NEWEST The new message is dropped JavaKotlin 
Flux<Price> prices = streams.messages(Price.class)
        .bufferSize(16)
        .overflow(ActorStreams.Overflow.DROP_OLDEST)
        .flux(ref -> ticker.tell(new Subscribe(ref)));

val prices: Flux<Price> = streams.messages(Price::class.java)
    .bufferSize(16)
    .overflow(ActorStreams.Overflow.DROP_OLDEST)
    .flux { ref -> ticker.tell(Subscribe(ref)) }

DROP_OLDEST suits values where only the latest matters, such as prices or positions.

docs.title: Backpressure to the sending actor
docs.text:
When nothing may be dropped, let the sending actor wait for the subscriber. With ackTo(sender, ack), the reference sends ack to sender each time a message has gone on to the subscriber. The sender sends its next message only after an ack:

JavaKotlinJavaKotlin 
Flux<Row> rows = streams.messages(Row.class)
        .ackTo(exporter, new Exporter.Ack())
        .completeWhen(row -> row.isLast())
        .flux(ref -> exporter.tell(new Exporter.Start(ref)));

val rows: Flux<Row> = streams.messages(Row::class.java)
    .ackTo(exporter, Exporter.Ack())
    .completeWhen { row -> row.isLast }
    .flux { ref -> exporter.tell(Exporter.Start(ref)) }

.onMessage(Start.class, (state, msg) -> {
    state.subscriber = msg.subscriber();
    state.sendNext();
    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
})
.onMessage(Ack.class, (state, msg) -> {
    state.sendNext();
    return SpringActorBehavior.same();
})

.onMessage(Start::class.java) { state, msg ->
    state.subscriber = msg.subscriber
    state.sendNext()
    SpringActorBehavior.same()
}
.onMessage(Ack::class.java) { state, _ ->
    state.sendNext()
    SpringActorBehavior.same()
}

With ackTo, there is no buffer, so bufferSize and overflow do not apply.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The bridges are tested on one node. The reference that messages creates lives on the subscriber's node.
  • An actor cannot fail a messages Flux; it can end it with completeWhen. To report an error, send a message that the subscriber maps to an error with Reactor's handle operator.

docs.title: Streaming to Clients
docs.text:
Send what actors produce to browsers and services over Server-Sent Events, WebSocket or gRPC. Each bridge builds on the messages Flux of Reactor Streams: a client gets a reference that actors send to, and when the client disconnects, the reference stops. An actor that watches it receives ActorTerminated and can forget the client or stop itself.

All three need actor-streams:

GradleMaven 
implementation("io.github.seonwkim:actor-streams:$version")

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.seonwkim</groupId>
    <artifactId>actor-streams</artifactId>
    <version>${actor.version}</version>
</dependency>
Transport Stack What you write Server-Sent Events Spring MVC or WebFlux A controller method that returns the messages Flux WebSocket WebFlux An ActorWebSocketHandler with a connector gRPC grpc-java or Spring gRPC ActorGrpc.respond(flux, responseObserver) in the service method

docs.title: Server-Sent Events
docs.text:
Return the Flux from a controller with produces = text/event-stream. Spring MVC and WebFlux both write each element as an event, and cancel the Flux when the client goes away:

JavaKotlin 
@RestController
public class PricesController {
    private final ActorStreams streams;
    private final SpringActorSystem actorSystem;

    public PricesController(ActorStreams streams, SpringActorSystem actorSystem) {
        this.streams = streams;
        this.actorSystem = actorSystem;
    }

    @GetMapping(path = "/prices", produces = MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE)
    public Flux<Price> prices() {
        return Mono.fromCompletionStage(actorSystem.actor(TickerActor.class).withId("ticker").getOrSpawn())
                .flatMapMany(ticker -> streams.messages(Price.class)
                        .bufferSize(16)
                        .overflow(ActorStreams.Overflow.DROP_OLDEST)
                        .flux(ref -> ticker.tell(new Subscribe(ref))));
    }
}

@RestController
class PricesController(
    private val streams: ActorStreams,
    private val actorSystem: SpringActorSystem,
) {
    @GetMapping(path = ["/prices"], produces = [MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE])
    fun prices(): Flux<Price> =
        Mono.fromCompletionStage(actorSystem.actor<TickerActor, _>().withId("ticker").getOrSpawn())
            .flatMapMany { ticker ->
                streams.messages(Price::class.java)
                    .bufferSize(16)
                    .overflow(ActorStreams.Overflow.DROP_OLDEST)
                    .flux { ref -> ticker.tell(Subscribe(ref)) }
            }
}

The ticker keeps its subscribers and forgets one when it stops, as shown in Reactor Streams.

When the client disconnects:

  • WebFlux notices at once, and the reference stops.
  • Spring MVC (a servlet container) notices only on its next write to that client. The reference stops after the next message the actor sends, which fails to write. If an actor may stay quiet for a long time, send a heartbeat now and then.

Use a small buffer with DROP_OLDEST for values where only the latest matters, so a slow client never holds many messages.

docs.title: WebSocket (WebFlux)
docs.text:
ActorWebSocketHandler is a WebFlux WebSocketHandler. For each connection it creates a client reference and calls your connector, which connects it to actors and returns where the client's text frames go:

JavaKotlin 
@Configuration
public class WebSocketConfig {

    @Bean
    public HandlerMapping chatSocket(ActorStreams streams, SpringActorSystem actorSystem) {
        ActorWebSocketHandler handler = new ActorWebSocketHandler(streams, (session, client) -> actorSystem
                .actor(UserActor.class)
                .withContext(new UserContext(UUID.randomUUID().toString(), client))
                .spawn()
                .thenApply(user -> text -> user.tell(new Incoming(text))));
        return new SimpleUrlHandlerMapping(Map.of("/ws/chat", handler), 1);
    }
}

@Configuration
class WebSocketConfig {

    @Bean
    fun chatSocket(streams: ActorStreams, actorSystem: SpringActorSystem): HandlerMapping {
        val handler = ActorWebSocketHandler(streams) { _, client ->
            actorSystem.actor<UserActor, _>()
                .withContext(UserContext(UUID.randomUUID().toString(), client))
                .spawn()
                .thenApply { user -> Consumer<String> { text -> user.tell(Incoming(text)) } }
        }
        return SimpleUrlHandlerMapping(mapOf("/ws/chat" to handler), 1)
    }
}

The user actor sends text to the browser with client.tell(json). To stop with the connection, it watches the reference (context is the actor's own SpringActorContext subclass, which carries the client reference):

JavaKotlin 
.withState(ctx -> {
    ctx.watch(context.client());
    return new UserState(ctx, context.client());
})
.onSignal(ActorTerminated.class, (state, signal) -> SpringActorBehavior.stopped())

.withState { ctx ->
    ctx.watch(context.client)
    UserState(ctx, context.client)
}
.onSignal(ActorTerminated::class.java) { _, _ -> SpringActorBehavior.stopped() }

When the client disconnects, the reference stops and the user actor stops with it. The other way round, when the outgoing Flux completes (see completeWhen below), the session closes.

The third constructor argument configures the outgoing messages, with the same settings as messages:

JavaKotlin 
new ActorWebSocketHandler(streams, connector, messages -> messages.bufferSize(64).completeWhen("bye"::equals));

ActorWebSocketHandler(streams, connector) { messages -> messages.bufferSize(64).completeWhen { it == "bye" } }

By default the reference buffers 256 messages the client has not taken yet, and closes the session with an error when the buffer is full.

The chat example uses this bridge.

docs.title: gRPC
docs.text:
ActorGrpc.respond sends a Flux (or a Mono, or any Reactive Streams Publisher) to a gRPC response stream. Call it in a server-streaming or unary method of a grpc-java service, or of a Spring gRPC service:

JavaKotlin 
@Service
public class PriceService extends PriceServiceGrpc.PriceServiceImplBase {
    private final ActorStreams streams;
    private final SpringActorHandle<TickerActor.Command> ticker; // spawned at startup, set in the constructor

    @Override
    public void watch(WatchRequest request, StreamObserver<Price> responses) {
        ActorGrpc.respond(
                streams.messages(Price.class).flux(ref -> ticker.tell(new Subscribe(ref))),
                responses);
    }

    @Override
    public void getPrice(PriceRequest request, StreamObserver<Price> responses) {
        ActorGrpc.respond(streams.ask(ticker.ask(new GetPrice(request.getSymbol()))), responses);
    }
}

@Service
class PriceService(
    private val streams: ActorStreams,
    private val ticker: SpringActorHandle<TickerActor.Command>, // spawned at startup
) : PriceServiceGrpc.PriceServiceImplBase() {

    override fun watch(request: WatchRequest, responses: StreamObserver<Price>) {
        ActorGrpc.respond(
            streams.messages(Price::class.java).flux { ref -> ticker.tell(Subscribe(ref)) },
            responses,
        )
    }

    override fun getPrice(request: PriceRequest, responses: StreamObserver<Price>) {
        ActorGrpc.respond(streams.ask(ticker.ask(GetPrice(request.symbol))), responses)
    }
}
  • It requests the next element only while the call is ready to send, so a slow client slows the Flux. With ackTo, the slowness reaches the sending actor.
  • When the client cancels or disconnects, the Flux is cancelled and the reference stops.
  • When the Flux fails, the call ends with the error's gRPC status (UNKNOWN unless the error is a StatusException or StatusRuntimeException).

actor-streams does not bring grpc-java: the application has it already (directly or through Spring gRPC). The bridge is built against grpc-java 1.83 and uses only its stable grpc-stub API.
